title: Documentation tiers and their use
scenario: A commentator writes: "Action 13 gave tax administrations a three-tier documentation package, but only the country-by-country report really matters, and even its value is blunted by the restrictions on how tax authorities may use it. Groups should prepare all three tiers once, centrally, and file the same package everywhere."

items.prompt: (a) Explain the content and purpose of each of the three tiers of transfer pricing documentation recommended in the OECD BEPS Action 13 report.

answer.model:
Action 13 (2015) recommends a three-tiered standardised approach. The master file gives tax administrations a high-level overview of the multinational group: its organisational structure and legal ownership, a description of its business, including the main drivers of profit, supply chain for the largest products and services, and important service arrangements, its intangibles (strategy, ownership, important agreements and related party transfer pricing policies for R&D and intangibles), its intercompany financing arrangements, and its financial and tax positions, including advance pricing agreements and rulings. It is a single document for the group and is intended to help the administration put the group's transfer pricing practices in their global economic, legal, financial and tax context for risk assessment.

The local file is entity-specific. It contains detailed information on the material related party transactions of the local entity: a description of the transactions and the context, amounts of payments and receipts by category, identification of the associated enterprises involved, copies of material intercompany agreements, a comparability and functional analysis, the selection and application of the most appropriate transfer pricing method and the reasons for it, financial information used, and relevant benchmarking or other support. It is the tier that supports the arm's length analysis under Article 9 and the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines.

The country-by-country report (CbCR) is a template filed by groups above the consolidated revenue threshold (EUR 750 million in the preceding fiscal year). Table 1 gives, for each tax jurisdiction, revenues (split between unrelated and related parties), profit or loss before income tax, income tax paid (cash basis), income tax accrued for the current year, stated capital, accumulated earnings, number of employees and tangible assets other than cash. Table 2 lists each constituent entity with its jurisdiction of residence and main business activities, and Table 3 allows additional explanatory information. Its purpose is high-level transfer pricing risk assessment and economic and statistical analysis, not a conclusive analysis of any transaction.

points.point: Master file: high-level group overview covering structure, business description, intangibles, intercompany financing and financial and tax positions
Local file: detailed entity-level information on material related party transactions, agreements, comparability analysis and method selection
CbCR content: allocation of income, taxes paid and accrued and indicators of economic activity by jurisdiction (Table 1), entity list with activities (Table 2)
States the purposes: master file and CbCR for risk assessment and context, local file to test the arm's length position
States the CbCR EUR 750 million revenue threshold

answer.grader_note: Accept equivalent wording. Do not credit a claim that the local file is prepared for the group as a whole.

items.prompt: (b) Critically evaluate the claim that the value of the CbCR is blunted by the limits on how it may be used.

answer.model:
The claim has force but is overstated. Action 13 states that CbCR information should be used for high-level transfer pricing risk assessment, and may also be used for assessing other BEPS-related risks and for economic and statistical analysis. It should not be used as conclusive evidence that transfer prices are or are not appropriate, and it should not be used to make transfer pricing adjustments based on an income allocation formula computed from the data. Adjustments by a tax administration on the basis of the CbCR alone are therefore inconsistent with the agreed standard, which reflects the OECD's rejection of formulary apportionment under the arm's length principle. The restriction is deliberate: the data are aggregated, unaudited in the transfer pricing sense, and not on a uniform accounting basis, so conclusions drawn directly from them would risk arbitrary results and double taxation.

The restriction limits the report's value to the administration receiving it, but the report still does useful work. It lets an administration see where profit, tax, staff and assets sit, spot patterns such as high profit with few employees and low tax in a low-tax jurisdiction, and select audits. Those enquiries can then proceed through the local file and ordinary audit powers. The conditions on filing and exchange (filing by the ultimate parent in its residence jurisdiction, automatic exchange under qualifying competent authority agreements, confidentiality and consistency of use, and local filing fallbacks if there is a systemic failure to exchange) are designed to give groups comfort that the report is protected.

Further limits matter more than the use restriction. The EUR 750 million threshold excludes many groups, and some developing countries argue that this, together with the allocation of information through the parent's jurisdiction and exchange agreements that need reciprocity and confidentiality capacity, leaves them with less benefit than larger economies. Thus the claim is partly right: the use restriction caps the report's evidential weight, but it is the coverage and access conditions that most limit its value to many administrations. On balance the CbCR remains a significant transparency tool, though a screening tool rather than a basis for assessments.

points.point: States that Action 13 limits CbCR to high-level risk assessment and statistical analysis
States that CbCR alone should not be used as conclusive evidence or as the basis for adjustments and that a formula-based allocation is not permitted, linking to the arm's length principle
Explains the data limitations (aggregated, different accounting bases) as the rationale for the restriction
Identifies the threshold and access limitations, including developing country concerns about exchange and parent-jurisdiction filing
Notes the exchange and confidentiality conditions and the local filing fallback
Reaches a reasoned conclusion on whether the claim is overstated

answer.grader_note: Credit any coherent view. A candidate who treats the report as binding evidence of transfer pricing outcomes should not exceed 4 marks.

items.prompt: (c) Assess whether groups should "prepare all three tiers once, centrally, and file the same package everywhere".

answer.model:
Central coordination is sensible but filing an identical package everywhere is not workable and carries risk. The CbCR is a single standardised template and the master file is a single group document, so central preparation of both is efficient and reduces inconsistency. Many jurisdictions have, however, set their own content, thresholds, deadlines, language and format rules for the master file and local file, and Action 13 left implementation to domestic law. A group will therefore need to check each country's rules, translate documents, and meet different filing and penalty regimes.

The local file cannot be a copy of a central document. It must describe the transactions of the local entity, use the comparables and economic analysis relevant to that entity and market, and reflect the local entity's actual functions, assets and risks. A one-size document risks being a generic analysis that does not meet local standards, which may remove penalty protection that depends on contemporaneous, adequate documentation.

Consistency is the real risk in either direction. Information in the master file, local files, CbCR, financial statements and tax returns will be compared by administrations that exchange information; unexplained differences invite audit. Central review is a control against this, but it must be matched by local input. A sensible approach is a central framework and review, local preparation of local files, and a protocol for aligning the narrative across all tiers, so that the commentator is right about coordination and wrong about uniformity.

points.point: Central preparation of master file and CbCR is efficient and promotes consistency
Local rules on thresholds, deadlines, language, content and penalties differ because Action 13 is implemented through domestic law
The local file must be entity and market specific, and a generic document risks failing local standards or penalty protection
Reasoned conclusion: central framework with local tailoring and consistency review across tiers, returns and accounts

title: Special categories of income in the treaty distributive rules
scenario: A policy paper states: "Articles 16 to 20 of the Model Conventions are exceptions to the ordinary rules for employment and business income. Each exception exists for a reason, but several of the reasons are weaker today than when the provisions were drafted, and the OECD and UN Models do not always agree."

items.prompt: (a) Explain how Article 16 (directors' fees) and Article 17 (entertainers and sportspersons) allocate taxing rights, and why each departs from the rules in Articles 7 and 15.

answer.model:
Article 16 allows the State of residence of the company to tax fees and other similar payments derived by a resident of the other State in the capacity as a member of the board of directors (or similar organ) of that company. It is a source rule in effect: the director need not be present in the company's State for the right to arise, and it applies to a resident of the other State whether or not the director performs any duties in the company's State. The rationale is practical. A director's services are difficult to locate geographically because board decisions have effects wherever the company operates, the company can often deduct the fee, and the company's State is the natural place to tax. The Commentary notes that it applies to remuneration for the director role and not to a separate employment, which falls under Article 15 (or Article 7 where the services are carried on independently; the OECD Model has no Article 14, and the UN Model 2021 numbering used Article 14 for independent personal services, which the UN Model 2025 deleted).

Article 17(1) allows the State where the performance takes place to tax income derived by an entertainer such as a theatre, film, radio or television artiste, or a musician, or by a sportsperson, from personal activities in that capacity, notwithstanding Articles 7 and 15. There is no PE or fixed base requirement, no duration threshold, and no minimum income threshold in the OECD text. Article 17(2) allows the performance State to tax income from the activity that accrues not to the performer but to another person, such as a company or a personal service entity, again notwithstanding Articles 7 and 15; this addresses star companies and similar arrangements. The justification is that performers are mobile, spend short periods in a State, and could otherwise escape source taxation through the 183-day or PE thresholds, so the Model gives the performance State a simple, unconditional right.

points.point: Article 16: company's State of residence may tax directors' fees of a resident of the other State, irrespective of where services are performed
Rationale for Article 16: difficulty of locating director services, deductibility and the company's State link; distinguishes separate employment under Article 15
Article 17(1): performance State taxes entertainers and sportspersons notwithstanding Articles 7 and 15, with no PE or day-count threshold
Article 17(2): look-through to income accruing to another person, aimed at star companies and similar arrangements
Rationale: mobility and short stays would otherwise escape source taxation under Article 7 and 15 thresholds

items.prompt: (b) Compare the OECD and UN approaches to Article 18 (pensions) and Article 19 (government service), and explain the position of students under Article 20.

answer.model:
Article 18 of the OECD Model gives exclusive taxing rights over pensions and similar remuneration for past employment to the State of residence of the recipient, subject to Article 19(2). This favours residence, the State in which the retiree lives and which bears the social cost, and avoids source State taxation of deferred compensation. The UN Model offers alternatives. Alternative A is similar to the OECD rule. Alternative B, which reflects a source orientation, lets the State of residence tax pensions and similar remuneration but also allows the State from which the payments arise to tax them where the payer is a resident of that State or the payment is borne by a permanent establishment there; the bilateral treaty decides whether Alternative B is adopted and on what terms. The UN approach recognises that a developing State may have allowed deductions for pension contributions and wants to tax the benefits.

Article 19 allocates taxing rights over salaries, wages and similar remuneration paid by a State, its local authority or a statutory body for government service to the paying State, unless the services are rendered in the other State and the individual is a resident and national of that State, or did not become resident of that State solely to render the services. Pensions paid by the State for government service follow the same pattern, with taxation in the paying State unless the recipient is a resident and national of the other State. This reflects the sovereign nature of government service and the principle of mutual respect between States. Government pay for activities of a business character is dealt with under Articles 15 to 18 instead.

Article 20 exempts, in the host State, payments received by a student or business apprentice, who was a resident of the other State immediately before visiting the host State and is present solely for education or training, for the purposes of maintenance, education or training, provided the payments arise from sources outside the host State. Its purpose is to avoid taxing temporary study-related support. The UN Model follows the same approach, and the Commentary notes that treaties may add bilateral conditions such as time limits.

points.point: OECD Article 18: exclusive residence State taxation of pensions, subject to Article 19(2)

UN Model Article 18 offers Alternative A (residence) and Alternative B with source State right for pensions, with a source State right where the payer is resident there or the payment is borne by a permanent establishment

Article 19: paying State taxes government service pay, with the exception where services are rendered in the other State by a resident national who did not become resident solely to render them; pensions follow similarly

Article 20: host State exempts maintenance, education and training payments from sources outside that State for a student or apprentice who was a resident of the other State immediately before visiting

answer.grader_note: Do not credit the statement that Article 18 gives taxing rights to the source State in the OECD Model.

items.prompt: (c) Evaluate the paper's claim that the reasons for these exceptions are weaker today.

answer.model:
The claim is partly right. For Article 17, the need to prevent mobile performers escaping source tax remains, and the Article 17(2) look-through still matters because performers commonly contract through companies. However, the lack of any threshold means that a minor engagement can be taxable in the performance State, which creates compliance and withholding burdens out of proportion to the revenue, and may discourage cultural exchange; many treaties add a de minimis amount or an exemption for publicly funded cultural exchanges, and the UN Commentary discusses such a provision. Digital performance also challenges the premise of physical presence: a streamed or recorded performance may not take place in the State where the audience is, and Article 17 turns on where the personal activities are exercised, which differs from where the economic benefit arises. The Commentary and some state practice treat royalties and payments for rights differently from payments for performance.

For Article 16, remote board participation weakens the rationale that director services are hard to locate; a director may attend by video and the company State has no territorial connection with the activity. Even so, the rule is simple, avoids disputes about place of performance, and aligns with the company's deduction. The strongest argument for retaining it is administrability.

For Articles 18 and 19, the main question is distribution of the tax base. Residence taxation of pensions suits capital-exporting States with many retirees abroad receiving pensions but disadvantages source States that gave deductions, which is why the UN Model gives an alternative. Article 19 remains sound in principle, but increasingly governments use business-like entities, and the Commentary distinction between government service and business activity is difficult to apply. For students, the rule's aim of avoiding tax on support from home is supported, though it can be exploited where payments are disguised remuneration. Overall, these provisions were designed for a more physical, less mobile world; some are still useful for administrability, but others would benefit from thresholds and anti-abuse tests. A reasoned view should acknowledge the Models' different balance between residence and source.

points.point: Article 17 is still justified by mobility of performers and the look-through for star companies
Article 17 weaknesses: no threshold, compliance burden, digital and remote performance, cultural exchange provisions
Article 16: remote participation weakens the location rationale but administrability and the company's State link support it
Articles 18 and 19: residence versus source balance, UN Alternative B, and difficulty of the government versus business distinction
Article 20: purpose and potential for abuse
Reasoned conclusion recognising the OECD and UN difference in orientation

answer.grader_note: Credit any developed argument supported by Articles and Commentary. A list of Article contents without evaluation earns no more than 3 marks.

title: Transparency about tax planning
scenario: A finance ministry official argues: "Mandatory disclosure of tax planning is more intrusive than automatic exchange of information, and it makes more sense to deal with abusive arrangements through general anti-avoidance rules than by requiring early reporting by advisers and taxpayers."

items.prompt: (a) Explain the modular approach taken in the OECD BEPS Action 12 report on mandatory disclosure rules.

answer.model:
The Action 12 final report (2015) does not prescribe a single rule. It sets out recommendations for countries that choose to introduce mandatory disclosure, in a modular framework, so that each State can design a regime to meet its own policy objectives. The principal aim is early information on aggressive or abusive transactions, arrangements or structures, which allows the administration to respond quickly by changing legislation or regulation, or by targeting audits, and also to deter promoters and users.

The modules cover: who must report, either the promoter or the taxpayer user, or both, with a mechanism to avoid duplicated reporting; what must be reported, which is determined by a combination of a generic test, usually a main benefit test, and specific hallmarks aimed at features of known risks; when to report, with time limits and the question of whether the obligation arises when the scheme is made available or implemented; how to report, including the information required and how reports are linked through reference numbers; and the consequences of non-compliance, such as penalties. The design also considers how disclosure relates to the confidentiality of information, legal professional privilege, and scheme identification numbers. Countries can also choose between a taxpayer-based approach (as in some systems) and a promoter-based approach. The framework is not a minimum standard, so there is no peer review or compulsory implementation, in contrast to the minimum standards on harmful tax practices, treaty abuse, dispute resolution and CbCR.

points.point: Action 12 offers modular recommendations, not a single rule or minimum standard
Purpose: early information on aggressive or abusive arrangements to enable quick policy response and audit targeting, and deterrence
Modules include who reports (promoter, user or both), what is reported (generic and specific hallmarks), when and how to report
Consequences and design issues such as penalties, scheme reference numbers and privilege
States that Action 12 is not a BEPS minimum standard

items.prompt: (b) Describe how hallmarks and the main benefit test operate in a mandatory disclosure regime, and discuss the difficulties of defining them.

answer.model:
Hallmarks are descriptions of features or characteristics of arrangements that indicate potential tax avoidance and act as a trigger to report. Generic hallmarks target features common to many schemes, such as confidentiality conditions, contingent or success-based fees, or standardised documentation that is marketed to many taxpayers. Specific hallmarks target known areas of concern, for example arrangements that convert income into capital, use losses in a specified manner, or involve circular cash flows or transactions with parties in low-tax jurisdictions. The Action 12 report suggests that countries combine hallmarks with a threshold, commonly a main benefit test, under which an arrangement is reportable only if the main benefit or one of the main benefits that might be expected is a tax advantage. The EU rules adopted in Directive 2018/822 (DAC6) used hallmarks with the main benefit test applying to some categories only.

There are difficulties. If hallmarks are too wide, taxpayers and advisers over-report ordinary commercial transactions, and the administration is flooded with information. If too narrow, planning is redesigned to avoid the hallmarks. The main benefit test involves a motive element that is difficult to apply, and it raises interpretation issues common to general anti-avoidance rules, such as what counts as a tax advantage and how to compare it with commercial benefits. Different jurisdictions define hallmarks differently, which creates compliance cost for cross-border groups. Hallmarks defined only by features may catch normal transactions, such as contingent fees in ordinary commercial advice. Regimes face the problem of reporting an arrangement before the law has decided whether it is abusive, which means that reporting does not itself imply illegality. These points bear on the proportionality of the burden and the quality of data received.

points.point: Defines hallmarks and distinguishes generic from specific hallmarks with examples
Explains the main benefit test as a threshold linked to the expected tax advantage
Identifies difficulty: over-reporting and under-reporting depending on breadth
Identifies difficulty: motive and tax advantage tests mirror anti-avoidance rule problems
Notes divergence between jurisdictions and cross-border compliance cost, and that reporting does not itself mean the arrangement is abusive

answer.grader_note: Credit accurate use of DAC6 or other examples. Do not credit the claim that all DAC6 hallmarks require the main benefit test.

items.prompt: (c) Evaluate the official's argument that mandatory disclosure is more intrusive than automatic exchange of information and less useful than a general anti-avoidance rule.

answer.model:
The two instruments have different functions, so the comparison is imperfect. Automatic exchange, such as under the Common Reporting Standard, provides information on financial accounts so that residence States can tax income and capital that residents hold abroad. It identifies taxpayers and assets. Mandatory disclosure instead reveals planning, that is, the design and marketing of arrangements before or soon after they are used. It is more intrusive in one respect: it places obligations on advisers and taxpayers to report on their own affairs and may touch on advice, and the Action 12 report acknowledges legal professional privilege, which many States protect. The OECD's 2018 Model Mandatory Disclosure Rules for CRS avoidance arrangements and opaque offshore structures show a narrower, targeted use to support the CRS itself, so the two tools can be complementary.

A general anti-avoidance rule (GAAR) allows an administration to counteract an abusive arrangement once it has found it. It does nothing to help find it and acts after the event, with uncertainty about when it applies. Mandatory disclosure can supply the information needed to apply a GAAR, allows legislative amendments, and deters promoters. Their respective weaknesses are therefore different: a GAAR provides the legal basis for counteraction, and disclosure provides intelligence and deterrence.

The argument is therefore weak as a statement of alternatives. The proportionality concern about intrusiveness is valid and should be met by tight hallmarks, protection for privilege and limited use of data. The cost of compliance, and reports which attract no consequence, can undermine confidence. Taken together, disclosure and a GAAR are complementary, with the better question being how to design disclosure so that the burden is proportionate.

points.point: Distinguishes the function of automatic exchange (accounts and assets) from disclosure (planning arrangements)
Acknowledges intrusiveness concerns including privilege and burden on advisers and taxpayers
Explains that a GAAR counteracts after discovery whereas disclosure supplies early information and deterrence
Reasoned conclusion that the tools are complementary and that design should be proportionate

title: Halden Systems and State S
scenario: Halden Systems Ltd (Halden) is resident in State R and builds and services water treatment equipment. In 2026 it entered into two contracts with customers in State S. Contract 1 is with Customer Ltd to install and commission a filtration plant on Customer Ltd's land in State S. Contract 2 is with Beta Ltd to advise on the operating efficiency of Beta's existing plant, with Halden employees visiting Beta's premises in State S. Halden also sells its equipment to other State S customers. These sales are negotiated by employees of Halden Sales S Ltd (Sales S), a wholly owned subsidiary resident in State S that sells only Halden products and is paid a commission. Sales S staff agree price, quantities and delivery terms with each customer. The draft contract is then sent to Halden in State R, which signs it, and in 2026 every one of the 41 contracts proposed in this way was signed without any change. Halden has no office or employees of its own in State S other than as described. Halden asks whether it is exposed to taxation in State S on business profits under the State R and State S treaty, and the treaty text on permanent establishments is to be considered under (i) the OECD Model 2025 and (ii) the UN Model 2025 as alternative drafts. Assume the Articles are in the Model form, including the changes made to Article 5(5) and 5(6) of the OECD Model in 2017, and that every day listed in Table 2 is a day of physical presence in State S.

exhibits.caption: Contract 1: work on Customer Ltd's site in State S
Contract 2: days of presence of Halden employees at Beta Ltd's premises in State S (each period inclusive)

items.prompt: (a) Explain whether Halden has a permanent establishment in State S in respect of Contract 1, under (i) the OECD Model and (ii) the UN Model, showing how you measure the duration.

answer.model:
Duration from 1 March to 15 December 2026: March 31 + April 30 + May 31 + June 30 + July 31 + August 31 + September 30 + October 31 + November 30 + December 15 = 290 days, or about 9.5 months.

A building site or installation project is a PE only if it lasts long enough. Article 5(3) of the OECD Model provides that a building site, or construction or installation project, constitutes a PE only if it lasts more than twelve months. It lasts 9.5 months, so, applying only that paragraph, there is no PE under the OECD Model. The measurement starts when the contractor begins its activities, including preparatory work, and continues until work is completed or permanently discontinued; time is not interrupted by seasonal breaks. There is no indication of connected projects at the same site by related enterprises, which the Commentary says may need to be aggregated if contracts are split artificially; this should be checked.

Article 5(3)(a) of the UN Model provides that a building site, construction, assembly or installation project, or supervisory activities in connection with it, is a PE if it lasts more than six months. It lasts 9.5 months, which exceeds six months, so Halden has a PE in State S under the UN Model for the installation project. The fixed place test in Article 5(1) is not needed for this result. State S could tax the profits attributable to the PE under Article 7, as determined by what the PE would earn as a separate and independent enterprise. For the OECD Model, Article 5(1) might also be tested: Halden has access to Customer's land, but a dedicated place of business at its disposal for 290 days would still be a building site question, and the specific rule in Article 5(3) governs, so no PE arises under the OECD Model unless the 12 month limit is exceeded.

points.point: Calculates the duration as 290 days (about 9.5 months)
OECD Article 5(3): building or installation site is a PE only if it exceeds twelve months, so no PE here on this paragraph
Explains the start and end rules for measuring duration (including preparatory work, no interruption for temporary breaks)
UN Article 5(3)(a): threshold is six months, so a PE exists for the installation project
Notes that profits attributable to the PE are taxable by State S under Article 7 (separate enterprise principle)
Notes anti-fragmentation and connected-project checks or that Article 5(3) is the specific rule

answer.grader_note: Candidates who apply the 12-month test under the UN Model, or conclude a PE exists under the OECD Model without a further fact, should lose the relevant marks.

items.prompt: (b) Explain whether Contract 2 gives rise to a PE under Article 5, calculating the days of presence, and discuss the position under the OECD Model.

answer.model:
Under UN Article 5(3)(b) (same numbering in the UN Model 2021 and 2025), the furnishing of services, including consultancy services, by an enterprise through employees or other personnel engaged for that purpose, creates a PE if activities of that nature continue (for the same or a connected project) within the State for a period or periods aggregating more than 183 days in any twelve month period commencing or ending in the fiscal year concerned.

Days of presence (each calendar day counted once, overlapping days not counted twice): A: April 30 + May 31 + June 30 = 91 days. B: 15 to 30 June is 16 days, July 31, August 31 = 78 days. A and B overlap on 15 to 30 June (16 days). Combined A and B: 1 April to 31 August, April 30 + May 31 + June 30 + July 31 + August 31 = 153 days. C: October 31 + November 30 = 61 days. Total = 153 + 61 = 214 days, all within the twelve month period from 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027. 214 exceeds 183 days, so a services PE exists under UN Article 5(3)(b), as the services are for one project and the twelve-month test is met. Halden should be advised that State S can tax the profits attributable to the services PE under Article 7, and that the PE comes into existence only once the 183 days is exceeded, though the profits attributable may cover the period depending on the treaty and domestic rules.

The OECD Model has no services PE rule. Halden would need a fixed place of business under Article 5(1). Beta's premises could be at Halden's disposal if employees performed their activities there for a sufficient time, but the OECD Commentary requires a degree of permanence, and a changing set of employees performing services, with no dedicated space, is less likely to meet that test. No PE would then arise under the OECD Model, provided no other ground is satisfied, although the outcome would depend on whether Halden has Beta's premises at its disposal for a sufficient time. This is a point of judgement.

points.point: Sets out UN Article 5(3)(b): services through employees, same or connected project, more than 183 days in any 12 month period
Calculates A and B combined as 153 days after removing the 16 overlapping days, and C as 61 days
Totals 214 days, exceeds 183, so a services PE exists under the UN Model
States that the OECD Model has no services PE rule so a fixed place test under Article 5(1) applies
Concludes with reasoning that the OECD fixed place test is unlikely but arguable (permanence and disposal)

answer.grader_note: The 12-month window should include all the dates shown. Penalise double-counting of the overlap (91 + 78 = 169 + 61 = 230 is wrong).

items.prompt: (c) Advise Halden whether Sales S creates a PE for it in State S under (i) the OECD Model (with the 2017 changes) and (ii) the UN Model 2025, including the effect of Article 5(6) in each Model.

answer.model:
The OECD Model Article 5(5), as amended in 2017, provides that where a person is acting in a State on behalf of an enterprise and in doing so habitually concludes contracts, or habitually plays the principal role leading to the conclusion of contracts that are routinely concluded without material modification by the enterprise, and those contracts are either in the name of the enterprise, or for the transfer of ownership or the right to use property, or for the provision of services by the enterprise, the enterprise has a PE in respect of that person's activities, unless the activities are limited to those in Article 5(4). Sales S staff agree price, quantity and delivery terms and Halden signed all 41 contracts without change in 2026. Although Sales S does not formally conclude the contracts, it plays the principal role leading to their conclusion, and the contracts are routinely concluded without material modification. Halden may argue that signing in State R means no contract was concluded by Sales S, which would be a successful argument under the old wording, but it fails under the amended text.

Article 5(6) (OECD Model 2025, and the UN Model 2025 after renumbering; in the UN Model 2021 numbering the independent agent paragraph is 5(7)) provides that Article 5(5) does not apply where the person is an independent agent acting in the ordinary course of its business. However, a person who acts exclusively or almost exclusively on behalf of one or more enterprises to which it is closely related is not an independent agent. Sales S sells only Halden products and is wholly owned, so it is closely related and not independent. Article 5(6) is therefore unavailable. Article 5(7) confirms that control of a company does not itself make it a PE of the parent, but that does not prevent Article 5(5).

Under the UN Model, Article 5(5) also treats a person who habitually concludes contracts or plays the principal role, and Article 5(5)(b) covers a person who habitually maintains a stock of goods from which it delivers regularly on behalf of the enterprise. Under the UN Model 2025 the principal role limb of Article 5(5) already applies to Sales S on the same reasoning as the OECD text; any older UN limb for securing orders wholly or almost wholly for the enterprise should be checked against the edition the treaty follows, and is not needed for the result. In the UN Model 2025 the independent agent rule is Article 5(6), the subsidiary rule is Article 5(7) and the closely related definition is Article 5(8), because the insurance rule formerly in Article 5(6) was deleted and replaced by Article 12C. (In the UN Model 2021 numbering Article 5(6) was the insurance rule and the independent agent rule was Article 5(7).) Sales S, acting almost wholly for Halden, is not independent. Both Models therefore produce a dependent agent PE, provided the treaty adopts the 2017 wording in the OECD case. If the treaty uses pre-2017 wording, which refers to authority to conclude contracts in the name of the enterprise, Halden's position would be better. Advice: Halden should expect State S to assert a PE, and attribution of profit under Article 7 should consider that the arm's length commission to Sales S may already cover much of the attributable profit, subject to the PE bearing risks of the contracts.

points.point: OECD 5(5): habitual principal role in concluding contracts routinely concluded without material modification, applied to Sales S and Halden's unchanged signing of 41 contracts
Notes the old authority to conclude wording could have helped Halden and so the treaty text must be checked
Article 5(6): independent agent exception unavailable because Sales S acts almost exclusively for a closely related enterprise
Article 5(7): subsidiary status does not of itself create a PE, but does not override 5(5)

UN Model 2025 Article 5(5): the principal role limb applies as in the OECD text so a PE also arises under the UN Model; the independent agent exception is Article 5(6) in the UN Model 2025 numbering (5(7) in the 2021 numbering)
Advice on profit attribution under Article 7, noting the arm's length commission already paid

title: Interest deductibility at Dorrin Ltd
scenario: Dorrin Ltd (Dorrin) is resident in State S and is the manufacturing subsidiary of the Atlas group, headed by Atlas Holdings Ltd in State U. In Year 1 Dorrin borrowed from a related finance company, Ferrum Finance Ltd (Ferrum), resident in State T, and from an unrelated bank. State S has introduced a fixed ratio rule following the OECD BEPS Action 4 report. It limits net interest deductions to 25 per cent of tax-EBITDA, with an optional group ratio rule under which an entity may instead use the ratio of the Atlas group's net third party interest expense to its consolidated EBITDA, if higher than 25 per cent. State S has no de minimis threshold. Disallowed interest may be carried forward. State S and State T have a treaty based on the OECD Model, and State T taxes Ferrum on its interest income at the ordinary rate. Dorrin's directors want to know how much interest is deductible, whether the group ratio rule helps, and whether other rules could still restrict the deduction, including whether the loan from Ferrum is on arm's length terms, where Ferrum has lent at a rate of 7 per cent when comparable bank loans to similar borrowers cost 5 per cent. All figures are illustrative.

exhibits.caption: Dorrin Ltd, Year 1 (amounts in millions)
Atlas group, consolidated, Year 1 (amounts in millions)

items.prompt: (a) Calculate the net interest deduction available to Dorrin under State S's fixed ratio rule, and the amount disallowed.

answer.model:
Tax-EBITDA = operating profit for tax purposes, after depreciation, plus tax depreciation = 24 + 6 = 30 million. (Operating profit is taken before interest, and the question gives no other adjustment or exempt income.)

Net interest expense = interest expense to Ferrum 8 + to the bank 4 less interest income 2 = 10 million.

Fixed ratio capacity = 25 per cent × 30 = 7.5 million.

Net interest expense of 10 exceeds capacity of 7.5, so the deduction is limited to 7.5 million and 2.5 million is disallowed in Year 1 (10 less 7.5). The disallowed 2.5 million is available for carry forward under the State S rules, subject to the carry-forward conditions. The Action 4 report recommends a fixed ratio rule that limits an entity's net interest deductions to a percentage of tax-EBITDA within a corridor of 10 to 30 per cent, with State S's 25 per cent falling within that range. The rule applies to net interest expense, so interest income is netted before testing against capacity, and applies to related and third party interest alike, which is why the 4 million paid to the bank is included.

points.point: Calculates tax-EBITDA as 30 million (24 + 6)
Calculates net interest expense as 10 million (8 + 4 less 2)
Calculates capacity as 7.5 million (25% × 30)
Deduction limited to 7.5 million and disallowed 2.5 million
States that the rule applies to net interest, covers related and third party interest, with the 10 to 30% Action 4 range and carry forward

items.prompt: (b) Calculate the position if Dorrin elects the group ratio rule, and explain how the group ratio rule is designed to work.

answer.model:
Group ratio = group net third party interest expense ÷ group EBITDA = 54 ÷ 135 = 40 per cent.

This is higher than the fixed ratio of 25 per cent, so the election is beneficial. Capacity = 40 per cent × Dorrin's tax-EBITDA of 30 = 12 million.

Dorrin's net interest expense of 10 million is below capacity of 12 million, so the full 10 million is deductible and nothing is disallowed in Year 1. Unused capacity is 2 million (12 less 10), which State S would carry forward only if its rules allowed it (the Action 4 report recommends optionally allowing carry-forward of unused capacity for a limited period).

The group ratio rule is designed to allow an entity in a highly leveraged group, which borrows from third parties for genuine commercial reasons, to deduct interest up to the group's own external leverage, so that a fixed ratio does not penalise groups that are naturally highly geared. It uses net third party interest expense, which excludes intragroup interest, and consolidated EBITDA, so a group cannot raise its ratio simply by lending between group members. The Action 4 report recommends it as an optional addition to the fixed ratio rule, and some States cap the group ratio at a level or add an uplift. The facts do not indicate any cap in State S.

points.point: Group ratio 54 ÷ 135 = 40%
Capacity 40% × 30 = 12 million, so 10 million is fully deductible and nothing disallowed
Notes unused capacity of 2 million and the optional carry forward
Explains the rationale: genuinely highly geared groups, using third party interest only to prevent manipulation

answer.grader_note: Credit a candidate who notes that the group ratio rule may be subject to a cap or uplift in other States, but the facts state none.

items.prompt: (c) Advise Dorrin on other rules that may restrict the deduction even if the fixed or group ratio rule is satisfied, and on whether the Ferrum loan is a problem.

answer.model:
A ratio rule is a limit on the amount of net interest, not a test of whether a particular loan is on arm's length terms, so it does not replace transfer pricing. Article 9 of the Models and the domestic transfer pricing rules in State S allow the administration to test the terms of the Ferrum loan. The OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines, Chapter X on financial transactions, require the accurate delineation of the transaction, including whether the debt level is one that an independent lender would have granted, and whether the interest rate is arm's length. Here Ferrum charges 7 per cent against 5 per cent for comparable bank loans. Interest of 8 million at 7 per cent implies a principal of about 114.3 million, and at 5 per cent the same principal would cost about 5.71 million (8 × 5 ÷ 7), so roughly 2.29 million is the excess over an arm's length rate. On these facts that excess would be disallowed or recharacterised (the principal is inferred, not stated, so it should be confirmed); any arm's length adjustment reduces net interest before the ratio rule is applied, so the figures in (a) and (b) would change, with the possibility of a corresponding adjustment under Article 9(2) in State T through the mutual agreement procedure. Dorrin should obtain a benchmarking analysis, consider the credit rating of Dorrin standing alone and the effect of group support, and consider whether the full principal would be borrowed on that basis.

The debt level may also be tested by a domestic thin capitalisation rule, if State S keeps one in addition to the ratio rule, and by rules on hybrid mismatches (Action 2) if the loan or Ferrum's treatment gives a deduction without inclusion, though the facts say that State T taxes Ferrum at the ordinary rate, so a mismatch is unlikely. The interest paid to Ferrum is also subject to the treaty: Article 11 of the OECD Model limits source State withholding tax on interest to 10 per cent if Ferrum is the beneficial owner, and the beneficial ownership concept, along with any limitation on benefits or principal purpose test under Article 29, could be relevant if Ferrum is a conduit. Article 11(6) provides that where the amount of interest exceeds what would have been agreed at arm's length, Article 11 applies only to the arm's length amount.

Non-discrimination in Article 24(4) requires interest paid to a non-resident to be deductible under the same conditions as to a resident, but the Commentary accepts that rules which apply Article 9(1) or limit interest are not discriminatory, and State S's rule applies regardless of the lender's residence, so no discrimination arises. Practically Dorrin should (i) elect the group ratio rule and prepare supporting group figures, (ii) seek an arm's length rate or restructure the loan, and (iii) document the position in the local file.

points.point: Explains that the ratio rule does not replace the arm's length test of the Ferrum loan under Article 9 and domestic transfer pricing rules
Applies Chapter X: delineation of the financial transaction, debt capacity and the 7% versus 5% comparison, indicating a likely adjustment to the excess rate
Notes possible corresponding adjustment in State T and mutual agreement procedure
Identifies other restrictions such as thin capitalisation and hybrid rules, and why a mismatch is unlikely on these facts
Article 11: withholding, beneficial ownership and Article 11(6) arm's length limit
Article 24(4): no discrimination because the rule applies irrespective of lender residence; practical advice

answer.grader_note: Credit sensible alternative structures. The final answer should recognise that the interest rate difference needs principal information; an unqualified calculation of a disallowance amount is not required.

title: Neutrality benchmarks and relief methods
scenario: A finance minister in State R, a capital-exporting State that taxes residents on worldwide income, tells parliament: "We should replace our ordinary foreign tax credit with a full participation exemption for foreign dividends and branch profits. Credit relief is the only method consistent with fairness between investors, and exemption simply lets our companies compete on lower foreign tax rates at the expense of our revenue." A think tank replies that exemption is the better method for a trading economy and that the real fairness problem lies elsewhere.

items.prompt: (a) Explain capital export neutrality and capital import neutrality, and identify which method of relief from double taxation is conventionally associated with each.

answer.model: Capital export neutrality (CEN) holds that a resident investor should bear the same total tax whether it invests at home or abroad, so that the investment location decision is not distorted by tax. It requires the residence State to tax foreign income at the home rate and to relieve foreign tax only up to the home tax on that income. The method associated with CEN is the ordinary credit: worldwide taxation with a credit for foreign tax, limited to the domestic tax attributable to the foreign income (a per country or per item limit), so that the total burden equals the higher of the two rates. Capital import neutrality (CIN) holds that all investors competing in the same source market should bear the same tax burden whatever their residence, so that a local and a foreign investor face the same tax on the same income. It requires the residence State to leave foreign income to the source State. The method associated with CIN is exemption, including the participation exemption for dividends and often for foreign branch profits, under which the residence State exempts the income (OECD and UN Articles 23A and 23B contain the exemption and credit methods respectively). Neither benchmark can be satisfied in full by one State acting alone, and the two are only equivalent when the home and foreign rates are identical. A related benchmark, national neutrality, treats foreign tax as a deduction, and capital ownership neutrality asks who is the best owner of an asset, regardless of tax; a strong answer may mention these but they are not required.

points.point: defines CEN as equal total tax burden on domestic and foreign investment by a resident
defines CIN as equal tax burden for all investors competing in the same source market
links CEN to the ordinary credit method with the limit at domestic tax on the foreign income
links CIN to exemption or the participation exemption
cites Articles 23A (exemption) and 23B (credit) of the OECD and UN Models, or states that the Models allow either method

answer.grader_note: Award half marks for correct definitions without the link to a relief method. Do not credit the claim that credit equals CIN.

items.prompt: (b) Critically evaluate the minister's claim that the credit method is the only method consistent with fairness, and that exemption lets companies compete at the expense of revenue.

answer.model: The claim is overstated because it treats CEN as the sole definition of fairness. Fairness can be defined between residents (CEN, supporting a credit) or between competitors in the source market (CIN, supporting exemption), and each is a coherent equity benchmark. Exemption is also consistent with the benefit view of tax, under which the source State has the primary claim to tax income generated by activity within its territory, and the residence State relinquishes its claim to avoid taxing twice. The credit method has practical weaknesses that weaken the claim that it is more principled. First, it needs the residence State to compute foreign tax paid, translate currencies, apply the limitation and often allow underlying credit for dividends from foreign subsidiaries, which is complex and gives rise to excess credit and excess limit positions, with the result that CEN is rarely achieved. Second, most credit systems defer residence taxation of subsidiary profits until dividends are paid, so a company can accumulate profits in a low-tax State and the system departs from CEN in practice; anti-deferral rules such as controlled foreign company regimes are needed to restore it. Third, a credit only relieves tax up to the domestic rate, so if the foreign rate is higher the excess is a cost to the investor unless carry-forward is allowed. Exemption is simpler to administer, avoids the lock-in effect that arises when repatriation triggers residence tax, and puts the company on equal terms with local competitors, which is the CIN case. The revenue criticism has force: exemption gives the residence State no revenue from low-taxed foreign profits, creating an incentive to shift profits and activities to low-tax States. A participation exemption normally carries conditions (minimum holding, holding period, a subject to tax or activity test, and switch-over to credit for low-taxed passive income) which answer part of the concern. The Pillar Two global minimum tax of 15 per cent now sets a floor, under which a jurisdiction applying the GloBE rules may collect top-up tax where low-tax profits were exempted, which reduces the revenue and competition concern with exemption. Whichever method a State chooses, treaty relief is normally offered under the Model in either form, and the choice is a matter of policy rather than of principle. The minister's all or nothing framing is therefore not supported, but the revenue and mobility risks are real and require anti-abuse protection.

points.point: states that fairness has competing meanings (CEN equity between residents, CIN equity between competitors), so credit is not the only fair method
notes exemption is consistent with source primacy or the benefit view
identifies practical limits of credit: complexity, excess credit or limit, and deferral departing from CEN
explains lock-in or repatriation effect and administrative simplicity as arguments for exemption
recognises the revenue and profit shifting risk of exemption as a valid part of the minister's concern
notes conditions or safeguards on a participation exemption (holding tests, subject to tax, switch-over, CFC rules)
reaches a reasoned conclusion that the claim is overstated, with a supported position

answer.grader_note: Either overall conclusion can score if it is argued from both sides. A one-sided answer caps at 5 of 9. The Pillar Two point is creditable but not required.

items.prompt: (c) The think tank says the "real fairness problem lies elsewhere". Discuss what other problems the choice between credit and exemption leaves unresolved, and how a State's choice of method interacts with source State taxation, tax sparing, and the allocation of taxing rights under treaties.

answer.model: The choice of relief method only addresses what the residence State does after the source State has taxed. It does not decide the extent of source taxation, which is where most double taxation disputes arise. First, the rate and base of source taxation: a high withholding tax rate on dividends, interest or royalties, or a source rule that taxes services on a thin nexus, produces a tax that either method must absorb. Treaties therefore limit source taxation (Articles 10 to 12, with Article 12A in the UN Model 2021 numbering or Article 12AA in the UN Model 2025 for fees for services, and the permanent establishment threshold in Article 5), so allocation of taxing rights under the treaty does more to set the burden than the relief article. Second, exemption of foreign income can interact with source taxation to produce double non-taxation where the source State exempts or offers a holiday and the residence State exempts under Article 23A, which is a base erosion concern. The OECD Commentary notes the risk and States respond with subject to tax conditions and, under Article 23A(4), the right to apply the credit method instead of exemption where the source State applies the Convention to exempt the income or to limit its tax under Article 10(2) or 11(2). Third, tax sparing credits allow the residence State to credit tax that was forgone under the source State's incentive; this preserves the incentive for a developing State, which is a CIN style outcome, but the OECD view is that it is open to abuse and reduces the revenue of the residence State, so many OECD members have declined to give it or conditioned it on safeguards, while the UN Model Commentary is more accepting, reflecting the interests of developing States. Fourth, mismatches in qualification of income or entities between the two States (for example when the source State treats a payment as royalties and the residence State as business profits) can lead to double taxation or none despite either method, and require mutual agreement procedures. Fifth, relief depends on who is the resident and on the beneficial owner: a conduit may be denied treaty benefits and an indirect credit may fail where the claimant is not the recipient. Sixth, the choice of method affects how the residence State treats losses and expenses allocated to exempt income, which is a significant practical distortion. A strong conclusion is that the think tank is right that relief method is only one part of the system: the more fundamental matters are the allocation of source and residence taxing rights, treaty anti-abuse provisions, and consistent qualification, and the relief method should be chosen after those are settled, with the UN Model giving more weight to source State rights than the OECD Model.

points.point: explains that relief method operates only after source taxation, so source taxation rules and rates drive the burden
identifies treaty limits on source taxation (Articles 5, 10 to 12) as the main allocation of taxing rights
identifies double non-taxation risk from exemption combined with source holidays and the Article 23A(4) response or subject to tax conditions
explains tax sparing, its purpose, and the OECD versus UN attitude
identifies conflicts of qualification of entities or income as unresolved by either method
notes beneficial owner or conduit issues and expenses or losses allocated to exempt income
reaches a reasoned conclusion on the think tank's position

answer.grader_note: Credit 1 mark for any two distinct additional problems if the discussion is shallow. Do not credit unsupported statements about particular States.

title: Entities across borders
scenario: A partnership formed under the law of State P is treated by State P as a separate taxable entity, while State Q treats a comparable partnership as fiscally transparent. A commentator argues: "The qualification problem is solved by treaties, because the Model already tells States how to treat transparent entities and a partnership resident in one State will always get treaty relief on income it receives from the other."

items.prompt: (a) Explain what is meant by transparent and opaque entities, how States decide which a foreign entity is, and why an entity may be recognised as a legal person but still be transparent for tax purposes.

answer.model: A transparent (or flow through) entity is not itself taxed on its income; the income is attributed to and taxed in the hands of the members or partners, who are taxed as if they had earned it directly. An opaque entity is a taxpayer in its own right, taxed on its profits, and members are taxed only on distributions. Recognition of a foreign entity as a legal person is a private international law question, usually decided by the law of incorporation or, in some States, the law of the real seat (siege reel). Whether it is transparent for tax is a separate question for the State of the tax claim, answered by domestic tax law. States use different methods: a classification by legal form (a company is opaque and a partnership is transparent); a comparison of the foreign entity's characteristics with those of the domestic entities (limited liability, separate legal personality, free transferability of interests, centralised management, and continuity of existence); or an elective regime such as the United States entity classification election, under which eligible entities choose to be taxed as a corporation or as a flow through. An entity can therefore have legal personality (it may own assets, sue and contract in its own name) and still be transparent, because tax classification does not depend on the existence of legal personality. The same entity can be treated as opaque by one State and transparent by another, which leads to the qualification issues in part (b) and (c).

points.point: defines transparent entity: income taxed in the hands of members
defines opaque entity: taxed itself, members taxed on distributions
explains recognition as a legal person is a private international law matter (incorporation or real seat) distinct from tax classification
describes at least two state practice approaches (legal form, characteristics test, election or check the box)
explains that legal personality does not decide transparency

answer.grader_note: Do not credit an answer that equates recognition with taxation status.

items.prompt: (b) Describe the problems that arise when two States classify the same entity differently, with examples of double taxation and of double non-taxation.

answer.model: A conflict of entity classification arises because each State applies its own tax law. Where State P treats the partnership as opaque and State Q as transparent, the income may be taxed by different persons or in different periods, which can give either result. Double taxation: suppose the partnership in State P receives dividends from State Q. State Q regards the partnership as transparent and so treats the partners as the recipients and applies the dividend withholding rate that would apply to each partner; State P regards the partnership as the owner and taxes it on the dividend. The partners, resident in a third State, are then taxed again on the distribution in that State, and no State gives a credit for the other's tax, because from each State's view the taxpayer is different. A second example is where the credit State does not recognise the foreign tax as paid by the same person who is claiming credit, so a credit is refused. Double non-taxation: a payment by an entity treated as a company in one State and transparent in another can produce a deduction in the payer State (as an interest or royalty payment to a partner) while the recipient State treats the same payment as a transparent distribution of profit that is not taxable (a deduction no inclusion mismatch), or an entity may be treated as opaque by the residence State of its owners, which exempts a dividend, and as transparent by the source State, so that the income is attributed to a partner resident in a State that does not tax it. These are hybrid mismatch arrangements. The BEPS Action 2 report (neutralising the effects of hybrid mismatch arrangements) recommends linking rules which match the tax treatment of the payer and the payee, with a primary response of denying a deduction and a defensive rule of requiring inclusion. For treaty purposes the Commentary identifies that conflicts of qualification may lead to non-taxation or double taxation, and that the mutual agreement procedure is available.

points.point: explains that each State applies its own law so the taxpayer differs between States
gives a correct worked example of double taxation (income taxed to different persons, no credit)
gives a correct example of double non-taxation such as deduction no inclusion or exemption in both
identifies hybrid mismatch arrangements as the term for such outcomes
refers to BEPS Action 2 linking rules (primary and defensive responses)
notes mutual agreement procedure as treaty route for qualification conflicts

items.prompt: (c) Critically evaluate the commentator's claim that the Models resolve the position and that a partnership resident in one State will always receive treaty relief.

answer.model: The claim is wrong in important respects. The OECD Model addresses transparent entities in Article 1(2), added in the 2017 update following BEPS Action 6 and 2, which provides that income derived by or through an entity or arrangement treated as wholly or partly fiscally transparent under the tax law of either Contracting State is considered income of a resident of a State only to the extent that the income is treated for the purposes of taxation by that State as the income of a resident. It therefore gives treaty benefits to the extent that a resident of the State is taxed on the income, but denies them where nobody in the State is taxed on it. The UN Model also contains a corresponding Article 1(2) in its recent versions (UN Model 2021 and 2025); a candidate should say that the UN text follows the same approach, and flag that it is the treaty text actually in force that matters, since many older treaties contain no such provision. Second, the treaty requires a person who is a resident under Article 4, that is liable to tax by reason of residence. A fiscally transparent partnership is generally not liable to tax and so is not itself a resident, which is the reason why Article 1(2) looks through to the partners. In the scenario, State P treats the partnership as opaque, so it may be a resident of State P; State Q treats it as transparent and may treat the partners (who might reside in other States) as the persons entitled to relief, potentially under their own treaties. Third, the claim that relief is automatic ignores the other conditions: beneficial ownership under Articles 10 to 12 must be satisfied by whoever receives the income, the limitation on benefits or principal purpose test under the 2017 text (OECD Model Article 29, including the PPT in Article 29(9), and the preamble; the UN Model 2025 Article 29 combines a qualified person test with a principal purpose test) applies, and a partnership may not be the beneficial owner. Fourth, where the qualification differs the question is not settled by Article 1(2) as such. The Commentary on Articles 23A and 23B and the 1999 OECD Partnership Report address conflicts of qualification arising from different treatments of an entity and recommend that the State of source follow the qualification of the State of residence for the purposes of applying the relief article, to avoid double taxation, but this is guidance in the Commentary not a rule, and the State of source may treat it differently when its treaty text differs. Where the conflict persists, mutual agreement under Article 25 is the remedy. Fifth, Action 2 domestic rules operate independently of treaties and may deny a deduction or require an inclusion. The commentator is therefore right that the Models give guidance but wrong that the problem is solved or that relief is guaranteed. A sound conclusion: Article 1(2) improves the position, but relief remains conditional on residence, beneficial ownership, anti-abuse provisions and consistent classification, and the MAP is required for residual conflict.

points.point: identifies Article 1(2) OECD Model (2017) and its to the extent rule for fiscally transparent entities
notes UN Model contains comparable provision or that actual treaty text decides, and older treaties may lack it
explains that a transparent partnership is not liable to tax and so not a resident under Article 4, hence the look through
identifies further conditions: beneficial ownership, limitation on benefits or principal purpose test
refers to the OECD Partnership Report 1999 or Commentary on conflicts of qualification and its non-binding status
notes Article 25 MAP for residual conflicts and domestic hybrid mismatch rules
reaches a reasoned conclusion that the claim is wrong or overstated

answer.grader_note: Accept any accurate paraphrase of Article 1(2). Do not require quotation. Do not credit a statement that Article 1(2) denies relief to partnerships generally.

title: Information sharing between tax authorities
scenario: State K, a financial centre, has agreed to a request-based information exchange agreement and to the automatic exchange of financial account information, but its minister says: "We have met the international standard; our banks can now be trusted to keep clients' affairs private from everyone except foreign tax authorities, who will receive only what they can show they need." A foreign tax authority has asked State K for details of all accounts held by residents of its State at one bank, without naming any taxpayer.

items.prompt: (a) Explain the scope of Article 26 of the OECD and UN Model Tax Conventions and the main limits on, and safeguards for, the exchange of information under it.

answer.model: Article 26 provides for exchange of information that is foreseeably relevant to carrying out the Convention or to the administration or enforcement of the domestic laws of the Contracting States concerning taxes of every kind and description, so that it is not limited to the taxes covered by the treaty or to residents of the Contracting States (Article 1 and Article 2 do not restrict it). The standard was changed from necessary to foreseeably relevant in 2005, and the Commentary explains that the aim is to allow the widest possible exchange while not permitting fishing expeditions, requests made speculatively without a link to an identifiable taxpayer or tax matter. Paragraph 2 requires that information received is treated as secret in the same manner as information obtained under the domestic law of the receiving State and disclosed only to persons or authorities concerned with the assessment, collection, enforcement or prosecution of taxes, or the determination of appeals, with use for other purposes permitted if the laws of both States allow and the competent authority of the supplying State agrees. Paragraph 3 sets limits: a State is not required to carry out administrative measures at variance with the laws and administrative practice of either State, supply information not obtainable under its laws or normal administrative practice, or supply information which would disclose a trade, business, industrial, commercial or professional secret or trade process, or whose disclosure would be contrary to public policy (ordre public). Paragraph 4 requires a State to use its information gathering measures to obtain information for the other State even where it has no domestic tax interest in it. Paragraph 5 provides that a State may not decline to supply information solely because it is held by a bank, other financial institution, nominee, agent or fiduciary, or because it relates to ownership interests in a person. The UN Model follows the same structure; assistance in collection is dealt with in the separate Article 27, not in Article 26, and the UN Commentary adds that the competent authorities may establish procedures through consultation.

points.point: states the foreseeably relevant standard and that it covers taxes of every kind and persons who are not residents
explains no fishing expeditions, the requirement of a link to an identifiable taxpayer or tax matter
describes the confidentiality requirement and permitted use (paragraph 2)
identifies the limits in paragraph 3 (domestic law and practice, trade secret, public policy)
identifies paragraph 4 (no domestic interest) and paragraph 5 (bank secrecy not a ground for refusal)

answer.grader_note: Paragraph numbers are not required if the content is right. UN Article 27 on collection is not required.

items.prompt: (b) Compare the Model treaty provision with tax information exchange agreements (TIEAs), the Multilateral Convention on Mutual Administrative Assistance in Tax Matters and the work of the Global Forum, and explain the three forms or standards of exchange the international framework recognises.

answer.model: A Model Convention Article 26 is one provision within a comprehensive double tax treaty, so it exists only between States that have concluded a full treaty, and it is tied to the treaty's coverage. TIEAs, based on the 2002 OECD Model Agreement on Exchange of Information on Tax Matters, were developed for jurisdictions, often low-tax or financial centres, with which the treaty partner was not willing to conclude a full convention: they contain only exchange provisions, are normally bilateral, are one way or reciprocal, and operate on request, with no relief or allocation of taxing rights. The Multilateral Convention (developed jointly by the OECD and the Council of Europe and amended by protocol in 2010 to open it to all States) is a single multilateral instrument providing for exchange on request, spontaneous and automatic exchange, simultaneous examinations and assistance in collection, with a wide range of participating jurisdictions, and it is the legal basis for most automatic exchange under the Common Reporting Standard. The Global Forum on Transparency and Exchange of Information for Tax Purposes is the multilateral body (with a large membership including developing States) that monitors implementation through peer reviews: an assessment of the legal and regulatory framework and of how it works in practice, with ratings of compliance. The three forms of exchange are: on request (a specific request about a particular taxpayer or matter, or an identified group (Article 26 Commentary, 2012)), spontaneous (the supplying State provides information it has found that it considers relevant to the other State without being asked), and automatic (routine systematic transmission of predefined information, such as financial account balances under the Common Reporting Standard, as in this scenario). The Global Forum standard is expressed in terms of exchange on request and automatic exchange, supported by availability of ownership and accounting information and access to it. Candidates may note that the exact count of standards varies in accounts and the answer should define what is meant.

points.point: explains Article 26 is within a comprehensive treaty and limited to treaty partners
describes TIEAs: 2002 Model, narrow scope, on request
describes the Multilateral Convention: amended 2010, multilateral, covers all forms of exchange and assistance in collection
describes the Global Forum and peer reviews of legal framework and practice
explains the three forms: on request, spontaneous, automatic, with CRS as example

answer.grader_note: The syllabus-wide phrase three standards is read as the three forms; accept an answer that treats the standards as on request, automatic and, with clear definition, a third item (such as availability of beneficial ownership information) if consistently explained.

items.prompt: (c) Advise whether the foreign authority's request for details of all accounts held by its residents at one bank without naming taxpayers meets the Article 26 standard, and critically evaluate the minister's statement about privacy and the adequacy of the international standard.

answer.model: The request is for information on an unnamed group of taxpayers, a group request. The Commentary (since 2012) accepts that a request may relate to a group of taxpayers not individually identified, provided the requesting State gives a detailed description of the group, the specific facts and circumstances leading to the request, an explanation of the applicable law and why there are reasonable grounds for believing that taxpayers in the group have been non-compliant, a demonstration that the information sought would assist in determining compliance, and, where relevant, that a third party is likely to hold the information. A bare request for all accounts of residents at one bank, without grounds, is a fishing expedition, because it lacks the foreseeable relevance link, so State K may decline and ask for supporting detail; the answer changes if the requesting authority can show, for example, that the bank has been associated with an identified non-compliance pattern. State K cannot rely on bank secrecy (Article 26(5)) or lack of domestic interest (Article 26(4)) as grounds for refusal. As to the minister's statement: it is wrong in two respects. First, the standard does not allow privacy against domestic or foreign authorities as a ground for refusal in properly founded requests, and automatic exchange transmits data without any request or specific showing of need, so the claim that foreign authorities receive only what they can show they need is not correct for the automatic exchange State K has agreed to. Second, meeting the standard on paper is not the end: the Global Forum assesses practice and effectiveness, and a State can be rated poorly for failing to answer requests in practice. There is a legitimate counterpoint that the safeguards (confidentiality, use restrictions, the speciality rule, data protection and the need for a foreseeable relevance link) protect taxpayers, and developing States raise concerns that they lack capacity to participate in automatic exchange or to reciprocate, so the standard may not operate evenly. A sound conclusion is that State K may reasonably ask for more detail on the group request, but not refuse on bank secrecy, and the minister overstates the privacy protection.

points.point: identifies this as a group request and states the Commentary conditions (detailed group description, facts, grounds for belief in non-compliance, how the information assists)
concludes that a bare request without grounds is a fishing expedition and may be declined or supplemented
states that bank secrecy and absence of domestic tax interest are not valid grounds for refusal
explains that automatic exchange does not depend on a request or need shown, so the minister's statement is wrong
notes the Global Forum assesses practice and effectiveness, not only legal compliance
notes safeguards (confidentiality, use limits) and developing State capacity concerns as counterpoints

title: Veltra Ltd: where is the company resident?
scenario: Veltra Ltd was incorporated in State R in Year 1 and is a wholly owned subsidiary of a listed group. State R taxes companies as resident if they are incorporated there. State S taxes a company as resident if its place of effective management is in State S. Veltra has five directors: the chair and one other reside in State R, and three reside in State S. In Year 5, 4 of 10 board meetings were held in State S, 2 in State R, and 4 by video link with the chair joining from State R and a majority of directors joining from State S. The chief executive, who is not a director, lives in State R and takes day to day operating decisions with a team in State R, while the board in practice approves strategy, financing and acquisitions. Veltra's only office and its employees are in State R. State S has assessed Veltra as resident and State R continues to tax it as resident. Veltra's taxable profit for Year 5 is 4,000,000 currency units (illustrative). The corporate income tax rate is 20% in State R and 30% in State S. The R to S treaty follows the 2017 OECD Model text on dual residence of companies, and Veltra wishes to know its position and how to obtain relief. The treaty also contains the standard time limit in the mutual agreement procedure article.

exhibits.caption: Year 5 board meeting record and tax rates (illustrative)

items.prompt: (a) Explain why Veltra is a dual resident for treaty purposes, and why dual residence matters.

answer.model: Article 4(1) of the OECD and UN Models defines a resident of a Contracting State as a person who, under the law of that State, is liable to tax there by reason of domicile, residence, place of management, place of incorporation or any other criterion of a similar nature. Veltra is incorporated in State R, so it is liable to tax in State R by reason of its place of incorporation, and it is assessed in State S because the S authorities contend that its place of effective management is there, a criterion of a similar nature. Each State therefore applies its own domestic test and both treat Veltra as a resident, so Veltra is resident in both States under Article 4(1) and falls within the dual residence rule in Article 4(3). Dual residence matters because each State taxes a resident on its worldwide income, producing residence to residence double taxation which is not relieved by the credit or exemption articles (Articles 23A and 23B), which assume one State of residence and one State of source. A person that is a resident of both States could claim treaty benefits in each against the other, which would risk abuse.
