It introduces a side-by-side safe harbour, available by election, under which groups headquartered in a jurisdiction with a qualifying regime, assessed against criteria, is treated so that US-parented groups are not subject to the IIR or UTPR of other States on their US profits, while the qualified domestic minimum top-up taxes and the other jurisdictions' rules continue. It also adds a UPE safe harbour (replacing the transitional UTPR safe harbour), further simplifications and safe harbours, including a permanent simplified effective tax rate safe harbour at 15 per cent (for fiscal years beginning on or after 31 December 2026), a one-year extension of the transitional country-by-country reporting safe harbour and a safe harbour for substance-based tax incentives. In favour of the package: it preserved the broad participation of the Inclusive Framework and the continuing application of GloBE in most States, gave certainty and lowered compliance costs for groups, and avoided competing unilateral responses. Against: it creates asymmetry, since US-parented groups are treated more favourably than groups from States that adopted GloBE, which undermines the level playing field that Pillar Two was designed to create; the exemption reduces revenue and weakens the backstop role of the UTPR; the safe harbours add complexity of their own, and a system with more than one standard of recognition is less coherent than a single common approach. The outcome should be judged against the objective of the project, which was to set a floor under competition on tax rates. My view is that the package preserves a smaller but workable system at the price of consistency. The status of detail should be checked, as it was still developing after agreement.

points.point: States that the package responds to the US position and the G7 2025 statement, exempting US-parented groups from IIR and UTPR under a qualifying regime
Identifies other elements: simplified ETR safe harbour, extended transitional CbCR safe harbour, substance-based incentive safe harbour
Gives arguments in favour (preserved participation, certainty, reduced compliance, avoided unilateral measures)
Gives arguments against (asymmetry and level playing field, revenue, UTPR backstop weakened, added complexity)
Reaches a reasoned conclusion on coherence

answer.grader_note: This area is recent: credit careful general wording. Do not penalise omission of detailed criteria.

title: Calder Tools Ltd and its State S branch
scenario: Calder Tools Ltd is resident in State R and manufactures power tools. In Year 1 it carried on sales activity in State S through a branch with a warehouse and eight employees, who negotiate and conclude contracts with State S customers, hold and manage the inventory, and bear the risk of unsold stock. Goods are made in State R and supplied to the branch by head office. The branch is accepted as a permanent establishment under Article 5 of the State R and State S treaty, which follows the OECD Model and its 2010 Article 7. The company wants to know the profit that State S can tax, the tax payable, and what happens in State R. All amounts are illustrative and in a common currency unit. The treaty relief method in State R is not specified in the extract, and Calder Tools Ltd asks for both Article 23A and Article 23B to be considered. The State S corporate rate is 25 per cent and the State R rate is 30 per cent. The Exhibit gives the relevant figures for Year 1. Head office general administration costs benefit the whole company and State S accepts a revenue allocation key. The company has not yet prepared a transfer pricing file for the dealing with the branch.

exhibits.caption: Year 1 figures for Calder Tools Ltd and its State S branch

items.prompt: (a) Explain how Article 7 of the OECD Model, as interpreted under the Authorised OECD Approach (AOA), requires the profits of a permanent establishment to be attributed, and note how the UN Model differs.

answer.model: Article 7(1) allows the State where a permanent establishment is situated to tax only the profits attributable to it. Article 7(2), as rewritten in 2010, requires attribution of the profits that the PE might be expected to make if it were a separate and independent enterprise engaged in the same or similar activities under the same or similar conditions, taking account of the functions performed, assets used and risks assumed through the PE and through the other parts of the enterprise. The AOA carries out the attribution in two steps. Step one is a functional and factual analysis, identifying activities and conditions, attributing assets and risks by reference to significant people functions performed in the PE, recognising dealings between the PE and other parts of the enterprise, and attributing capital on the basis of the assets and risks. Step two is to determine the profits of the PE's dealings and activities by applying the Transfer Pricing Guidelines by analogy, so that dealings are priced at arm's length. Article 7(3) provides for the corresponding adjustment by the residence State where the source State has attributed profits. The UN Model's Article 7 also adopts the separate enterprise approach in 7(2), but differs in retaining a limited force of attraction rule in 7(1), under which sales of the same or similar goods in the source State may be attributed to the PE, and it has been less ready to adopt the AOA wholesale. The treaty text and its date therefore matter.

points.point: States Article 7(1): only profits attributable to the PE may be taxed in the PE State
Describes the functionally separate enterprise hypothesis in Article 7(2) (functions, assets, risks)
Explains AOA step one: functional analysis, significant people functions, assets, risks, capital, dealings
Explains AOA step two: pricing dealings under the Transfer Pricing Guidelines by analogy
Identifies the UN Model difference (limited force of attraction, wider approach)

answer.grader_note: UN Article 7 wording differs between editions; credit a candidate who states the force of attraction point with care.

items.prompt: (b) Calculate the profit attributable to the permanent establishment of Calder Tools Ltd in State S for Year 1, and State S's tax on it. Show each step.

answer.model: Step 1: revenue from State S customers: 20,000,000. Step 2: the dealing under which goods are sold by head office to the branch, priced at arm's length: cost of goods 13,500,000, so the gross profit is 20,000,000 minus 13,500,000, which is 6,500,000. Step 3: the PE's direct expenses of 2,400,000 are deducted: 6,500,000 minus 2,400,000 equals 4,100,000. Step 4: head office general administration of 3,000,000 is a cost that benefits the whole enterprise. The Exhibit states that a revenue allocation key is accepted, giving the PE a share of 20,000,000 ÷ 100,000,000, which is 20 per cent, so 600,000 is deductible: 4,100,000 minus 600,000 equals 3,500,000. Step 5: capital attribution. The PE's net assets used and risks are 10,000,000 and the capital allocation approach attributes 40 per cent as free capital, which is 4,000,000. The remaining 6,000,000 is funded by debt and the arm's length interest is 4 per cent, which is 240,000, deductible: 3,500,000 minus 240,000 equals 3,260,000. Step 6: tax at State S's 25 per cent: 3,260,000 multiplied by 0.25 equals 815,000. The attributable profit is therefore 3,260,000 and the tax is 815,000. Note that Article 7(2) as read under the AOA requires that expenses be attributed on the same basis whether incurred in the State of the PE or elsewhere, and that the allocated head office costs and the dealing price are subject to challenge on their fairness.

points.point: Attributes gross profit of 6,500,000 (20,000,000 less 13,500,000) using the arm's length internal dealing
Deducts direct expenses of 2,400,000 to reach 4,100,000
Allocates head office costs of 600,000 using the 20 per cent revenue key (3,000,000 x 20,000,000 ÷ 100,000,000)
Calculates attributed free capital of 4,000,000 and debt of 6,000,000
Deducts interest of 240,000 to reach profit of 3,260,000
Calculates State S tax of 815,000

answer.grader_note: Award follow-through marks for consistent arithmetic from an earlier error.

items.prompt: (c) State R, where Calder Tools Ltd is resident, taxes the company at 30 per cent. Advise on the double taxation consequences for Year 1 under Articles 23A and 23B, and on what could happen if State R computes the PE's profit differently.

answer.model: State R must give relief for State S's tax. Under the exemption method in Article 23A, State R exempts the PE profit of 3,260,000, so no State R tax arises on it and the combined burden is 815,000. Under the credit method in Article 23B, State R taxes the company on its worldwide profit, including the 3,260,000, which at 30 per cent is 978,000, and gives credit for State S tax of 815,000, since the credit is limited to the lesser of the foreign tax paid and the State R tax attributable to that income. The credit is therefore 815,000 and State R collects 163,000, which is 978,000 minus 815,000, so the total is 978,000 and the burden is at the State R rate. The treaty's actual article determines the method. If State R computes the profit differently, for example because it does not follow the AOA, does not accept the dealing price or the allocated head office cost, then State R might regard the PE profit as lower, for example 2,600,000. State R would then give relief only for its own calculation under the exemption method, or limit the credit, and economic double taxation arises on the difference. Article 7(3) requires State R to make a corresponding adjustment if it agrees that the State S figure is justified. If not, the company can use the mutual agreement procedure in Article 25 and, if the State R treaty has it, arbitration under the MLI, to resolve the difference. Time limits and documentation matter, and a transfer pricing file supporting the dealing would be advised. State R's relief is also limited by its own domestic rules, which may still apply in the absence of corresponding treaty articles.

points.point: Applies Article 23A exemption: no State R tax, total burden 815,000
Applies Article 23B credit: State R tax 978,000, credit 815,000, residual 163,000
Identifies the credit limit as the lesser of foreign tax and State R tax on that income
Explains possible mismatch where State R computes a different PE profit and the risk of economic double taxation
Advises on Article 7(3) corresponding adjustment and MAP under Article 25 (and possibly arbitration)

answer.grader_note: Accept a different illustrative State R figure if the logic of limited relief is correct.

title: Vale Holdings and the State S dividend
scenario: Zephyr Group is headed by Zephyr Parent Ltd, resident in State X. State X has no treaty with State S. In Year 1 Zephyr Parent Ltd interposed Vale Holdings Ltd, resident in State M, as the 100 per cent holder of Delta Mining Ltd, a State S company that Zephyr Group had decided to acquire. Vale was acquired from a third party in the course of a regional reorganisation that the board minuted before the Delta investment was approved. Vale has three directors resident in State M who meet in State M, holds four other subsidiaries in the region and has arranged local bank funding. It has two employees. In Year 3 Delta paid Vale a dividend of 10,000,000 (illustrative currency units). Within 45 days Vale paid 9,000,000 on to Zephyr Parent Ltd as a dividend. State M exempts dividends received from subsidiaries and levies no withholding tax on dividends paid to State X. The State S and State M treaty follows the OECD Model and both are parties to the MLI with the PPT applied. State S domestic withholding tax on dividends is 30 per cent. State S has issued a notice that it intends to deny the treaty rate. Zephyr Group asks for advice.

exhibits.caption: State S and State M treaty, dividend withholding rates (paraphrased extract)

items.prompt: (a) Explain the beneficial owner requirement and the principal purposes test (PPT), and how they may apply to Vale Holdings Ltd.

answer.model: The reduced rate in Article 10(2) of the OECD and UN Models is available only where the dividends are paid to a resident of the other State who is the beneficial owner. The Commentary explains that a conduit with very narrow powers over the income, acting as a fiduciary or administrator on behalf of another party, is not the beneficial owner, and the 2014 Commentary changes confirm that this is a substance-based reading, not a technical domestic-law meaning. The Danish cases of 2019 before the Court of Justice of the European Union, albeit on EU directives, indicated that abuse can be established with objective factors, and courts in several States have examined conduits. The principal purposes test in Article 29(9) of the 2017 and later OECD Models, also introduced by Article 7 of the MLI, denies a benefit if it is reasonable to conclude, having regard to all the facts and circumstances, that obtaining the benefit was one of the principal purposes of an arrangement or transaction that resulted directly or indirectly in the benefit, unless it is established that granting it would be in accordance with the object and purpose of the relevant provisions. Article 29(10) allows the competent authority to grant relief on request. Here, Vale passes on most of the dividend within weeks and has few employees, which are indicators that it is a conduit. But it also has local directors and several subsidiaries, which point the other way. The UN Model's anti-abuse provision, Article 29 (Entitlement to benefits), combines a qualified-person limitation on benefits with a principal purpose test, and the PPT works in the same way.

points.point: States that Article 10(2) requires a beneficial owner resident in the other State and explains the conduit concept
Describes the PPT in Article 29(9) OECD (one of the principal purposes, object and purpose exception) and its MLI source
Mentions Article 29(10) discretionary relief or the UN Model equivalent
Applies to the facts: indicators for conduit status (pass-through, thin staff) and against (local directors, other subsidiaries)

answer.grader_note: Accept reference to Indofood or the Danish cases if correct. Do not credit overstating the Danish cases as treaty cases.

items.prompt: (b) Calculate the State S withholding tax on the dividend if the treaty rate applies and if it does not, and the amount at stake. Then explain what other factors may decide whether State S may deny the reduced rate.

answer.model: Treaty rate: the Exhibit shows a 5 per cent rate for a company that is the beneficial owner holding at least 10 per cent of the capital. 10,000,000 multiplied by 5 per cent equals 500,000. Vale holds 100 per cent, so the holding condition is met. Without the treaty, domestic law applies at 30 per cent: 10,000,000 multiplied by 30 per cent equals 3,000,000. The amount at stake is 3,000,000 minus 500,000, which is 2,500,000. If Vale were not the beneficial owner but its parent were, the treaty would not apply to the parent unless a treaty between State S and State X existed, and the Exhibit shows none, so 3,000,000 is the exposure. The 15 per cent rate for other cases would give 1,500,000, but it is not relevant since the holding exceeds 10 per cent and the rate depends on beneficial ownership. Other factors include whether State S's domestic law has a general anti-avoidance rule or substance rules that apply even if the treaty is available, how the treaty is interpreted under domestic law, whether the treaty includes a limitation on benefits clause, and the burden of proof. The relevant State S authority will consider the length of time Vale has held the shares, its decision-making, the risk it bears and its funding. State S must also consider whether the group had a commercial purpose that was more than tax, such as a regional holding for financing.

points.point: Calculates treaty withholding of 500,000 (5% x 10,000,000) and notes the holding condition is met
Calculates domestic withholding of 3,000,000 (30%) and exposure of 2,500,000
Notes absence of a State S and State X treaty, so no fallback relief for the parent
Identifies other factors: domestic GAAR or substance rules, LOB, burden of proof, commercial purpose

items.prompt: (c) Advise Zephyr Group on the strength of State S's position, the points in its favour and against, and how it might reduce the risk in future structures.

answer.model: State S has a respectable case. The dividend is mostly passed on within 45 days, Vale's income is exempt in State M, the group interposed Vale after deciding to acquire Delta, and the saving is large at 2,500,000. Those facts suggest the benefit was a principal purpose of at least the interposition of Vale, which is enough under the PPT, not the sole purpose. For Zephyr: Vale has three local directors who take decisions, holds four other subsidiaries in the region, arranges local bank funding, and was acquired for a regional reorganisation planned before the State S investment, which indicates a genuine commercial purpose. The PPT does not apply merely because the structure saves tax; the object and purpose exception applies if relief is consistent with treaty purposes, which include encouraging cross border investment, and the Commentary's examples show that a genuine regional holding with substance should qualify. The beneficial owner test is a separate question. Passing on the dividend as a dividend, rather than under a contractual obligation to pay the same amount, supports Vale's discretion. Advice for the future: build substance in State M with staff and decision making at the right level, keep documentary evidence of the commercial rationale before the investment, avoid automatic pass through, retain profits where commercially justified, consider an advance ruling or a request under Article 29(10), document the position in the treaty file, and consider the alternative of a direct investment from State X on the domestic rate if no treaty relief is justified. The outcome is therefore uncertain and fact specific; I would advise the group to expect a challenge, and to prepare evidence, with a prudent provision for the 2,500,000 difference.

points.point: Identifies facts supporting State S: rapid pass-through, exempt receipt in State M, timing of formation, size of saving
Identifies facts supporting the group: substance, local directors, other subsidiaries, planned regional rationale
Explains that PPT requires one of the principal purposes and the object and purpose exception, with a regional holding example
Distinguishes beneficial owner from the PPT
Gives practical advice: substance, evidence, avoid automatic pass-through, rulings or Article 29(10), alternative structures
Reaches a balanced, reasoned conclusion on the risk

answer.grader_note: Either outcome acceptable if reasoned. The question is designed so that the facts cut both ways.

title: Taxation, fundamental rights and State conduct
scenario: A commentator argues: "Human rights instruments were written for police stations and courtrooms, not for tax offices. They give taxpayers some procedural protection but do nothing to discipline how States design their tax systems, and international law offers no remedy against a State that lures mobile profits away from its neighbours with a very low rate."

items.prompt: (a) Explain how the European Convention on Human Rights and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights can apply to tax measures, giving examples of the rights most often engaged.

answer.model: Neither instrument contains a tax code, but both bite on how tax is assessed, enforced and shared. Under the European Convention, Article 1 of the First Protocol protects the peaceful enjoyment of possessions and expressly preserves the State's right to enforce laws to secure the payment of taxes. The Strasbourg Court therefore grants States a wide margin of appreciation on tax policy, but it asks whether the burden is proportionate and whether the individual bears an excessive burden. In N.K.M. v Hungary (2013) a very high severance tax imposed on a civil servant's pay-off was held to breach the Article, so the margin is wide but not unlimited. Article 6 guarantees a fair hearing. Ordinary tax assessments are generally outside the civil limb, but tax surcharges and penalties of a punitive and deterrent character fall within the criminal limb, as the Court held in Bendenoun v France (1994) and, with a softened approach for lower-level penalties, in Jussila v Finland (2006). Article 8 (private life, home and correspondence) is engaged by search and seizure, by bulk demands for taxpayer data and by exchange of information, which must have a legal basis and be proportionate. Article 14 prohibits discrimination in the enjoyment of Convention rights, and Article 4 of Protocol 7 (ne bis in idem) has been tested against dual tax and criminal proceedings, for example in A and B v Norway (2016). The ICCPR contains parallel guarantees: Article 14 (fair trial and equality before courts), Article 17 (privacy), Article 26 (equality before the law and non-discrimination) and Article 15 (no retrospective criminal penalty). There is no property right in the ICCPR. The key point is that the instruments regulate individual treatment and process, with substantive tax policy left largely to the legislature.

points.point: states that the ECHR and ICCPR contain no general tax provisions but apply to tax measures through general rights
identifies Article 1 of Protocol 1 (property) and that it preserves the State's right to enforce tax laws
explains the wide margin of appreciation and proportionality or excessive individual burden test, ideally with N.K.M. v Hungary
explains that Article 6 civil limb generally excludes ordinary tax assessments
explains that tax surcharges and penalties can be criminal charges (Bendenoun or Jussila or Engel criteria)
identifies Article 8 ECHR and Article 17 ICCPR for searches and information exchange, requiring legal basis and proportionality
identifies non-discrimination (ECHR Article 14 or ICCPR Article 26) and ne bis in idem (Protocol 7 Article 4)
identifies ICCPR Article 14 fair trial and notes that the ICCPR lacks a property right

answer.grader_note: Credit other correct cases or rights. Do not credit invented case holdings.

items.prompt: (b) Assess whether a State that adopts a very low corporate tax rate to attract mobile profits commits an internationally wrongful act, and what international regimes nevertheless respond to such conduct.

answer.model: State responsibility under customary international law, as codified in the ILC Articles on Responsibility of States for Internationally Wrongful Acts (2001), requires conduct attributable to the State that breaches an international obligation in force for it. The first question is therefore whether any obligation exists. Taxation is an exercise of sovereignty and there is no general customary rule that limits a State's choice of rate or base, nor a rule that requires a State to tax at a minimum level. A low rate is attributable to the State, but it breaches nothing unless a treaty says so. The commentator is accurate on this point. Arguments for a wider rule, based on the duty not to intervene in another State's affairs, or on abuse of rights, have little State practice behind them, because the effect of a low rate on a neighbour's base is a lawful consequence of the neighbour's own choices, and coercion is absent. Obligations can nevertheless arise from specific sources. Treaty-based examples include the law of the European Union (State aid rules for selective measures, and the Code of Conduct on business taxation, which is political commitment rather than law) and trade agreements where the measure is a prohibited export subsidy. In the OECD context the 1998 report on harmful tax competition, the Forum on Harmful Tax Practices and the BEPS Action 5 minimum standard on preferential regimes (nexus approach for IP regimes, transparency on rulings) operate through peer review and the Inclusive Framework, which is soft law, though its effects are real because of the threat of defensive measures. Pillar Two, through the global minimum tax, now responds to low rates through top-up taxes rather than through any finding of unlawfulness. Overall, the conduct is lawful in itself, and international regimes work by cooperation and counter-measures.

points.point: identifies State responsibility requires attributable conduct breaching an international obligation (ARSIWA)
states that tax rate and base are matters of sovereignty and there is no general customary limit on low rates
evaluates and rejects or qualifies arguments from non-intervention or abuse of rights
identifies treaty-based obligations such as EU State aid or trade rules as possible sources of illegality
identifies OECD harmful tax practices work (1998 report, FHTP) and BEPS Action 5 as peer-review soft law
identifies Pillar Two or defensive measures as responses that do not depend on unlawfulness
reaches a reasoned conclusion that the conduct is not in itself wrongful absent a specific obligation

items.prompt: (c) Critically evaluate the claim that human rights law offers little to discipline State tax policy, and consider whether it could or should be developed to do more, whether on the design of tax systems or on tax competition.

answer.model: The claim is largely right about positive tax design but overstated overall. Courts defer to legislatures because tax raising involves distributive choices, expertise and democratic accountability, which explains the wide margin of appreciation. Extreme cases such as N.K.M. show a ceiling exists, but it is high and rarely reached, so rights give little guidance on rates, bases or the balance between direct and indirect taxes. Where rights bite is process (fair hearing, penalties, privacy and data protection in information exchange, retrospective legislation) and discrimination, for example on grounds of nationality or sex in the tax code. That matters in practice because automatic exchange regimes, tax investigations and penalty systems depend on legal safeguards, and a taxpayer can use these rights to challenge procedure. The case for development is stronger at the level of economic and social rights. Under the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights each State must use its maximum available resources to progressively realise rights, and it is argued that aggressive tax competition, abuse and illicit financial flows reduce those resources, so that low-tax practice can be linked to rights outcomes, including extraterritorially through the idea of obligations of cooperation. Counter-arguments are significant: causation is difficult to prove because spending choices and corruption matter as much as revenue; extraterritorial obligations on tax are contested; and the ICESCR obligation is progressive and non-justiciable in most systems. There is also a risk that an expanded rights approach would constrain legitimate competition and tax sovereignty of developing States, which rely on incentives. My conclusion is that rights are best used as a procedural and non-discrimination floor, with soft-law and treaty regimes (OECD, UN) doing the real work on competition, but that reporting and monitoring on the impact of tax practices on rights would be a realistic and valuable development, in preference to a new justiciable duty.

points.point: explains why courts defer to legislatures on tax design (margin of appreciation, distributive choices)
accepts that rights offer little on rates and bases, with extreme cases as a ceiling
identifies that rights are effective on procedure, penalties, privacy and discrimination, with practical examples
identifies economic and social rights (ICESCR) and the maximum available resources argument for linking tax competition to rights
considers extraterritorial obligations and cooperation arguments
identifies counter-arguments: causation, progressive and non-justiciable nature, risk to developing States and legitimate competition
gives a reasoned conclusion on what development, if any, is realistic

answer.grader_note: Candidates may reach a different conclusion if argued with authority. Credit balance more than the direction taken.

title: Consumption taxes and the rules of international trade
scenario: State X zero-rates exports under its value added tax and taxes imports at the border at the same rate as domestic supplies. State Y has no value added tax but a corporate income tax, and rebates part of that tax on exports. The Government of Y says it is doing no more than State X. A trade partner of Y disagrees.

items.prompt: (a) Explain the origin and destination principles for consumption taxes and how a value added tax is designed to give effect to the destination principle in cross-border trade.

answer.model: Under the destination principle consumption is taxed in the jurisdiction in which the goods or services are finally consumed, regardless of where they were produced. Under the origin principle the jurisdiction where production or supply takes place taxes it. The destination principle is dominant in practice because it preserves competitive neutrality: all goods sold on a market bear that market's tax, whether imported or local, and a State cannot gain by lowering its consumption tax to subsidise its producers abroad. The origin principle would distort the location of production and would give tax revenue to the State of production rather than the State where the burden is intended to fall. A value added tax gives effect to destination in three ways. Exports are zero-rated, so that no tax is charged on the supply but the exporter recovers input tax, giving a fully relieved export. Imports bear tax at the border or through a reverse charge at the same rate as domestic supplies, so that the burden on the imported item matches the local one. For services and intangibles, the place of supply rules allocate the right to the State of consumption, normally the customer's location for business to business supplies and a proxy for the consumer's usual residence for business to consumer supplies. The OECD International VAT/GST Guidelines (2017) express this approach, recommend neutrality, and favour the jurisdiction of the customer for business to business services. A retail sales tax operates similarly through exemptions for sales for resale or export, and the effects are the same though there is a different collection point. Neither system is perfect: cross-border online sales, small consignments and imports for consumer use need special registration and collection regimes.

explains neutrality or competitive reasons for the dominance of destination
explains zero-rating of exports with recovery of input tax
explains taxing imports at the border or by reverse charge at the same rate as domestic supplies
explains place of supply rules for services, B2B (customer location) and B2C

items.prompt: (b) Explain how GATT and GATS treat border tax adjustments for indirect and direct taxes, and assess the position of State Y in the light of the WTO disputes on tax rebates.

answer.model: GATT Article III:2 requires that imported products are not subject to internal taxes in excess of those applied to like domestic products, and the Japan Alcoholic Beverages II case (1996) read this with directly competitive or substitutable products in mind. Article II:2(a) allows a charge equivalent to an internal tax to be imposed on imports. The Agreement on Subsidies and Countervailing Measures defines as a prohibited export subsidy the full or partial exemption, remission or deferral of direct taxes specifically related to exports, while the remission or exemption of indirect taxes on exported products beyond those levied on the product sold domestically is also prohibited, but the remission of indirect taxes in line with the amount levied on like products for domestic consumption is not a subsidy (the Illustrative List of Export Subsidies in Annex I to the SCM Agreement and its footnotes). The result is an asymmetry: border adjustment is tolerated for indirect taxes and not for direct taxes. Under State Y's system the corporate income tax is a direct tax, and a rebate linked to exports looks like a prohibited export subsidy, subject to the argument that it is a refund of some other tax. The United States foreign sales corporation regime was found by WTO panels and the Appellate Body to involve prohibited export subsidies in the United States Foreign Sales Corporations dispute (1999 to 2002), which is the best authority for a direct tax measure. Under GATS, Article XVII national treatment applies to services, and Article XIV(d) allows differences in treatment where aimed at the equitable or effective imposition or collection of direct taxes, which confirms that direct taxes receive special treatment but only within limits. State Y's claim that it does no more than X is therefore weak, because the legal characterisation of the tax decides the question, not the economic effect.

points.point: explains GATT Article III:2 national treatment for internal taxes and like or directly competitive products
explains that border tax adjustments for indirect taxes on exports and imports are permitted (Article II:2(a) and SCM Annex I)
explains that exemption or remission of direct taxes related to exports is a prohibited export subsidy
identifies the asymmetry between indirect and direct taxes
cites the US Foreign Sales Corporation dispute (or another correct WTO dispute) as authority on direct tax
explains the GATS provisions: national treatment and the Article XIV(d) direct tax exception
applies the analysis to State Y with a reasoned conclusion that characterisation is decisive

answer.grader_note: Do not require exact article numbers within the SCM Agreement. Credit the principle.

items.prompt: (c) Critically evaluate whether the distinction between direct and indirect taxes for border adjustment purposes is economically justified, and discuss how digital trade and proposals for a destination-based income tax test it.

answer.model: The traditional justification is that indirect taxes are borne by consumers and are passed forward in prices, so an exemption of exports only relieves the consumption tax of the exporting State, while a direct tax on income is borne by the owners or workers of a firm and is not shifted into the price, so a rebate would be a true subsidy. Many economists dispute this. Corporate income tax is likely to be shifted partly to workers, customers or investors, while a value added tax may be borne by sellers who cannot raise price in competitive markets, and the incidence of both depends on elasticities and exchange rates. Theory also suggests that a uniform destination-based tax is equivalent to a uniform origin-based tax once exchange rates or wages adjust, so the practical justification for adjusting indirect taxes rests more on legal and administrative convenience and on the wish to avoid double taxation and under-taxation than on incidence. Against this, the distinction has clear practical advantages: border adjustment under a VAT is mechanical, auditable through invoices, and has been accepted for decades, whereas adjusting an income tax would need a view on what part of a firm's profit relates to exports. Digital trade shows a different strain: intangible supplies are hard to locate, and the destination principle for value added tax is now applied through registration and collection by non-resident suppliers, with the OECD Guidelines promoting the customer location. For direct taxes, proposals for a destination-based cash flow tax would exempt export revenue and deny deduction for imported inputs, which replicates a VAT in part, and supporters say it would stop profit shifting. Critics say it would clash with the WTO rule on direct tax adjustment, as the border treatment would be a prohibited subsidy under current wording, and would be hard to fit with treaty rules on business profits and with exchange-rate assumptions. My assessment is that the distinction is difficult to defend economically but it remains a settled trade law rule, so any reform of income taxes to a destination basis would need either WTO reform or a defence based on equivalence to a consumption tax, neither of which is assured.

points.point: explains the traditional incidence rationale (indirect taxes passed to the consumer, direct taxes not)
critically challenges the rationale (shifting of corporate tax, incidence depends on market conditions)
explains the equivalence of destination and origin taxes under exchange-rate or wage adjustment, or the legal and administrative rationale
identifies administrative advantages of invoice-based VAT adjustment
explains difficulty of locating digital supplies and the registration or collection solution
explains a destination-based cash flow tax and the WTO objection
