title: Where income is taxed: source rules and their collisions
scenario: "A State taxes non-residents on income from sources within its territory, yet the concept of source is not defined by any international rule. Each State defines it in the way that suits its revenue, and the consequence is that the same item can have two sources, or none."

items.prompt: (a) Describe the main source rules used in State practice for the principal categories of income and gains, and explain why they differ.

answer.model: Source rules usually follow a link to either the place where an economic activity or asset is located, or the place where the payer or benefit is located. For employment income the usual rule is that the income arises where the employment is exercised, with some States adding a rule for directors' fees by reference to the residence of the company. For business profits the source is the place where the business activity is carried on or where a permanent establishment is located, though some States tax profits on sales or services where the customer is located. For dividends the rule is generally the residence of the paying company. For interest, one family of States uses the residence of the payer and another the place where the borrowed funds are used or where the debt is secured. Royalties follow either the residence of the payer, the place where the intangible is used, or the place where the right is exercised. Income from immovable property is sourced where the property is situated. Gains on immovable property and on shares deriving their value from it follow the same logic, and gains on other assets are sourced by residence of the seller in some systems and by situs of the asset in others. Fees for services may be sourced where the work is performed, where the benefit is received, or by the residence of the payer. The differences arise because each rule serves different aims: to tax activities that use the State's infrastructure, to protect a deduction base where the payer deducts the payment, to reduce administrative cost by using the payer as withholding agent, and to preserve revenue. Developing States tend to favour wider source rules, including use or payment, as they are more often net importers of capital and services, which is also the policy reflected in some UN Model provisions.

points.point: states the principle that sources follow location of activity, asset, payer or use
employment: where exercised
business profits: place of activity or permanent establishment
dividends: residence of the payer
interest and royalties: payer residence versus place of use, with the divergence identified
immovable property and gains: situs; other gains vary between residence of seller and location
explains differences by policy: administrative convenience, deduction protection, capital importing versus exporting positions

items.prompt: (b) Explain how conflicts of source arise and how they may result in double taxation, and how tax treaties and domestic relief mechanisms respond.

answer.model: A conflict of source arises when two States each treat the same income as arising in their own territory. A typical example is interest paid by a company resident in State R to a lender in State S for a loan whose proceeds are used in State T. State R sources it by payer residence, State T by use, and both may levy withholding tax. The resident State of the lender gives a foreign tax credit only for tax on foreign-source income as defined by its own law, so if it regards the interest as arising in State R and nowhere else it may deny credit for State T's tax, leaving unrelieved double taxation. A second source of conflict arises where a State's source rule gives a different characterisation of the item, for example a payment as a royalty in one State and as business profits in another. Treaties respond by allocation rules that fix the right to tax regardless of domestic source rules. Under the OECD Model, Article 11(5) deems interest to arise in the State where the payer is resident, unless it is borne by a permanent establishment, in which case it arises where the establishment is situated, and the UN Model has equivalent wording. Article 12 of the OECD Model gives exclusive taxing rights on royalties to the State of residence, while the UN Model allows source taxation. Articles 23A and 23B oblige the residence State to relieve double taxation, and the Commentary addresses conflicts arising from differences in domestic law, including the view that the residence State should follow the source State's interpretation of facts or treaty provisions where the source State applies the treaty in accordance with its own reading. Where no treaty exists, relief depends on unilateral credit or exemption provisions, which may be limited by domestic source rules, and the mutual agreement procedure is not available. Source conflicts are therefore best resolved by treaty source rules, with domestic re-sourcing rules as a supplement.

points.point: explains conflict of source as two States each claiming the income arises in their territory
gives a correct example, such as interest sourced by payer residence in one State and place of use in another
explains that credit relief depends on the foreign source characterisation under domestic law, leading to unrelieved double taxation
identifies conflict of characterisation between States
explains treaty source rules, such as OECD Article 11(5) or UN equivalent, and Article 12 differences
explains Articles 23A and 23B relief, the Commentary on conflicts, and absence of treaty relief where no treaty exists

items.prompt: (c) Critically evaluate whether source rules need to be harmonised or redefined for modern business, including digital services, and discuss the UN Model's approach to fees for technical services and automated digital services (state which edition you use: the 2021 edition has Articles 12A and 12B, the 2025 edition has Articles 12AA and 12B).

answer.model: The argument for harmonisation is that unrelieved double taxation and double non-taxation both result from divergent rules, and that the digital economy makes the location of activity, the user, the asset and the customer easy to dispute. A shared definition would provide certainty and reduce disputes. The arguments against are strong. Source rules are an exercise of sovereignty, they reflect the position of each State as a capital importer or exporter, and agreement would likely settle on lowest common denominator rules, which could favour residence States. The OECD Model has historically limited source taxation of services and royalties, preferring residence taxation and the permanent establishment threshold, while the UN Model, which gives more weight to source taxation, includes Article 12A (technical services fees, added in the 2017 update; UN Model 2021 numbering, replaced together with Article 14 by a single Article 12AA on fees for any service in the UN Model 2025) allowing a withholding tax on fees for technical, managerial or consultancy services irrespective of presence, and Article 12B (automated digital services, added in the 2021 update and retained with the same number in the UN Model 2025) which allows source taxation of income from automated digital services at a gross or net election. The UN approach illustrates that a State can expand source taxation by treaty, and it responds to the claim that an enterprise can earn income from a market without any presence. The OECD Pillar One work (Amount A), which would reallocate a part of residual profit to market jurisdictions but whose multilateral convention was never opened for signature, is another proposed response to the same issue. Weaknesses of the UN approach include the use of gross-based withholding with the potential for over-taxation, the definitional difficulties of automated digital services, the risk of double taxation where residence States do not give credit, and adoption only where bilateral treaties include it. My conclusion is that full harmonisation is unrealistic, but a convergence on market-based sourcing for highly digitalised services is under way through different instruments, and the best policy would combine clearer definitions with net basis taxation, to reduce disputes and over-taxation, while recognising that the decisive questions are distributive rather than technical.

points.point: explains the case for harmonisation (certainty, disputes, double taxation, double non-taxation)
explains the case against (sovereignty, capital importer versus exporter positions, lowest common denominator)
describes UN Model Article 12A (fees for technical services, UN Model 2021 numbering, replaced by Article 12AA in the UN Model 2025) correctly
describes UN Model Article 12B (automated digital services) correctly
mentions OECD Pillar One or another alternative response
assesses weaknesses of the UN approach (gross basis, definitions, credit, bilateral adoption)
gives a reasoned conclusion

answer.grader_note: The UN Model update in which 12A was added is the 2017 update and 12B the 2021 update; the UN Model 2025 replaced 12A (and Article 14) with Article 12AA. Accept either numbering if the candidate names the edition, and accept general wording if dates are omitted.

title: Dividends from Mirro Co through Kestrel Holdings
scenario: Mirro Co is resident in State R and operates manufacturing plants there. On 1 July 2026 Kestrel Holdings Ltd, resident in State H, acquired 30% of the capital and voting rights of Mirro Co. Kestrel is a wholly-owned subsidiary of Parent Plc, resident in State P, and bought the shares with a 6,000,000 loan from Parent Plc (all amounts are illustrative currency units). On 15 March 2027 Mirro Co paid a dividend of 2,000,000 to Kestrel. Kestrel rents a small office, has two part-time directors who take decisions for it in State H, and holds a small portfolio of other shares, but 95% of its income in the year is the Mirro dividend. Within 30 days of receipt Kestrel paid 1,800,000 (90% of the dividend) to Parent Plc as interest on the loan, at a rate fixed in the loan agreement of 2026. State H does not tax dividends received by a company from a 25% holding and does not levy withholding tax on interest paid abroad. State R's domestic law imposes withholding tax of 30% on dividends paid to non-residents. Parent Plc says it holds the Mirro shares through Kestrel for commercial reasons connected with State H's banking facilities, and Kestrel has no plan to dispose of the shares. Mirro Co asks what withholding tax it must deduct.

exhibits.caption: Paraphrased dividend articles of the two treaties (illustrative; each is based on Article 10 of the OECD Model)
Both treaties contain a principal purposes test modelled on Article 29(9) of the OECD Model

items.prompt: (a) Calculate the withholding tax on the 2,000,000 dividend under (i) State R's domestic law, (ii) the State R and State H treaty at each of the two rates, and (iii) the State R and State P treaty if Parent Plc had held the 30% directly. State the number of days that Kestrel had held the shares on 15 March 2027 (counting both 1 July 2026 and 15 March 2027) and whether the 365 day period was complete at that date.

answer.model: (i) Domestic: 30% × 2,000,000 = 600,000. (ii) State R and State H treaty: at 5%, 2,000,000 × 5% = 100,000; at 15%, 2,000,000 × 15% = 300,000. (iii) State R and State P treaty if Parent Plc held directly: 30% holding is at least 10%, so the 10% rate applies, 2,000,000 × 10% = 200,000. Holding period: July 31 + August 31 + September 30 + October 31 + November 30 + December 31 = 184 days to the end of 2026; January 31 + February 28 = 59, giving 243; plus 15 days of March = 258 days counting both end dates. The shortfall against 365 days is 365 − 258 = 107 days, so the period was not complete at the date of payment, although the 365 day period only has to include the date of payment and the holding could be completed by 30 June 2027. The 25% capital condition is met, as the holding is 30%.

points.point: domestic withholding 600,000
treaty R-H at 5% is 100,000
treaty R-H at 15% is 300,000
treaty R-P at 10% is 200,000, with identification that the 30% holding exceeds 10%
holding period 258 days
period incomplete by 107 days at payment
notes that the test requires a period including the date of payment so it could be satisfied later, and that the 25% threshold is met

answer.grader_note: Accept 257 days if the candidate counts only one end date and states the convention.

items.prompt: (b) Discuss whether Kestrel is the beneficial owner of the dividend, taking account of the arguments on both sides.

answer.model: The term beneficial owner in Article 10 was introduced to deny treaty relief to a conduit that receives a dividend as an agent or nominee, or acts as a mere intermediary with limited powers. The OECD Commentary, in its 2003 and later revisions, states that the concept is not limited by domestic law meaning and is to be read in context and in light of the treaty's object and purpose, and that a recipient does not qualify if its right to use and enjoy the dividend is constrained by a contractual or legal obligation to pass the payment on to another person. This treatment was confirmed in the Indofood decision of the English Court of Appeal in 2006 (the beneficial owner is a person who receives for his own benefit and not as a conduit), the Prevost Car case in Canada, which held that a holding company was the beneficial owner as it had discretion over the dividend and was not a mere agent, and the Danish beneficial ownership cases (CJEU 2019), in which the Court said that a conduit company which passes dividends on without being able to use and enjoy them is not the beneficial owner, and that an abuse can be established by a combination of factors such as the pass-through of the income shortly after its receipt. For the taxpayer: Kestrel has a legal existence, an office, directors who decide in State H, and some other investments; its obligation to Parent is under a loan agreement that predates the dividend, creates an ordinary debtor and creditor relationship, and does not oblige it to pass on the dividend itself; the dividend and interest are separate cash flows, and the payment of interest by a holding company out of whatever income it has is normal. For the tax authority: 90% of the dividend was paid to Parent within 30 days, 95% of the income comes from Mirro, the business is thin, the payment of interest is out of proportion to the other income, State H does not tax either flow, and the loan was apparently used to buy the very shares. The Commentary says that a pass through is relevant where it is a contractual or legal obligation or where facts show that the recipient has in substance no right to use and enjoy; it does not treat servicing a loan as a conduit automatically, since a debtor in the ordinary course repays its creditor. My assessment is that the better view is that Kestrel's position is arguable but vulnerable: the fixed loan terms and genuine debt support its status as beneficial owner, but the timing, the 90% pass-through, minimal substance and the absence of other income would persuade many authorities and courts to treat it as a conduit, particularly with the Danish cases in view. The result depends on evidence, including whether the loan was commercial, whether Kestrel could have used the funds otherwise and how directors actually decided.

points.point: states the purpose of the beneficial owner requirement (denying relief to conduits, agents or nominees)
states that the Commentary treats beneficial ownership as an international and not a domestic law concept, with obligation to pass on as the key test
cites Indofood or Prevost Car or the Danish cases correctly
identifies facts for the taxpayer: substance, separate loan agreement, ordinary debtor creditor relationship
identifies facts against: 90 percent pass-through within 30 days, concentrated income, thin business, no tax in State H
recognises that servicing a loan is not automatically conduit behaviour
reaches a reasoned conclusion that depends on evidence

answer.grader_note: Both conclusions can be credited if the analysis is balanced. A candidate who ignores the facts that cut the other way gets no more than half marks for the analysis.

items.prompt: (c) Advise Mirro Co on the withholding tax it should apply and on the other points that State R's authority could raise, including the minimum holding period and the principal purposes test.

answer.model: Mirro Co is the withholding agent and bears liability if it deducts too little, so it should be cautious. The 25% capital condition is met, but the holding period condition in the paraphrased treaty requires a 365 day period that includes the date of payment. On 15 March 2027 Kestrel had held for 258 days. On the wording of the paraphrased treaty (a 365 day period that includes the day of payment) the period need not end before the payment, so the condition can still be satisfied if Kestrel holds until 30 June 2027, though practice varies and some States require the period to be complete before relief applies, so I would treat this as less certain. In practice Mirro Co has three options: deduct at 15%, 300,000, and let Kestrel claim a refund of the excess of 200,000 once the period is complete and beneficial ownership is established; deduct at 5%, 100,000, with a written confirmation from Kestrel and a risk of a later assessment on Mirro for the shortfall of 200,000 against the 15% rate; or deduct at the State P treaty rate of 10%, 200,000, only if Parent could be treated as holding the shares directly, which the 'directly' condition in Table 1 makes doubtful (otherwise 15% applies). Even if Kestrel meets the beneficial owner test, the principal purposes test may apply, as the structure was put in place with a loan from Parent and the stated reasons (banking facilities) do not explain the choice of Kestrel as holder rather than Parent. If the test is applied, the benefit of the R-H treaty can be denied, but the taxpayer may argue that Parent would have been entitled to an equivalent benefit under another treaty, here State P at 10% if it held directly, although the Commentary treats this as one factor and not a safe harbour, so the proper result would be 200,000 rather than 600,000 domestic tax. A State R authority could also apply domestic anti-avoidance rules, and could raise the interest deduction and the withholding rules for the interest leg. I would advise deducting at 15% (300,000) as the prudent course, documenting the facts, and noting that if Kestrel keeps the shares until 30 June 2027 and the beneficial owner and purposes questions are resolved, a refund of 100,000 to 200,000 could be claimed, depending on the final rate (200,000 refund at 5%, or 100,000 if 10% applies).

points.point: identifies that Mirro Co is the withholding agent with liability for under-deduction
identifies that the 25% capital condition is met but the 365 day condition is not complete at payment
explains the point that the period need only include the payment date and may be completed later, noting uncertainty in practice
sets out options: 15% with refund, 5% at risk, or alternatively 10% under the P treaty
explains the principal purposes test and its application to the structure
explains that an equivalent benefit under another treaty may be argued (State P at 10%)
gives a reasoned recommendation with correct amounts (300,000 withheld, refund of 200,000 or 100,000)

answer.grader_note: Accept any reasoned recommendation that gives correct arithmetic. 300,000 minus 100,000 = 200,000 refund at 5%; 300,000 minus 200,000 = 100,000 refund at 10%.

title: Two structures of the Veldt Group
scenario: The Veldt Group is headed by Veldt Holdings, resident in State P. All amounts are illustrative currency units and none of State P, State L, State B or State S has yet introduced rules following the OECD report on hybrid mismatch arrangements (Action 2 of the BEPS project), and none has updated their legislation for the structures below. Structure 1: in Year 1 Lender Co, a wholly-owned subsidiary of Veldt Holdings resident in State L, subscribed 20,000,000 for a perpetual instrument issued by Borrower Co, a wholly-owned subsidiary resident in State B. The instrument pays an annual return of 5%, which is 1,000,000 a year, payable only if Borrower has distributable profits. State B treats the instrument as debt and allows the 1,000,000 as a deduction at its corporate rate of 25%. State L treats it as equity, and the return is a dividend that is fully exempt under its participation exemption. Structure 2: Veldt Holdings owns Subco in State S. Subco is a company under State S law and is taxed there as a resident company, but State P treats it as transparent under an election, so State P taxes Veldt Holdings on Subco's income as if earned directly. Subco borrowed 5,000,000 from an unrelated bank at 4%, which is 200,000 a year of interest. Subco has operating income of 120,000 a year before interest. State S allows the interest as a deduction against Subco's income. State P, through the look-through, allows Veldt Holdings to deduct the same interest against its other taxable income, at State P's rate of 30%. Veldt Holdings asks what the rules in the Action 2 report would do to the two structures.

exhibits.caption: Summary of Structure 1 and Structure 2 (illustrative)

items.prompt: (a) Quantify the mismatches in each structure: the deduction without inclusion in Structure 1, and the double deduction in Structure 2, identifying the dual inclusion income and the amount that would be denied under the Action 2 rules, and calculate the extra tax in each State if the denial applies.

answer.model: Structure 1: Borrower deducts 1,000,000 and Lender includes nothing (the dividend is exempt), so the deduction without inclusion mismatch is 1,000,000. If the deduction is denied in State B, the extra taxable profit is 1,000,000 and the extra tax is 25% × 1,000,000 = 250,000. Structure 2: the same interest of 200,000 is deducted twice, once in State S (against Subco income) and once in State P (through the look-through). The dual inclusion income is the income that is included in both States: Subco's operating income of 120,000 is taxed in State S as Subco's own income and in State P as Veldt Holdings' income through the look-through, so dual inclusion income is 120,000. Under the Action 2 hybrid entity rule the double deduction is permitted only up to the dual inclusion income, so the excess is 200,000 − 120,000 = 80,000. If State P denies the deduction of that excess, the extra taxable income in State P is 80,000 and the extra tax is 30% × 80,000 = 24,000. The 80,000 may normally be carried forward and set against future dual inclusion income.

points.point: Structure 1 mismatch is 1,000,000 (deduction, no inclusion)
extra tax of 250,000 in State B (25% × 1,000,000)
identifies the double deduction of 200,000 in Structure 2
identifies dual inclusion income as 120,000 and explains why (income included in both States)
excess deduction of 80,000 (200,000 − 120,000)
extra tax in State P of 24,000 (30% × 80,000)
states that denied excess can be carried forward against future dual inclusion income

answer.grader_note: Accept a reasoned alternative if the candidate states that the denial falls on State S instead; the amount is the same but the tax rate differs.

items.prompt: (b) Explain which State applies the primary rule and which State applies the defensive rule in each structure, and what each rule requires.

answer.model: The Action 2 report recommends a linking rule in which one State's treatment follows the other's, with a primary rule and a defensive rule. In Structure 1, which is a hybrid financial instrument producing a deduction without inclusion between related parties (Lender and Borrower are in the same group, passing the 25% relatedness threshold in the report), the primary rule applies in the payer State: State B should deny the deduction to the extent of the mismatch, which is the full 1,000,000. If State B has not enacted the rule, the defensive rule applies in the payee State: State L should include the payment in ordinary income to the extent that it was deductible in State B, and it should override its participation exemption for this purpose. Here neither State has legislated, so there is no response and the mismatch continues unless State P or another State has an imported mismatch rule. In Structure 2, a hybrid entity gives rise to a double deduction. The primary rule applies in the parent State: State P, as the State that gets the second deduction through the look-through, should deny the deduction to the extent that it exceeds dual inclusion income, which here is 120,000, so the excess to be denied is 80,000. The defensive rule applies in the subsidiary State: if State P does not deny it, State S should deny the deduction in Subco to the same extent. The rules differ in that the primary rule for the double deduction sits with the parent State, while for the deduction without inclusion rule it is with the payer State. The linking is achieved by looking to what the other State does, and there is no obligation to look at what a State in a third country does except under imported mismatch rules. Both rules apply only to the extent of the mismatch, and timing differences that reverse within a period are not caught. An example of implementation is the EU Anti-Tax Avoidance Directive 2 (2017), which applies the same sequence, but I should state that the specific wording differs between the report and each State's legislation.

points.point: explains the linking rule and the order primary rule then defensive rule
Structure 1: identifies a hybrid financial instrument between related parties meeting the relatedness test
Structure 1: primary rule in payer State B denies the deduction (full 1,000,000)
Structure 1: defensive rule in State L includes the payment in income, overriding the exemption
Structure 2: primary rule in parent State P denies the deduction above dual inclusion income
Structure 2: defensive rule in State S denies the deduction in Subco
notes that rules apply only to the extent of the mismatch and that none applies here until States legislate
mentions implementation such as ATAD2 or Part 6A TIOPA, or imported mismatch rules

answer.grader_note: Avoid crediting recommendation numbers; the substance is what matters.

items.prompt: (c) Advise Veldt Holdings on the limits of the Action 2 rules as they could apply to these structures and on the risks of relying on them remaining unaffected by legislative change in State B and State S.

answer.model: Veldt Holdings should not treat the present legislative gap as stable. Both States may adopt the rules, and many have done so, in which case the group faces denial of 1,000,000 of deductions in Structure 1 (a cost of 250,000 per year at State B's rate) and 80,000 of deductions in Structure 2 (24,000 per year in State P). Limits of the rules also matter. They apply to related parties (25% threshold, including parties acting together) and to structured arrangements, so a fully unrelated lender would be outside Structure 1 unless the arrangement is structured. The hybrid financial instrument rule applies to payments under a financial instrument, and there is an exception where the mismatch is due to the payee's circumstances such as a tax exempt status, rather than the terms of the instrument. Timing differences are tolerated where the payment is included within a reasonable period, which in some implementations is 12 months. The double deduction rule in Structure 2 does not apply to the extent of dual inclusion income, which is why 120,000 is allowed. An imported mismatch rule can deny a deduction where a hybrid arises elsewhere in the chain, so intragroup financing is exposed in other States. Interaction with treaties is also relevant: the 2017 OECD Model Article 1(2) deals with transparent entities and governs whether Veldt Holdings can claim benefits for income earned through a fiscally transparent Subco. The Action 2 rules also overlap with general anti-avoidance rules and with the principal purposes test. My advice is to restructure to remove the mismatches (for example, make the instrument debt for both States or equity for both; elect that Subco is treated consistently in State P and State S), to quantify the exposure, and to avoid relying on a transitional gap, which could result in assessments, interest, penalties, and unfavourable reputational consequences. I would also review the group under the global minimum tax and any other changes as the reporting and deduction positions interact.

points.point: advises that the legislative gap is unlikely to be stable and quantifies the exposure (250,000 and 24,000 per year)
identifies relatedness (25%) and structured arrangement limits
identifies exceptions or limits: payee circumstances, timing differences, dual inclusion income
identifies imported mismatch rules as a further risk
identifies interaction with treaties (OECD Article 1(2) and transparent entities) or general anti-avoidance rules
recommends restructuring and gives a reasoned conclusion

answer.grader_note: Credit any reasoned advice. The figures must be consistent with part (a).

title: Treaties inside the domestic legal order
scenario: A finance minister of State R tells parliament: 'Our tax treaties bind us in international law, but what a taxpayer can actually claim depends on our own constitution and on what we legislate later. Where a later Act conflicts with a treaty, parliament is entitled to have the last word.' A colleague replies that the treaty network is only as credible as the State's willingness to honour it.

items.prompt: (a) Explain how a tax treaty may be incorporated into domestic law under monist and dualist approaches, and why the approach matters to a taxpayer who wishes to rely on the treaty.

answer.model: In a monist system international law and domestic law form one legal order. A treaty, once validly concluded and ratified, takes effect domestically without a separate statute, is often directly applicable to the extent its terms are sufficiently precise, and in many monist States ranks above ordinary legislation. A taxpayer may then invoke an Article of the treaty directly before a tax authority or court, and a conflicting earlier domestic rule is displaced. In a dualist system treaties bind the State internationally but have no domestic effect until parliament enacts them, usually by a short Act giving the treaty the force of law or by a general provision in the income tax code authorising the executive to make treaties effective by order. The taxpayer relies on the enacting provision, not on the treaty as such, and the domestic hierarchy decides the outcome. Intermediate positions exist: some States give treaties the force of law but rank them equal to statute, so that the later in time prevails under the lex posterior rule; others, by constitutional or statutory rule, give treaties priority over later statute or require a later Act to express an intention to override. The approach matters because it determines (i) whether the treaty can be relied on directly, (ii) its rank against domestic law, (iii) how it is interpreted, since a dualist court may read the enacting Act and the treaty together, and (iv) what relief is available if domestic law is later amended. Treaties generally limit taxing rights and do not create them, so in most systems a treaty can only reduce domestic liability, which is a further reason why the taxpayer, not the authority, normally invokes it. A conclusion that the incorporation method is a matter of domestic law is correct, but the State remains internationally responsible for performance whichever method it chooses (Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, Articles 26 and 27).

points.point: explains the monist approach: treaty part of domestic law on ratification, often directly applicable and ranked above statute
explains the dualist approach: legislation or an enabling provision is needed to give domestic effect
notes intermediate positions, e.g. treaty has statutory force but later statute may prevail unless the legislature expresses override
explains consequences for the taxpayer: ability to invoke the treaty directly, ranking, interpretation
notes treaties normally restrict and do not create taxing rights, and that international responsibility persists whichever method is used (VCLT Arts 26 and 27)

answer.grader_note: Credit accurate use of examples from any named jurisdiction only if correct. Do not credit statements that treaties automatically override domestic law everywhere.

items.prompt: (b) Discuss what is meant by treaty override, whether it is lawful in international law, and how the Commentary to the OECD Model deals with the issue.

answer.model: Treaty override occurs where a State enacts domestic legislation that, expressly or in effect, applies in a manner inconsistent with a treaty it has concluded, so that a rule the treaty would restrict is applied regardless. Examples include a later anti-abuse rule declared to apply 'notwithstanding any tax treaty', a change in the definition of residence that cuts across treaty tie-breakers, or a withholding tax applied in breach of a reduced treaty rate. Override may be express, where the Act states it prevails, or implied, where the court concludes from later in time and clear purpose that parliament intended to depart from the treaty. In international law the answer is clear: pacta sunt servanda (VCLT Article 26) requires treaties in force to be performed in good faith, and Article 27 provides that a party may not invoke its internal law as justification for failure to perform. Override therefore breaches international law and engages State responsibility, although the practical remedies are limited to diplomatic protest, termination or suspension, or dispute settlement where available. Domestically, in a dualist system or one where treaty and statute rank equally, the court may be bound to apply the later statute, while in systems giving constitutional priority to treaties the override fails. The OECD Commentary (Introduction to the Model and the Commentary on Article 1, on improper use of the Convention) recognises the problem, takes the view that a State acts inconsistently with the treaty where domestic rules are applied in a manner contrary to it, and distinguishes override from the legitimate use of domestic anti-abuse rules that the Commentary accepts as consistent with treaties, in particular where the abuse is of domestic law. This distinction is the core of the debate on whether, say, a general anti-avoidance rule or controlled foreign company rule is override at all. A reasoned conclusion is that override is unlawful internationally yet practically tolerated, and that it undermines the certainty that treaties exist to provide, which is why many States accept limits through constitutional rules and why the MLI relied on agreed changes rather than unilateral action.

points.point: defines treaty override and gives an example (express or implied)
explains that override breaches pacta sunt servanda and the rule that internal law is no justification (VCLT Arts 26 and 27)
explains the domestic position: depends on rank, lex posterior, constitutional priority
explains the OECD Commentary position and the distinction between override and legitimate domestic anti-abuse rules
reaches a reasoned conclusion on legitimacy and practical consequences for certainty

answer.grader_note: Do not penalise a candidate who states that the Commentary does not itself prohibit unilateral legislation but regards the conduct as a treaty breach. Paragraph numbers are not required.

items.prompt: (c) Distinguish the main types of tax treaty and critically evaluate the factors that influence how a State negotiates a bilateral income tax treaty.

answer.model: Treaties vary by scope and parties. A comprehensive bilateral income (and often capital) tax treaty, built on the OECD or UN Model, allocates taxing rights across income categories and provides for relief, non discrimination and mutual agreement. Limited treaties cover one subject only, such as international shipping and air transport income, estate and inheritance tax, social security contributions, or exchange of information (TIEAs). Multilateral instruments are rarer: the Multilateral Convention to Implement Tax Treaty Related Measures to Prevent BEPS modifies many existing bilateral treaties at once and works by matching of elections, while the Convention on Mutual Administrative Assistance in Tax Matters covers cooperation. Regional or group treaties, for example within a customs union, also exist. Negotiation usually starts from a model: OECD, UN, a State's own model (such as the US or Dutch model) or a hybrid. The OECD Model favours residence taxation and low source rates, so it suits capital exporting, developed economies; the UN Model keeps more source taxation (a lower permanent establishment threshold such as the building site period, services PE provisions, Article 12A on technical fees and Article 14 on independent personal services, which are UN Model 2021 numbering; the UN Model 2025 deleted Article 14 and replaced Article 12A with Article 12AA on fees for services) and suits capital importers. Factors that shape the position include the balance of investment and trade flows, since a net capital importer wants higher withholding rates and a wider source concept; the revenue cost of concessions; the aim of attracting investment through lower rates or tax sparing; the domestic law constraints, including how the treaty is incorporated; the State's exposure to treaty shopping and its wish for anti abuse provisions such as a principal purpose test under MLI Article 7 or Article 29 of the OECD Model; and the policy on exchange of information and dispute resolution, including arbitration. Critically, bargaining power is unequal, models are starting points not rules, and a rate cut that suits investors may leak to third parties through conduit structures. A State that negotiates well links each concession to a measurable gain and checks the interaction with existing treaties, because a most favoured nation clause can extend a concession to others.

points.point: distinguishes comprehensive bilateral, limited scope treaties (e.g. shipping, estates, TIEAs) and multilateral instruments such as the MLI
explains the role of the OECD Model, UN Model and State models as starting points
identifies and explains at least three negotiation factors: capital flows, revenue cost, investment attraction, anti-abuse, exchange of information
evaluates critically: bargaining power, treaty shopping leakage, MFN effects
gives a reasoned conclusion or practical recommendation

answer.grader_note: Accept any sound set of factors. Do not credit invented treaty names.

title: Technology and the international tax system
scenario: A policy paper circulated in State S argues that crypto-assets, decentralised platforms and artificial intelligence expose three weaknesses in the international tax framework: taxpayers cannot be found, income cannot be located, and rules written for physical presence cannot be applied. The paper concludes that no new treaty rules are needed because existing concepts adapt.

items.prompt: (a) Discuss the principal tax challenges raised by crypto-assets for a tax authority, and explain the international response to the problem of information.

answer.model: Crypto-assets raise problems of characterisation, valuation, residence, source and compliance. A holding may be treated as property, a currency, an intangible or an investment, so the same transaction can produce capital gains, ordinary income or no taxable event, and the characterisation can differ between States, creating double taxation or double non taxation (for example on staking rewards or mining receipts). Valuation is hard because tokens trade on many venues at different prices, and the time of the taxable event, such as exchanging one token for another, may not involve fiat currency. Pseudonymous addresses and self hosted wallets mean the authority may not know who owns the assets, and cross border exchanges can lie outside its reach. Source and residence rules rely on a place of performance, payer or management, which are hard to apply to a distributed ledger. These weaknesses have encouraged under reporting. The international response has centred on transparency. The OECD developed the Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF), approved in 2022, under which reporting crypto-asset service providers collect information on users and transactions and the information is exchanged automatically between jurisdictions that implement it, following the model of the Common Reporting Standard. The CRS itself was amended at the same time so that certain electronic money products and central bank digital currencies are brought within reporting, and the amendments are intended to be applied in tandem with CARF. Participation depends on domestic legislation and a competent authority agreement, so coverage is uneven and implementation dates differ by State. A reasoned view is that reporting addresses visibility but not characterisation, so substantive rules on gains, income and valuation remain a domestic matter and an area of divergence.

points.point: identifies characterisation problems (property, currency, income) and resulting double taxation or non taxation
identifies valuation and timing issues, including token to token exchanges
identifies identification and pseudonymity problems and weak residence or source anchors
explains CARF: reporting service providers, automatic exchange modelled on the CRS
notes CRS amendments and that implementation is uneven and does not resolve substantive characterisation

answer.grader_note: Do not require dates or numbers of participating States. A candidate who states CARF applies to all jurisdictions automatically should not receive the last two marks.

items.prompt: (b) Evaluate whether the existing permanent establishment and residence concepts can be applied to activities carried out through a blockchain or decentralised autonomous organisation (DAO).

answer.model: The Article 5 concept requires a fixed place of business through which business is wholly or partly carried on, or a dependent agent who habitually concludes contracts or plays the principal role in their conclusion (OECD Article 5(5) as amended following BEPS Action 7). Applied to a blockchain network, the nodes and validators are spread across many States, and a node owned by an enterprise might be argued to be a fixed place at its disposal, but the Commentary requires that the business be carried on through the place, and automated validation by software, possibly operated by independent participants, rarely amounts to the enterprise's own business activity. A smart contract is not a person and cannot be a dependent agent, although a development team or foundation that instructs and manages the protocol might create a PE for the developers or promoters if it has a fixed place of business or acts as dependent agent. Residence is similarly difficult. Article 4 refers to a person liable to tax by reason of domicile, residence, place of management or similar criterion. A DAO may have no legal personality; some States treat it as a partnership or unincorporated association and look to members, and others to the persons exercising control. Place of effective management or its equivalent may be impossible to find where decisions are made by token holder votes from many States. The tie breaker for persons other than individuals in the 2017 OECD Model Article 4(3), which refers the case to the competent authorities to settle by mutual agreement, gives limited help. Evaluating the paper's conclusion, existing concepts can be stretched but at the cost of uncertainty, and so jurisdictions may prefer reporting rules and domestic anti avoidance rules to treaty redesign. Candidates who cite the UN Model should note the services PE in Article 5(3)(b), which could catch services by personnel present, but not automated services.

points.point: states the PE tests: fixed place and dependent agent (Art 5(1), 5(5) with BEPS Action 7 changes)
analyses nodes, validators and smart contracts, and why automated activity is hard to attribute
analyses the residence difficulty for a DAO: legal personality, control, place of management and the Art 4(3) tie breaker
notes the UN Model services PE and its limits
evaluates the paper's conclusion with reasons

answer.grader_note: The 2017 OECD Model Art 4(3) refers to competent authorities settling residence of a person other than an individual by mutual agreement. Accept this or a general statement.

items.prompt: (c) Critically assess the issues that artificial intelligence raises for international taxation, both as a tool of tax administration and as a feature of multinational businesses.

answer.model: As a tool of administration, AI supports risk assessment, selection of audit targets, matching of third party data, analysis of country by country report data and chatbots for taxpayer service. Benefits are efficiency, wider coverage and the ability to detect patterns in transfer pricing or VAT data that humans would miss. Risks include bias in training data, opacity of decision making (a taxpayer may not be told why a return was selected), data protection and confidentiality limits on cross border sharing, and legality: decisions with legal effect must normally be made by an accountable official and be reviewable. Treaty confidentiality under Article 26 restricts using exchanged information outside its permitted purposes, which constrains training of systems on pooled data. For multinationals, AI creates valuable intangibles, models and data sets, the ownership and location of which are uncertain. Under the transfer pricing guidelines the DEMPE analysis (development, enhancement, maintenance, protection and exploitation) is used to allocate returns to entities performing important functions and controlling risk, so legal ownership of a model gives no more than a risk adjusted return on funding, or no return at all, unless the owner performs and controls the relevant functions. This is hard where training uses data generated by users in many States and compute in a third. AI may also substitute for people at a location, weakening PE thresholds based on personnel presence, and may allow rapid restructuring of supply chains. Where AI automates routine functions, the residual profit shifts to intangibles, increasing the pressure on the allocation rules and on Amount A style approaches under Pillar One, although the Amount A multilateral convention was never opened for signature, so this remains policy pressure and not a rule. Overall the existing frameworks can be applied, but tax authorities will need greater access to technical expertise, and international coordination on data sharing and safeguards is a precondition for effective use. A balanced conclusion recognises that AI in administration must be governed by legal safeguards, while the tax treatment of AI assets is largely a question of applying DEMPE to difficult facts.

points.point: explains uses of AI in tax administration with benefits
explains risks: bias, transparency, legality, data protection and Art 26 confidentiality
explains DEMPE and the allocation of returns from AI intangibles
identifies PE and presence issues and connection to profit allocation reform
reasoned critical conclusion

answer.grader_note: Do not credit assertions that Pillar One Amount A is specifically designed for AI. A short comment that it targets large digital and consumer facing businesses is acceptable.

title: Prevention and resolution of pricing disputes
scenario: A multinational group operating in many States complains that transfer pricing audits are slow, outcomes uncertain and relief from double taxation unreliable. Tax authorities respond that agreement in advance and simplified rules can reduce disputes, but that each tool has costs.

items.prompt: (a) Explain what an advance pricing agreement (APA) is, distinguish unilateral, bilateral and multilateral APAs, and assess the advantages and disadvantages for taxpayer and tax authority.

answer.model: An advance pricing arrangement is an arrangement that determines, in advance of controlled transactions, an appropriate set of criteria (the method, comparables and adjustments, critical assumptions) for determining the transfer pricing for those transactions over a fixed period, typically three to five years, often with a rollback to earlier years. A unilateral APA is agreed between the taxpayer and one tax authority only; it gives certainty in that State but does not bind the foreign counterparty, so the other State may adjust and double taxation may remain. A bilateral APA involves the taxpayer and two tax authorities and is negotiated under the mutual agreement procedure of the relevant treaty (Article 25 OECD and UN Models); it provides certainty in both States and eliminates the risk of double taxation. A multilateral APA involves more than two authorities and suits groups with an integrated value chain. The OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines (Annex to Chapter IV) set out guidance on bilateral APAs. Advantages for the taxpayer are certainty, reduced compliance and audit cost for the covered period and protection from penalties; for the authority, an agreed approach can conserve audit resources and improve understanding of the business. Disadvantages are the cost and time of the process (often well over a year), disclosure of commercially sensitive information, the risk that critical assumptions fail so the agreement lapses, and the fact that the authority commits resources to a taxpayer whose pricing it might have accepted anyway. A reasoned assessment is that bilateral or multilateral APAs suit large, recurring and complex transactions, such as intangibles or financial transactions, while unilateral APAs are of limited value unless the counterparty State will follow.

points.point: defines an APA including covered period, method, critical assumptions, rollback
distinguishes unilateral, bilateral and multilateral APAs, with the MAP basis for bilateral ones
advantages for taxpayer and tax authority
disadvantages: cost, disclosure, failure of critical assumptions
reasoned assessment of when each type is suitable

items.prompt: (b) Discuss the role of safe harbours in transfer pricing, including the reasons for and against their use and the simplified approach for baseline marketing and distribution activities developed under Pillar One (Amount B).

answer.model: A safe harbour is a provision applying to a defined category of taxpayers or transactions that relieves them from certain obligations under the general transfer pricing rules, for example by allowing a prescribed margin or rate instead of a full arm's length analysis. The OECD Guidelines (Chapter IV, section E) recognise the benefits: simpler compliance, certainty and reduced administrative burden, particularly for small taxpayers or low value adding services where a fixed markup (the low value adding intra-group services simplified approach, with a five per cent markup in the Guidelines) is used. Against this, the Guidelines identify risks: a safe harbour can depart from the arm's length principle and so lead to double taxation or double non taxation if the counterparty State does not accept it, may be exploited by sophisticated taxpayers who structure transactions to fit it, may distort pricing decisions and may raise equity concerns. For these reasons the Guidelines favour bilateral or multilateral safe harbours, which give certainty to both States, over unilateral ones. In February 2024 the OECD Inclusive Framework approved a report on Amount B, a simplified and streamlined approach to pricing baseline distribution and marketing activities performed by related parties, which was incorporated into the Guidelines as an annex to Chapter IV. It prices qualifying transactions using a matrix of operating margins set by industry grouping, asset and expense intensity, with a cap and collar to deal with data poor jurisdictions. It applies at the election of jurisdictions for fiscal years commencing on or after 1 January 2025 and is aimed at relieving the capacity constraints of low capacity jurisdictions and reducing disputes. Amount B is optional for jurisdictions, and its relationship with the existing treaty obligations depends on domestic implementation. It stands apart from Amount A, whose multilateral convention was never opened for signature, and the 2025 OECD Model Commentary on Article 25 now addresses it. Overall safe harbours trade accuracy for simplicity and are best targeted at routine, low risk activities, and bilateral where possible.

points.point: defines a safe harbour and gives an example such as low value adding services
benefits and risks per Chapter IV (certainty, simplicity vs departure from arm's length, double taxation, manipulation)
preference for bilateral or multilateral safe harbours
describes Amount B: simplified pricing of baseline marketing and distribution by matrix, annex to Chapter IV, approved 2024
notes that application is by election and aimed at reducing disputes and capacity burdens

answer.grader_note: Candidates are not expected to recall margin figures. The 2024 Amount B report and its optional implementation are as published by the OECD; exact start dates may be given in general terms.

items.prompt: (c) Evaluate the mechanisms available under tax treaties and the OECD framework for resolving a transfer pricing dispute between two States, including the interaction of Article 9(2) with Article 25.

answer.model: Where a State adjusts the profits of an enterprise under Article 9(1) so that profits taxed in the other State are included, double taxation arises. Article 9(2) obliges the other State, where it agrees that the adjustment is justified in principle and amount, to make a corresponding adjustment to the tax charged there. The obligation is conditional on agreement and the competent authority is to consult. Article 25 provides the process: a taxpayer who considers the actions of one or both States result in taxation not in accordance with the treaty may present the case to the competent authority of either Contracting State, which seeks to resolve it by mutual agreement with the other. The OECD Model provides for the agreement to be implemented notwithstanding domestic time limits (Article 25(2)). The weakness of the MAP is that the authorities are obliged to endeavour but not to reach agreement, so cases can remain unresolved and long. Responses include mandatory binding arbitration: Article 25(5) of the OECD Model since 2008 provides that if the competent authorities cannot agree within two years, the unresolved issues may be submitted to arbitration at the request of the person, and Part VI of the MLI offers arbitration as an option for States that choose it; the UN Model contains alternative provisions on arbitration (Alternative B in Article 25, under which either competent authority may request arbitration after three years, whereas OECD Article 25(5) lets the person request it after two years). BEPS Action 14 established a minimum standard on improving dispute resolution, including timely handling of cases, an average time of 24 months as a target and peer review of States. The EU Arbitration Convention and the EU Dispute Resolution Directive apply in the European Union. Domestic procedures such as appeals or the use of APAs reduce the number of cases. A reasoned evaluation is that MAP with arbitration offers the best prospect of eliminating double taxation, but it relies on States accepting arbitration, and many developing States are cautious about binding arbitration because they fear loss of sovereignty and capacity.

points.point: explains Art 9(1) adjustment, double taxation and the corresponding adjustment duty in Art 9(2) subject to agreement
explains Article 25 MAP: presentation by taxpayer, endeavour to resolve, implementation despite domestic time limits
identifies the limitation: no obligation to agree
arbitration: Art 25(5) OECD 2008, MLI Part VI, UN alternative
BEPS Action 14 minimum standard and the 24 month target
reasoned evaluation including developing State concerns

title: A shareholder leaves State R
scenario: Ilmari Voss, a citizen of State R, has been resident in State R for many years. He owns 100 per cent of the shares in Voss Components Ltd, a trading company resident in State R. On 1 July Year 3 he moves with his spouse and children to State S to run a new business there. His children start school in State S and his spouse takes up a job. He sells his family house in State R but keeps a small flat in State R, which he furnishes and which is available for his use, and he returns for about 60 days a year to oversee the company, whose management stays in State R. State R taxes individuals on worldwide income while resident, and deems a resident individual to dispose of shares in a company at market value on ceasing to be resident (an exit charge) at a flat 20 per cent, with an option to pay the tax in five equal annual instalments (interest ignored for this question) provided security is given. State S taxes residents on worldwide income and, for gains on a later sale, treats the acquisition cost of assets of a new arrival as their market value at the date of arrival. In Year 6 Mr Voss sells all the shares in Voss Components Ltd for 4,600,000. The two States have a treaty based on the OECD Model, with Article 13(5) as in the OECD Model. All figures are illustrative.

exhibits.caption: Facts about the shares (illustrative currency units)

items.prompt: (a) Calculate the State R exit charge arising on 1 July Year 3 and the amount of each annual instalment if the instalment option is chosen.

answer.model: Deemed gain = market value 4,000,000 minus cost 500,000 = 3,500,000. Exit charge = 20% x 3,500,000 = 700,000. Five equal annual instalments = 700,000 ÷ 5 = 140,000 each (interest ignored). The charge arises on the deemed disposal even though no cash is received, which is why the instalment option and security matter for liquidity.

points.point: instalments 700,000 ÷ 5 = 140,000, noting no cash proceeds arise

items.prompt: (b) Determine, applying Article 4 of the OECD Model, in which State Mr Voss is resident for treaty purposes during the period after 1 July Year 3, explaining the competing arguments.

answer.model: Under domestic law State R may still treat Mr Voss as resident, because he retains a permanent home there, is a national and manages the company from there, while State S treats him as resident from 1 July Year 3 as he lives there with his family. If both States treat him as resident, he is a resident of both under Article 4(1) and the tie breaker in Article 4(2) applies in sequence. (a) Permanent home: he has a home available in both States (the flat in State R is furnished and available, and the home in State S), so no result at this stage; the Commentary asks whether the home is available at all times continuously, and a small flat that is used on short business visits and is always available may count. (b) Centre of vital interests: personal and economic relations. Family, children's schooling, spouse's job and the new business are in State S, which point to State S; the company, management of it, the flat and nationality connect him to State R. Personal relations are usually given greater weight than business ties, and a stay of about 60 days a year in State R does not outweigh the family move, so the centre of vital interests is probably State S, although the dominant economic asset and its management remain in State R, which gives State R an argument. (c) Only if this cannot be decided would habitual abode be considered (clearly State S given 60 days in State R), then nationality (State R), then competent authority agreement. The likely result is residence in State S from 1 July Year 3 under Article 4(2)(b). Consequences: State R loses residence based taxing rights under Articles 10, 11, 13(5) after that date and keeps source rights only where the treaty allows, and the exit charge is a domestic measure for the period before treaty residence changed. Treaties do not generally prevent an exit charge on gains accrued while resident.

points.point: identifies potential dual residence under domestic law and Art 4(1)
applies permanent home test and identifies it as inconclusive
analyses centre of vital interests with facts on both sides and weights personal over business ties
states later tie breakers in sequence and reaches a reasoned conclusion that State S is likely
notes the exit charge is a domestic measure and treaty residence consequences

answer.grader_note: Accept a conclusion for State R if reasoned. Credit explicit use of the Commentary on the permanent home concept.

items.prompt: (c) Calculate the State S tax on the Year 6 sale, and the total tax suffered on the whole gain of 4,100,000 across both States on the assumption that State R exit charge of 700,000 is paid and State R does not tax the Year 6 sale.

answer.model: State S acquisition cost = market value at arrival 4,000,000. Gain = 4,600,000 minus 4,000,000 = 600,000. State S tax = 25% x 600,000 = 150,000. Whole economic gain = 4,600,000 minus 500,000 = 4,100,000. Of this, 3,500,000 accrued while resident in State R and was taxed by State R at 700,000 (payable by instalments of 140,000 if elected), and 600,000 accrued after arrival and was taxed by State S at 150,000. Total tax = 700,000 + 150,000 = 850,000, with each part of the gain taxed once, so there is no double taxation because State S rebased the cost. Without the rebasing State S would have taxed 4,100,000 x 25% = 1,025,000, giving 1,725,000 in total and double taxation of 3,500,000.

points.point: State S cost base 4,000,000 and gain 600,000
total tax 850,000 over the whole gain of 4,100,000, 3,500,000 plus 600,000
notes the rebasing prevents double taxation, contrasted with 1,725,000 if not rebased

items.prompt: (d) Advise Mr Voss whether State R could tax the Year 6 sale under the treaty if the treaty followed the UN Model Article 13(5), and what other planning points he should consider.

answer.model: Under OECD Article 13(5) the gain on shares that are not land rich (13(4)) is taxable only in the State of residence of the seller, so in Year 6 State S alone taxes the sale if Mr Voss is resident there. The UN Model Article 13(5) differs: gains from the alienation of shares in a company resident in a Contracting State may be taxed in that State if the alienator held, directly or indirectly, at least a specified percentage (a bilateral figure left blank in the Model, with 25 per cent the usual illustration) at any time during the 365 days preceding the alienation in the UN Model 2025 text (paragraph 13(5) in both the 2021 and 2025 editions; some earlier texts expressed the period as 12 months). Mr Voss owns 100 per cent, so State R could tax the Year 6 gain under a UN style treaty, creating double taxation of the 600,000 post arrival gain, which State S would need to relieve by credit under Article 23B (limited to the State S tax on that income) or exemption. He should check the actual treaty wording, whether State R will tax a gain accrued after departure, whether the exit charge is itself creditable, the effect of a deferred rather than paid exit charge, the security cost, and any rule that cancels the exit charge if he returns within a set period.

points.point: OECD Article 13(5): residence State only, so State S taxes
UN Article 13(5): source State may tax holdings of at least the specified percentage within the preceding period (365 days in the UN Model 2025, 12 months in some earlier texts)
applies the 100 per cent holding and relief under Art 23A or 23B
further practical points: wording, creditability of exit tax, deferral and security, return rules

answer.grader_note: Do not penalise a candidate who states the UN threshold as 'a specified percentage, for example 25 per cent'.

title: Sale of shares in a mining company
scenario: Cobalt Holdings Ltd is resident in State R. It owns 100 per cent of Halden Mining Ltd, resident in State S, which owns a mine, land and buildings in State S and also holds cash, equipment and receivables. Cobalt acquired the shares for 3,000,000 several years ago. Under a contract concluded in Year 5, Cobalt sells all the shares in Halden to an unrelated buyer for 9,000,000 on 31 December Year 5. State S taxes gains made by non-residents on shares deriving their value from immovable property in State S at 30 per cent. State R taxes the gain at 25 per cent. The treaty between State R and State S follows the OECD Model 2025 Article 13(4) (more than 50 per cent of value, derived directly or indirectly from immovable property situated in the other State, at any time during the 365 days preceding the alienation) and uses the credit method in State R (Article 23B). Cobalt says State S has no right to tax because the shares are not themselves immovable property. Halden's asset values at certain dates are in Table 1. All figures are illustrative.

exhibits.caption: Halden Mining Ltd: market value of assets (illustrative currency units, debts ignored)

items.prompt: (a) Calculate, for each date in Table 1, the percentage of Halden's total asset value attributable to immovable property in State S, and state on which dates the 50 per cent threshold is exceeded.

answer.model: 31 January: 4,800,000 ÷ 10,000,000 = 48.0 per cent, not more than 50. 31 March: 5,100,000 ÷ 10,200,000 = 50.0 per cent exactly, not more than 50 per cent so the threshold is not exceeded. 30 September: 5,600,000 ÷ 10,700,000 = 52.3 per cent (0.52336), exceeds 50. 31 December: 4,900,000 ÷ 10,500,000 = 46.7 per cent (0.46667), not exceeded. The threshold is therefore exceeded on 30 September only among the dates given. Debts are ignored: the Commentary compares the value of the immovable property with the value of all assets owned by the company, without deducting liabilities.

points.point: 48.0% at 31 January, and 46.7% at 31 December
50.0% at 31 March, correctly not more than 50 per cent

items.prompt: (b) Advise whether State S may tax the gain under Article 13(4), addressing Cobalt's argument and the significance of the 365 day period.

answer.model: Cobalt's argument that shares are not immovable property is answered by Article 13(4), which exists precisely to treat shares deriving more than 50 per cent of their value directly or indirectly from immovable property as equivalent to the property for allocation of taxing rights. If it applies, State S, as the State where the property is situated, may tax the gain without limit as to rate (the treaty allows tax, it does not set the rate). The test is not applied only at the date of sale. Under the 2017 and later wording it applies if at any time during the 365 days preceding the alienation the shares derived more than 50 per cent of their value from such immovable property. Table 1 shows that the threshold was exceeded on 30 September Year 5, within 365 days of 31 December Year 5, although on the date of sale the figure was only 46.7 per cent. This 365 day look back prevents a taxpayer from disposing of immovable property or adding other assets shortly before the sale to defeat the test. Cobalt may argue that the 52.3 per cent figure was a temporary peak, and that valuation date and method matter; but the wording is 'at any time', so a temporary excess is sufficient and the burden is practical evidence of values. Immovable property is defined by Article 6 and includes land, buildings and, by Article 6(2), rights to work mineral deposits, so the mine falls within it, subject to the domestic law of State S. The Commentary notes that the value is compared with all assets of the company, directly or indirectly held, so a holding through lower tier companies is also caught. A further point is the Multilateral Instrument, Article 9, which for States that adopt it substitutes the same 365 day period and adds comparable interests, so the treaty wording should be checked against the State R and State S positions. Conclusion: State S may tax the gain of 6,000,000 under Article 13(4), and Cobalt's argument fails. The conclusion is secure only if the values are accepted, so the facts and valuation should be reviewed.

states the test: more than 50% of value from immovable property, direct or indirect, at any time in the 365 days preceding
applies the table: exceeded on 30 September within the period, though not at the date of sale

conclusion with caveat on valuation, or reference to MLI Art 9

answer.grader_note: A candidate who relies only on the sale date value should receive no credit for the application mark.

items.prompt: (c) Calculate the tax in State S, the tax in State R before relief, the foreign tax credit allowed by State R under Article 23B, the net State R tax, and any unrelieved State S tax.

answer.model: Gain = 9,000,000 minus 3,000,000 = 6,000,000. State S tax = 30% x 6,000,000 = 1,800,000. State R tax before relief = 25% x 6,000,000 = 1,500,000. Under Article 23B the credit is limited to the part of the State R tax attributable to the income that may be taxed in State S, so credit = lower of 1,800,000 and 1,500,000 = 1,500,000. Net State R tax = 1,500,000 minus 1,500,000 = 0. Unrelieved State S tax = 1,800,000 minus 1,500,000 = 300,000 (an excess credit that is lost unless domestic law allows carry forward). Total tax = 1,800,000.

State R tax before relief 1,500,000
credit limited to the lower figure, 1,500,000, with net State R tax of nil
excess State S tax 300,000 unrelieved

items.prompt: (d) Explain how the position would differ if the treaty followed the UN Model and how the structure of the holding could affect the outcome.

answer.model: The UN Model Article 13(4) (same paragraph number in the 2021 and 2025 editions) is drafted in the same way as the OECD Model on land rich entities (more than 50 per cent, 365 days) but the UN Model also contains Article 13(5), which permits the State where a company is resident to tax gains on the alienation of shares in that company where the seller held at least a specified percentage (for example 25 per cent) at any time during the 365 days before in the UN Model 2025 text (12 months in some earlier texts). So even if the land rich test were not met, State S could tax a 100 per cent seller under a UN style treaty. Under the OECD Model Article 13(5) the gain would be taxed only in State R. Structure matters: if Cobalt held Halden through an intermediate company in State T, the treaty between State T and State S would decide the outcome, and the State T treaty might lack a land rich rule, which invites treaty shopping; the MLI principal purpose test (Article 7) and the 365 day look back may deny the benefit. Selling the shares in the intermediate company instead may also be caught by the indirect wording of Article 13(4).

OECD Art 13(5): residence State only if the 13(4) test is not met
effect of an intermediate holding company in a third State and relevant treaty
anti avoidance: MLI principal purpose test and indirect wording of 13(4)

title: Intermediaries and the permanent establishment threshold
scenario: "The post-BEPS changes to Article 5 have ended the commissionaire structure. A principal can no longer sell through a local intermediary without creating a permanent establishment, and fragmenting its local operations no longer helps." Consider this statement in the light of the OECD Model Tax Convention 2025 and the UN Model Tax Convention 2025.

items.prompt: (a) Explain the changes made to Article 5 of the OECD Model as a result of BEPS Action 7, covering agency, independent agents, the specific activity exemptions and fragmentation of activities.

answer.model:
Action 7 of the BEPS project produced changes that were included in the OECD Model from 2017. First, the dependent agent rule in Article 5(5) was widened. Under the older text a person created a permanent establishment only if it habitually exercised an authority to conclude contracts in the name of the enterprise. Now a person who habitually concludes contracts, or habitually plays the principal role leading to the conclusion of contracts that are routinely concluded without material modification by the enterprise, can create one. The contracts must be in the name of the enterprise, or be for the transfer of ownership of, or the grant of a right to use, property owned by the enterprise or which it has the right to use, or be for the provision of services by that enterprise. The second limb reaches a commissionaire who negotiates the key terms with customers while the contract is formally signed in the commissionaire's own name.

Second, the independent agent exception in Article 5(6) was narrowed. It no longer applies to a person who acts exclusively or almost exclusively on behalf of one or more enterprises to which it is closely related, and closely related is defined in Article 5(8) by reference to control and a greater than 50 per cent beneficial interest, or a third party who controls both.

Third, in Article 5(4) the exemptions for storage, display, delivery, purchasing, collecting information and other activities, which in older texts applied to the activities in subparagraphs (a) to (d) without any further test, now each apply only where the activity is of a preparatory or auxiliary character.

Fourth, Article 5(4.1) is an anti-fragmentation rule. The exemptions are denied where the enterprise or a closely related enterprise carries on business at the same or another place in the State and that place is a permanent establishment, or the overall activity from combining the activities at the two places is not preparatory or auxiliary, provided the activities are complementary functions that are part of a cohesive business operation. The UN Model has taken up some of this but not all, and it retains its own provisions such as the services rule in Article 5(3)(b), while the UN Model 2021 numbering has an insurance agent rule in Article 5(6), which the UN Model 2025 deleted and replaced with a new Article 12C on insurance premiums (so the independent agent rule moves from Article 5(7) to Article 5(6)), and a candidate must read the UN text of the edition in use separately.

points.point: States that Article 5(5) now covers a person who habitually plays the principal role leading to the conclusion of contracts routinely concluded without material modification
Identifies the contract categories (name of the enterprise, property owned or usable by the enterprise, services by the enterprise), including the commissionaire in its own name
Explains that the old test was habitually exercising an authority to conclude contracts
Explains that Article 5(6) no longer protects an agent acting exclusively or almost exclusively for closely related enterprises
Mentions the definition of closely related enterprises in Article 5(8)

States that each Article 5(4) exemption is now subject to the preparatory or auxiliary condition, and explains the anti-fragmentation rule in Article 5(4.1) (cohesive business operation, complementary functions)

Notes the source (BEPS Action 7 Final Report, 2015) and that the UN Model adopts the changes only in part, with UN-only provisions such as the services rule in Article 5(3)(b) and insurance (Article 5(6) in the UN Model 2021 numbering, deleted in the UN Model 2025 and replaced by Article 12C)

answer.grader_note: Do not credit paragraph numbering that is wrong. Accept the 2017 or later Model as the source of the changes. UN Model detail is not required beyond recognising a difference.

items.prompt: (b) Critically evaluate the statement. To what extent do the changes end the use of commissionaire arrangements and the fragmentation of local operations?

answer.model:
The statement overstates the position, although the direction of the reform is clear. Before the reform, a principal could sell its goods in a State through a commissionaire that contracted in its own name. Courts in several jurisdictions, for example the French Conseil d'Etat in Zimmer and the Norwegian Supreme Court in Dell, held that the principal was not bound by those contracts and so had no permanent establishment. The new principal role limb in Article 5(5) is aimed squarely at this. Where the commissionaire negotiates price and the essential terms and the principal's standard terms are then accepted without material modification, a permanent establishment can arise even though the principal never signs.

There are, however, real limits. The words 'principal role' and 'routinely concluded without material modification' are open textured. The Commentary offers examples, but the line between persuading a customer to accept standard terms and negotiating them will be disputed. The contract categories also matter: the sub-paragraph on property requires that the property is owned by the enterprise or that the enterprise has the right to use it. If the local entity buys the goods and resells them as a buy-sell distributor, taking title and the risk, the structure is not an agency at all, and no permanent establishment arises under Article 5(5). A group can therefore move from a commissionaire to a limited risk distributor and remain outside the rule, which shifts the dispute to transfer pricing under Article 9 rather than to Article 5. The independent agent exception also still protects an agent that is genuinely independent and sells for several unconnected principals.

On fragmentation, Article 5(4.1) applies only if the places are operated by the same or closely related enterprises and are complementary parts of a cohesive operation. A group that splits warehouse, delivery and sales support between unrelated contractors falls outside it. Even where a permanent establishment is found, profit attribution under Article 7 may be small if the intermediary is already rewarded at arm's length, so the revenue gain to the source State can be modest. Finally, the reforms do nothing about remote sales without any personnel, which is the concern behind Pillar One and UN Article 12B.

In conclusion, the changes narrow the commissionaire structure considerably and raise the cost of fragmentation, but they do not end either. They move disputes from the existence of a permanent establishment to the facts of contract negotiation and to the attribution of profit.

points.point: Explains the pre-reform position (principal not bound by commissionaire contracts, so no permanent establishment)
Cites the Zimmer and Dell decisions, or states that courts in several jurisdictions reached that result
Explains that the principal role limb is aimed at negotiated contracts concluded on standard terms
Identifies uncertainty in 'principal role' and 'material modification' as a source of disputes
Identifies that the property contract category depends on property owned or usable by the enterprise, so a buy-sell distributor remains outside
Recognises that restructuring into a limited risk distributor moves the issue to Article 9
Notes that a genuinely independent agent for several principals is still protected
