Recognises that anti-fragmentation applies only to same or closely related enterprises and complementary functions
Notes that profit attribution under Article 7 may limit the revenue effect
Reaches a reasoned conclusion that the changes narrow but do not end the structures (credit judgement shown by weighing both sides)

answer.grader_note: Any well argued view is acceptable if it engages with both limbs of the statement. Do not credit a statement that the new rule applies to a buy-sell distributor.

items.prompt: (c) Discuss how and when these changes affect a pair of States whose existing treaty was signed before 2017.

answer.model:
The reforms are changes to the text of the Model, and a treaty signed before 2017 contains whatever text the two States agreed at the time. New wording therefore has no effect on an existing treaty until the treaty is amended. The routes are bilateral renegotiation or the Multilateral Convention to Implement Tax Treaty Related Measures to Prevent BEPS (the MLI), signed in 2017 and in force from 1 July 2018. The MLI contains Article 12 on artificial avoidance of permanent establishment status through commissionaire arrangements and similar strategies, Article 13 on artificial avoidance through specific activity exemptions, where a party chooses Option A or Option B or neither, and Article 15 on the definition of a person closely related to an enterprise.

The MLI modifies only a Covered Tax Agreement, meaning one that both States have listed, and its provisions apply only where the matching choices and notifications of the two States allow it. A State may reserve against Article 12 or Article 13, and many States did. A reservation by either State blocks the change for that treaty. The timing of effect is set by Article 35 of the MLI, with different rules for withholding taxes (events on or after the first day of the next calendar year that begins on or after the latest entry into force for both States) and for other taxes (taxable periods beginning on or after six calendar months after that entry into force).

The Commentary updates raise a separate issue. Changes that clarify the meaning of existing language can be taken into account in interpreting older treaties, according to the OECD view, but a substantive change of wording, such as the extension of Article 5(5), cannot be read back into a treaty with the earlier text. Treaties based on the UN Model need their own analysis. In practice, an adviser must check each treaty one by one, together with the reservations and notifications, and the domestic definition of a permanent establishment, because many treaties still carry the older text and the structures may continue to work.

points.point: States that a change to Model text does not alter an existing treaty until amended
Identifies bilateral renegotiation and the MLI as the routes
Names MLI Articles 12, 13 and 15 and their subject matter
Explains that the MLI applies only to Covered Tax Agreements and only where the States' choices and notifications match
Notes that reservations (for example against Article 12) block the change
Refers to the timing rules in MLI Article 35
Distinguishes interpretive Commentary changes from substantive text changes for older treaties
Concludes that each treaty must be checked separately and that many older treaties retain the old text

answer.grader_note: MLI Article 13 detail (options and anti-fragmentation) is marked leniently; credit any accurate description.

title: Domestic anti-avoidance and treaty benefits
scenario: "A State that wants to counter abusive structures needs no treaty-based rule at all, because its own general anti-avoidance rule will always prevail over a tax treaty." Discuss this proposition with reference to the OECD and UN Models and to State practice.

items.prompt: (a) Explain the main approaches that States take in domestic law to counter tax avoidance, and the distinction between avoidance and evasion.

answer.model:
Tax evasion is the illegal non-payment of tax, usually involving concealment or misstatement, and attracts penalties and sometimes prosecution. Tax avoidance is arranging affairs to reduce tax within the letter of the law, and the line between acceptable planning and unacceptable avoidance is the subject of the doctrines below.

First, courts in many States apply judicial doctrines. These include substance over form, the rejection of sham transactions (where the documents do not reflect the real transaction), business purpose tests, step transaction and the purposive reading of the statute. In a common law State the older rule that a taxpayer may arrange affairs to minimise tax has been qualified by approaches that look at the real commercial effect of a composite arrangement.

Second, many States have enacted a statutory general anti-avoidance rule (GAAR). These typically require an arrangement with a tax advantage as a main or principal purpose and some form of abuse, or conduct that is not a reasonable course of action, and they permit the tax authority to counteract the advantage.

Third, there are specific anti-avoidance rules aimed at known risks: transfer pricing, thin capitalisation and interest limitation, controlled foreign company rules, and rules on hybrid mismatches and on the use of conduit companies. A specific rule gives certainty but is only as good as the drafting, and planners can structure around it.

Fourth, in the European Union, the Court of Justice held in the Danish beneficial ownership cases (26 February 2019) that abuse of rights is a general principle of EU law which a State may rely on to deny directive benefits even without a domestic or treaty rule. Common issues across all of these are legal certainty, the burden of proof and whether the rule applies to the foreign element of the transaction.

points.point: Defines evasion (illegal, concealment) and avoidance (within the letter of the law) and states the line is contested
Describes judicial doctrines such as substance over form, sham and business purpose
Describes statutory GAAR features (purpose test, abuse, counteraction)
Describes specific anti-avoidance rules with examples (CFC, thin capitalisation, transfer pricing, hybrid rules)
Refers to the Danish beneficial ownership cases and the general principle of abuse of rights in EU law
Identifies a common issue such as legal certainty or burden of proof

items.prompt: (b) Critically evaluate the principal purposes test in Article 29(9) of the OECD Model as a treaty anti-abuse rule, comparing it with a limitation on benefits provision.

answer.model:
Article 29(9) denies a treaty benefit if it is reasonable to conclude, having regard to all relevant facts and circumstances, that obtaining the benefit was one of the principal purposes of any arrangement or transaction that resulted directly or indirectly in the benefit, unless it is established that granting the benefit would be in accordance with the object and purpose of the relevant provisions. The threshold of one of the principal purposes is low: it does not have to be the sole or main purpose. The taxpayer can rebut by showing that the benefit is consistent with the object and purpose of the treaty, and the Commentary supplies examples to guide this.

A limitation on benefits (LOB) provision, as in the qualified person paragraphs of Article 29, works differently. It sets objective tests for who is a qualified person, such as listed companies, ownership and base erosion tests, and an active conduct of a business test, with derivative benefit rules and a discretionary relief mechanism. It gives certainty and is administrable by reference to facts, but it is long and complex and may be over inclusive, denying benefits to a bona fide group, and under inclusive, because a treaty shopper can sometimes find a qualifying entity. It also assumes that the State has the capacity to administer detailed ownership tests.

The PPT is shorter and flexible, catches arrangements an LOB cannot foresee, and applies to transactions as well as entities, but it creates uncertainty because a decision turns on the tax authority's view of purpose, on which courts are only starting to rule, and may result in conflicting views of the two States.

Under the BEPS Action 6 minimum standard, a State must adopt a statement of common intention in the preamble and then either a PPT alone, a PPT with an LOB, or an LOB with an anti-conduit mechanism. The MLI gives effect to this through Article 6 for the preamble and Article 7 for the PPT, with an optional simplified LOB in Article 7. The UN Model Article 29 (entitlement to benefits) combines a qualified person limitation on benefits with a principal purpose test. On balance the PPT's flexibility is its strength and its weakness, and combining the two gives the best protection against abuse while preserving claims by genuine investors.

points.point: States the PPT: one of the principal purposes of an arrangement, reasonable to conclude, all relevant facts
Identifies that the threshold is low (not sole or main purpose)
Explains the taxpayer's rebuttal based on the object and purpose of the provisions
Describes the LOB as objective tests of a qualified person (the LOB paragraphs of Article 29), with derivative benefits and discretionary relief
Evaluates the LOB (certainty and administrability against complexity and over or under inclusion)
Evaluates the PPT (flexibility against uncertainty and risk of inconsistent application)
Explains the Action 6 minimum standard options (PPT alone, PPT with LOB, LOB with anti-conduit mechanism)
Refers to MLI Articles 6 and 7 as the implementation route
Reaches a reasoned conclusion on the relative merits or on combining them

answer.grader_note: Credit a correct reference to a UN Model anti-abuse provision but do not require paragraph numbers.

items.prompt: (c) Discuss whether a State may apply its domestic anti-avoidance rules to deny the benefits of a tax treaty, and assess the proposition in the light of your answer.

answer.model:
Under the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, a State must perform a treaty in good faith (Article 26) and may not invoke its internal law as justification for failing to perform it (Article 27). On that basis a domestic rule that denied a treaty benefit would appear to breach the treaty. How far a treaty prevails in domestic law depends on the constitution: in a monist State a treaty ordinarily takes precedence over inconsistent statute, whereas in a dualist State a later statute may override it as a matter of domestic law even if the State is in breach internationally.

The OECD Commentary on Article 1 takes the view that there is no conflict between domestic anti-abuse rules and the treaty, because treaties are not intended to give benefits in abuse cases and the application of a domestic rule to prevent abuse therefore does not contradict the treaty. It also states a guiding principle that a benefit is not available where one of the main purposes of the arrangement is to obtain it and granting the benefit would be contrary to the object and purpose of the provisions. UN Model Commentary takes a broadly similar approach. Courts have not been uniform. Some have accepted that domestic abuse doctrines apply to treaty claims, particularly where the abuse is of a general legal principle, as the Court of Justice did in the Danish beneficial ownership cases in the EU context. Others have required a specific treaty rule before benefits could be refused.

Since 2017 the preamble states an intention not to create opportunities for non taxation or reduced taxation through avoidance, including treaty shopping, and the PPT now makes the rule express. This reduces the conflict argument but also invites the argument that the express treaty rule displaces a broader domestic rule.

The proposition is therefore overstated. A GAAR will not always prevail over a treaty: the result depends on the constitutional position, the terms and Commentary of the treaty, the facts and the view taken by the other State, which may seek relief through the mutual agreement procedure. A State that wishes to be certain should rely on an express treaty rule.

points.point: States the VCLT obligations (Article 26 good faith, Article 27 no reliance on internal law)
Distinguishes monist and dualist treatment of treaties in domestic law
States the OECD Commentary view that there is no conflict because treaties do not give benefits in abuse cases
States the guiding principle (main purpose and contrary to object and purpose)
Notes that courts have reached different results and some require an express treaty rule
Notes the effect of the post 2017 preamble and the PPT
Refers to the EU position (Danish cases) or the UN Commentary
Concludes that the proposition is overstated and depends on several factors, including the other State's view and MAP

title: Who earns the return on an intangible
scenario: "Legal ownership of an intangible should determine who earns the profit from it. Tax authorities that look beyond the contract, and use hindsight when prices turn out to be wrong, undermine the arm's length principle." Consider this statement with reference to the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines (2022) and the UN Practical Manual on Transfer Pricing.

items.prompt: (a) Explain how the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines allocate the return from an intangible among members of a multinational group, including the roles of legal ownership, DEMPE functions, assets and risk.

answer.model:
Chapter VI of the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines starts from the accurate delineation of the controlled transaction: the intangible is identified, the legal ownership and contractual terms are noted, and then the conduct of the parties is compared with the contract through a functional analysis. Legal ownership, by itself, does not entitle the owner to the whole return. The owner is entitled to the return from exploiting the intangible only if it performs and controls the important functions and bears and controls the risks, and has the financial capacity to bear them.

The functions in question are development, enhancement, maintenance, protection and exploitation, abbreviated DEMPE. Of these, the Guidelines treat as important functions such matters as the design and control of research and development programmes, the control of budgets and strategic decisions about the protection of the intangible, and the decisions on defence against infringement. Group members that perform these functions are entitled to arm's length compensation, and in some cases to a share of the residual return, particularly where their contribution is unique and valuable.

An entity that only funds the development, and has the financial capacity but does not control the risk, is entitled only to a risk free return on its funding, not to a premium for the risk. Using the six step analysis of risk in Chapter I, the Guidelines ask which entity controls the risk and has the capability to assess and decide, and allocate risk accordingly. If the legal owner does not perform or control the DEMPE functions, it is entitled only to an arm's length compensation for any functions it does perform, which could be little more than a return for holding title. The UN Manual on Transfer Pricing adds a focus on location specific advantages and local market features which can create value in the market jurisdiction, and which may give that State an argument for a larger share of profit.

points.point: States that accurate delineation looks at contract terms and the actual conduct of the parties
States that legal ownership alone does not entitle the owner to the return
Names and defines DEMPE
Identifies important functions (control of R&D, budget and protection decisions)
Explains control over risk and financial capacity as the conditions for entitlement to the risk related return
States that a funder without control of risk earns a risk free return
States that DEMPE contributors are compensated at arm's length or share residual profit where contributions are unique and valuable
Refers to UN Manual emphasis on location specific advantages and local market features

items.prompt: (b) Critically evaluate the DEMPE based approach. Does it improve the allocation of profit from intangibles compared with the contractual ownership approach, and what difficulties does it create?

answer.model:
The strength of the DEMPE approach is that it aligns profit with the functions that create value and so is harder to manipulate. Under a contractual ownership approach a group could place an intangible in a low tax entity with no staff, and claim the whole residual return for the cost of a few legal documents. Independent parties would not accept that a passive owner with no capability would take the upside.

There are, however, difficulties. It is hard to identify and weigh the contribution of each group member. Development may be carried out by several teams in different States, marketing may add as much value as the underlying technology, and the Guidelines accept that where several members make unique and valuable contributions, a transactional profit split may be the most appropriate method, which brings its own uncertainty about splitting factors. The idea of control also requires judgement: an entity must have the capability and actually exercise the decision making, and this turns on evidence such as who has the people, who takes the decisions and where. Different States may weigh the same evidence differently and take inconsistent positions, resulting in double taxation that must then be resolved under the mutual agreement procedure.

There is also the compliance cost of documenting these decisions, and the risk of retrospective challenge. On the other hand the approach creates a real incentive to align substance, with people and decisions, where the returns are booked, which is a result that BEPS Actions 8 to 10 sought. Critics argue that the approach departs from what independent parties do, since in third party arrangements a financier or a passive licensor frequently earns a contractual return without performing DEMPE functions, and that the approach is hard to apply to acquired intangibles.

Overall the approach is a reasonable improvement on pure contractual ownership as a protection against base erosion, but it increases the need for evidence and the likelihood of disputes. It works best where the facts about who does what are clear and documented.

points.point: Explains that it aligns return with value creating functions
Explains the weakness of the contractual ownership approach (passive owner with no capability)
Identifies the difficulty of identifying and weighing DEMPE contributions
Notes that a profit split may be needed where contributions are unique and valuable
Discusses the control concept and its evidential basis
Identifies the risk of conflicting positions and double taxation, with MAP as the remedy
Identifies compliance cost or retrospective challenge
Notes the incentive to align substance and the criticism that it departs from arrangements between independent parties
Reaches a reasoned overall conclusion

items.prompt: (c) Explain the guidance on hard to value intangibles and assess whether the use of ex post outcomes is consistent with the arm's length principle.

answer.model:
Hard to value intangibles (HTVI) are intangibles, or rights in intangibles, for which at the time of the transaction no reliable comparables exist and the projections of future cash flows or income, or the assumptions used in valuing them, are highly uncertain, so that it is difficult to predict the level of eventual success. The guidance, added by the 2017 Guidelines and carried into the 2022 edition, addresses the information asymmetry between taxpayer and tax authority: at the time of the transaction the group knows far more about the prospects than the authority.

The tax authority may use the actual outcomes (ex post results) as presumptive evidence about the appropriateness of the pricing arrangements agreed at the time, and may make adjustments. The presumption can be rebutted by the taxpayer. The exemptions are broadly where the taxpayer provides details of the ex ante projections and shows that these were properly prepared, with proper regard to foreseeable events and risks, and the significant difference between projections and outcomes is due to unforeseeable developments; or the transaction is covered by a bilateral or multilateral advance pricing arrangement; or the difference between the outcome and the projections does not change the compensation determined at the time of the transaction by more than 20 per cent; or a commercialisation period of five years has passed since the first unrelated party revenues, in which the difference from the projections did not exceed 20 per cent.

The reasoning is that independent parties, faced with the same uncertainty, would have used a price adjustment clause or a shorter term, so the authority is entitled to apply the price that independent parties would have agreed. Critics argue this is hindsight, which is contrary to the arm's length principle's focus on conditions at the time of the transaction, and creates uncertainty. The safeguards, the exemptions and the focus on tax authorities' use of outcomes only as evidence about what could have been foreseen, limit the effect. Overall, the approach is consistent with the principle if the outcomes are used as a pointer to what was foreseeable and not as a basis to reprice.

points.point: Defines HTVI (no reliable comparables, highly uncertain projections)
Explains the information asymmetry rationale
States that ex post outcomes are presumptive evidence of the ex ante pricing
States that the presumption may be rebutted by the taxpayer through documented ex ante projections and unforeseeable developments
States the exemptions for an APA, a difference of less than 20 per cent, and a five year commercialisation period
Explains that independent parties would have used a price adjustment clause or short term
Presents the hindsight criticism
Concludes on consistency with the arm's length principle, noting the safeguards

answer.grader_note: Accept a description of the exemptions that is accurate even if the order differs.

title: A royalty adjustment and the treaty process
scenario: Harrow Plc is a company resident in State P. It owns patents that it licenses to its wholly owned subsidiary, Tessel Ltd, resident in State Q. In Year 3 Tessel paid Harrow a royalty of 1,000,000 and deducted it in computing profits in State Q. The tax authority in State Q audited Tessel. On 14 March Year 4 it sent Tessel its first written notice that it considered an arm's length royalty to be 700,000. The audit notice was followed by a formal assessment on 10 November Year 4, reducing Tessel's royalty deduction by 300,000. Tessel appealed to the court in State Q and the appeal is pending. State P taxed the whole 1,000,000 royalty received by Harrow in Year 3 and has made no adjustment. The tax rates are 30 per cent in State Q and 20 per cent in State P. The treaty between State P and State Q follows the OECD Model, including Article 9(2) and Article 25 with the arbitration provision in paragraph 5. On 20 February Year 7 Harrow filed a written request for mutual agreement procedure with the competent authority of State P. State P's competent authority sent the case to the competent authority of State Q on 15 March Year 7. State Q's competent authority confirmed on 1 June Year 7 that it had received all the information it needed to begin substantive consideration of the case. Harrow's directors are asking what they may expect. All figures are illustrative.

exhibits.caption: Facts about the royalty (illustrative)

items.prompt: (a) Advise whether Harrow's request is within the time limit in Article 25(1) of the OECD Model, and state the earliest date on which Harrow could ask for arbitration under Article 25(5).

answer.model:
Article 25(1) allows a person who considers that the actions of one or both States result or will result in taxation not in accordance with the treaty to present the case to the competent authority of either State (the 2017 and later OECD text; older OECD text refers to the State of residence, and the wording in the UN Model depends on the edition, so check it). The case must be presented within three years of the first notification of the action resulting in taxation not in accordance with the treaty. Harrow is resident in State P and filed with State P's competent authority, which is the correct place. The first notification can be argued to be the written notice of 14 March Year 4 or the assessment of 10 November Year 4. Three years from the earlier date is 14 March Year 7, and filing on 20 February Year 7 is inside that period, so the request is in time whichever date is taken.

Article 25(5) provides that unresolved issues are submitted to arbitration at the request of the person who presented the case, where the competent authorities have not reached agreement within two years from the presentation of the case to the competent authority of the other State. In the OECD text the period runs from the date on which all the information required by the competent authority of the other State to begin substantive consideration has been provided. That date is 1 June Year 7, not 20 February or 15 March, so two years runs to 1 June Year 9, and Harrow could request arbitration from that date, if the competent authorities have not resolved the case.

points.point: States that the case may be presented to the competent authority of either State (Harrow chose State P, its State of residence) and that the time limit is three years from first notification
Considers both the notice of 14 March Year 4 and the assessment of 10 November Year 4 as possible start dates
Concludes that the request is in time on either view
States the arbitration trigger of two years from when the information needed to begin substantive consideration is provided
Calculates 1 June Year 9 and rejects the earlier dates

answer.grader_note: Credit a correct statement that domestic time limits are not relevant to the treaty three year period.

items.prompt: (b) Calculate the amount of tax that is paid twice as a result of State Q's adjustment, the effect of a full corresponding adjustment by State P, and the cost to the group that no corresponding adjustment can remove.

answer.model:
State Q treats 300,000 of the royalty as Tessel's profit. Additional State Q tax = 300,000 x 30% = 90,000.

State P taxed the same 300,000 as Harrow's royalty income. State P tax on it = 300,000 x 20% = 60,000. So the 300,000 is taxed in State Q (90,000) and again in State P (60,000), a total of 150,000 on the same income.

If State P agrees with the adjustment and makes a corresponding adjustment under Article 9(2), Harrow's income falls by 300,000 and State P refunds 60,000. The income is then taxed only in State Q, with total tax of 90,000. The double taxation eliminated is therefore 60,000, the tax paid in State P on the 300,000.

The corresponding adjustment does not return the group to the position before the audit. Before the audit the 300,000 was taxed in State P at 20%, a tax of 60,000 on the group. After the adjustment and relief, the same income bears 90,000 in State Q. The group is worse off by 90,000 minus 60,000 = 30,000, which reflects the 10 percentage point difference in rates applied to 300,000 (10% x 300,000 = 30,000). The treaty gives relief from double taxation and not from the rate difference, so the 30,000 cannot be recovered through the mutual agreement procedure. Interest and any penalties charged by State Q are not dealt with here.

points.point: Calculates State Q additional tax: 300,000 x 30% = 90,000
Calculates State P tax on the same income: 300,000 x 20% = 60,000
States that 150,000 is taxed in total on the same 300,000, with 60,000 the double tax
States that a corresponding adjustment gives a refund of 60,000 in State P, leaving 90,000 total
Calculates the residual cost of 30,000 as the rate difference (10% x 300,000)
Explains that the treaty relieves double taxation but not the rate difference

items.prompt: (c) Advise Harrow whether State P is obliged to make a corresponding adjustment under Article 9(2), and what the competent authorities must do under Article 25.

answer.model: Article 9(2) provides that where one State includes in the profits of an enterprise, and taxes accordingly, profits on which an enterprise of the other State has been charged to tax in that other State, and the profits so included are profits which would have accrued to the enterprise of the first State if the conditions had been those between independent enterprises, then the other State shall make an appropriate adjustment to the amount of the tax charged on those profits. The adjustment is conditional: State P must agree that the adjustment made by State Q is justified in principle and in amount. State P is not bound to accept State Q's figure of 700,000 without examination, and if it does not agree it should consult State Q. Under Article 25(2), the competent authority of State P, if it considers the objection to be justified and it is not itself able to arrive at a satisfactory solution, shall endeavour to resolve the case by mutual agreement with the competent authority of State Q, with a view to the avoidance of taxation not in accordance with the treaty. That is an obligation of best endeavours and does not guarantee agreement, which is the reason for arbitration. Any agreement must be implemented notwithstanding any time limits in the domestic law of the States. If the competent authorities have not resolved the case within the two year period, Harrow may request arbitration and the arbitrators could decide the price in dispute.

points.point: States the Article 9(2) condition that State P must agree the adjustment is justified in principle and amount
States that State P is not bound to accept State Q's figure, and should consult
States the Article 25(2) duty to endeavour to resolve by mutual agreement if the objection appears justified
Explains that this is a duty of best endeavours and not a duty to reach agreement
States that agreements are implemented notwithstanding domestic time limits
Links the lack of a duty to agree with the arbitration provision

items.prompt: (d) Advise on how the arbitration process under Article 25(5) works and its limits, including whether Harrow's pending domestic appeal in State Q matters.

answer.model:
Article 25(5) of the OECD Model (the arbitration paragraph keeps this number in the OECD Model 2025, which added only a new paragraph 6 on the GATS to Article 25) provides that where a person has presented a case to the competent authority of a State under paragraph 1 on the ground that the actions of one or both States have resulted in taxation not in accordance with the treaty, and the competent authorities cannot resolve the case within two years of the relevant date, any unresolved issues shall, if the person so requests in writing, be submitted to arbitration. The decision is binding on both States, unless a person directly affected by the case does not accept the mutual agreement that implements the arbitration decision, and it must be implemented notwithstanding any time limits in domestic law. The arbitration is not available where a decision on these issues has already been rendered by a court or administrative tribunal of either State.

That last point matters for Harrow. Tessel has a pending appeal in State Q. If the court gives a decision on the arm's length royalty before the arbitration starts, the arbitration cannot decide the same issues. Many competent authorities require the taxpayer to suspend or withdraw domestic proceedings, or agree to accept the result, before they will accept a case, so Harrow should plan the order of events and take advice about the position in State Q.

The arbitration provision is not universal. Paragraph 5 appears in the OECD Model, and States include it only if they negotiate it. The UN Model offers arbitration as an optional Alternative B of Article 25 (paragraph 5: three years from presentation of the case to the other competent authority, and either competent authority may request it, unlike the OECD rule where the person requests after two years); there is no Article 25A. The MLI offers an optional arbitration part to those States that choose it, and many have not. The Action 14 minimum standard requires access to mutual agreement and timely resolution, with a target of an average of 24 months, but it does not require arbitration. Since the facts say this treaty includes the provision, Harrow should keep its right alive by documenting the date of complete information and making a written request on the due date.

points.point: States the two year trigger and the written request by the person who presented the case
States that the decision is binding on the States, subject to the taxpayer's right not to accept the implementing agreement
States that arbitration is unavailable where a court or tribunal has already decided the issues
Applies this to Tessel's pending appeal in State Q and the need to plan the order of proceedings
Notes that competent authorities may require domestic proceedings to be suspended or withdrawn
Notes that arbitration is optional (OECD text only if negotiated, MLI optional part, UN Model optional article)
Refers to the Action 14 minimum standard (access to MAP, 24 month target) which does not itself require arbitration

answer.grader_note: Credit accurate statements about the UN Model arbitration article without requiring numbering. The 24 month average target is the Action 14 peer review benchmark.

title: A group with entities in three low tax places
scenario: Calder Group is a multinational group within the scope of the Pillar Two GloBE rules. Its ultimate parent entity, Calder Holdings, is resident in State U, which has implemented an income inclusion rule consistent with the GloBE Model Rules and owns 100 per cent of every subsidiary. Three subsidiaries are relevant. Rowan Ltd operates in State R, which has no minimum tax of any kind. Quill Ltd operates in State Q, which has introduced a qualified domestic minimum top-up tax (QDMTT) that is also a qualified rule for the purposes of the safe harbour for such taxes. Birch Ltd operates in State B, which has no minimum tax. Each is the only constituent entity in its jurisdiction. For fiscal year 2026 the percentages that apply for the substance-based income exclusion are assumed, for this exercise only, to be 8 per cent of eligible payroll costs and 6 per cent of the carrying value of eligible tangible assets (a simplification: the GloBE transition percentages start at 10 and 8 per cent and decline each year). Assume that GloBE income equals the profit before tax shown in the country by country report and that covered taxes equal the income tax expense shown there. The group wishes to know its Pillar Two position for the year and whether safe harbours are available. All figures are illustrative.

exhibits.caption: Entity data for fiscal year 2026 (illustrative)

items.prompt: (a) Calculate the jurisdictional top-up tax for Rowan, using the GloBE rules without any safe harbour.

answer.model:
Step 1, effective tax rate: covered taxes ÷ GloBE income = 600,000 ÷ 10,000,000 = 6%.
Step 2, top-up tax percentage: minimum rate 15% minus 6% = 9%.
Step 3, substance-based income exclusion: payroll carve-out = 8% x 2,000,000 = 160,000; tangible asset carve-out = 6% x 5,000,000 = 300,000; total = 460,000.
Step 4, excess profit: GloBE income minus the exclusion = 10,000,000 minus 460,000 = 9,540,000.
Step 5, top-up tax = 9% x 9,540,000 = 858,600.
State R has no qualified domestic minimum top-up tax, so State R collects nothing. The top-up tax is allocated first to the income inclusion rule in State U, which, as the owner of 100 per cent, charges the whole 858,600 on Calder Holdings. If State U had no such rule the undertaxed profits rule would be the backstop. If State R later introduces a QDMTT, the amount would be collected there and would reduce what State U may charge.

points.point: Calculates the ETR of 6% and top-up percentage of 9%
Calculates the payroll carve-out of 160,000
Calculates the tangible asset carve-out of 300,000 and total of 460,000
Calculates excess profit of 9,540,000
Calculates top-up tax of 858,600
States that the income inclusion rule in State U collects the top-up tax because State R has no QDMTT
Notes that the undertaxed profits rule is the backstop and that a later QDMTT in State R would take priority

items.prompt: (b) Calculate the top-up tax for Quill and explain how the QDMTT in State Q affects the income inclusion rule in State U.

answer.model:
ETR = 400,000 ÷ 4,000,000 = 10%. Top-up tax percentage = 15% minus 10% = 5%. Substance-based income exclusion: payroll = 8% x 500,000 = 40,000; tangible assets = 6% x 1,000,000 = 60,000; total = 100,000. Excess profit = 4,000,000 minus 100,000 = 3,900,000. Top-up tax = 5% x 3,900,000 = 195,000.

Because State Q has a QDMTT, the 195,000 is charged in State Q on Quill. The QDMTT is designed to be computed on the GloBE basis, so the amount collected locally is the same as the jurisdictional top-up tax, and the jurisdictional top-up tax that would otherwise be charged by State U's income inclusion rule is reduced by the QDMTT paid to nil. State Q therefore collects the revenue, and not State U, and the group pays 195,000 in total and not twice. Where the QDMTT is also within the QDMTT safe harbour, State U may treat the top-up tax for State Q as zero for IIR purposes without recomputing it.

points.point: Calculates ETR of 10% and top-up percentage of 5%
Calculates the exclusion of 100,000
Calculates excess profit of 3,900,000
Calculates top-up tax of 195,000
States that the QDMTT is collected in State Q and the IIR top-up tax is reduced by the QDMTT paid
Refers to the QDMTT safe harbour as removing the need for State U to recompute

items.prompt: (c) Advise the group on whether the transitional country by country reporting safe harbour could apply to Rowan, Quill and Birch for fiscal year 2026, and discuss what the safe harbours and the OECD's January 2026 side by side package mean for the group.

answer.model:
The transitional country by country reporting safe harbour deems the top-up tax for a jurisdiction to be zero if one of three tests is met on the basis of qualified country by country report data. The de minimis test needs revenue and profit below low thresholds, and the revenue is above the threshold in all three jurisdictions, so it does not apply. The simplified effective tax rate test needs a rate at or above a transitional rate, which is 17 per cent for fiscal years beginning in 2026. Rowan has 6 per cent (600,000 ÷ 10,000,000) and Quill 10 per cent (400,000 ÷ 4,000,000), and Birch has 1 per cent (8,000 ÷ 800,000), so none meet it. The routine profits test needs profit before tax at or below the substance-based income exclusion for the jurisdiction. For Rowan, profit of 10,000,000 exceeds the exclusion of 460,000, and for Quill 4,000,000 exceeds 100,000, so neither passes. For Birch, the exclusion is 8% x 6,000,000 = 480,000 plus 6% x 7,000,000 = 420,000, a total of 900,000, and profit of 800,000 is below it, so Birch passes the routine profits test and its top-up tax is deemed zero. Without the safe harbour Birch would also have no top-up tax, since excess profit would be nil, so the safe harbour saves compliance work and not tax.

Rowan therefore has top-up tax of 858,600 collected through State U's rule. Quill's top-up tax is collected by State Q, and the QDMTT safe harbour would apply if the State Q rules meet the conditions, relieving State U from computing the top-up tax for State Q.

The transitional safe harbour is time limited: the January 2026 package extended it by one year to fiscal years beginning on or before 31 December 2027 (with 17 per cent also applying for 2027), and it then expires, so the group must plan for the full computation afterwards. The side by side package, published by the OECD Inclusive Framework in January 2026, adds a safe harbour for groups whose ultimate parent entity is in a jurisdiction with a qualifying side by side regime, a related safe harbour from the undertaxed profits rule for qualifying parent jurisdictions, and further simplifications, including a simplified effective tax rate safe harbour and a safe harbour for tax incentives that relates to the substance-based income exclusion. It leaves QDMTTs unaffected, so State Q's QDMTT continues to apply even if a group qualifies for a safe harbour. Since State U has an ordinary income inclusion rule consistent with the Model Rules, the side by side safe harbour for qualifying regimes would not apply to this group in its own right. Details and start dates should be checked against the OECD text.

points.point: States that the safe harbour deems the top-up tax to be zero if one of three tests is met on qualified CbCR data
Rejects the de minimis test on the facts (revenue above threshold)
States the transitional simplified ETR of 17% for 2026 and shows that Rowan (6%), Quill (10%) and Birch (1%) fail
Applies the routine profits test and shows Rowan and Quill fail
Calculates Birch's exclusion of 900,000 and shows that Birch passes the routine profits test
Observes that Birch would have no top-up tax without the safe harbour, which saves compliance and not tax
States that the QDMTT safe harbour can relieve State U for Quill and that Rowan's tax is collected through State U
States that the transitional safe harbour is time limited
Describes the January 2026 side by side package accurately (side by side safe harbour for qualifying regimes, related UTPR safe harbours, simplified ETR, QDMTTs unaffected)
Concludes that the side by side safe harbour does not apply because State U has an ordinary IIR

answer.grader_note: Credit hedged wording on the exact dates of the side by side safe harbours. The 17% rate for 2026 is the transitional safe harbour rate (15% for 2024, 16% for 2025, 17% for 2026).

title: Reach of tax jurisdiction and the limits of enforcement
scenario: A commentator writes: 'A State may impose tax on whatever it chooses, provided it has some connection with the taxpayer. Its real limit is not the right to tax but the ability to collect, because no State will enforce another State's tax claim.' Several States now tax their citizens on worldwide income wherever resident, and some require foreign financial institutions to report on accounts held by their nationals.

items.prompt: (a) Explain the connecting factors on which States base jurisdiction to tax and the limits that public international law places on the exercise of that jurisdiction.

answer.model: States exercise jurisdiction to tax by reference to a connection between the taxpayer or the income and the taxing State. The principal connecting factors are residence (or domicile), which supports taxation of worldwide income on a personal or unlimited basis; source or situs, which supports taxation of income arising in, or assets located in, the territory on a limited or territorial basis; and, in a minority of States, citizenship or nationality, which supports worldwide taxation regardless of residence. Presence, permanent establishment and the location of immovable property operate as refinements of source. Public international law recognises that sovereignty over territory and over persons gives a State jurisdiction to prescribe. The accepted view is that there must be a genuine or substantial link between the State and the person or transaction taxed. Public international law has few binding rules that confine tax jurisdiction: there is no general prohibition on taxing worldwide income on a thin link, and State practice is wide. The constraint is therefore weak in respect of prescriptive jurisdiction (the power to make and apply tax law) but strong in respect of enforcement jurisdiction, which is territorial: a State may not send its officials to exercise coercive powers such as seizure or audit on another State's soil without consent. The consequence of overlapping claims is international double taxation, which is relieved by unilateral rules and by treaties rather than by any rule of customary law. A good answer notes that an unreasonable exercise of jurisdiction may be challenged as an abuse of right, but that this has rarely been applied to tax.

points.point: identifies residence/domicile as a connecting factor supporting worldwide taxation
identifies source/situs as a connecting factor supporting territorial taxation
identifies citizenship/nationality as a connecting factor used by a minority of States
distinguishes unlimited from limited tax liability
states that international law requires a genuine or substantial link or recognises sovereignty over territory and persons
recognises that international law places few binding limits on prescriptive tax jurisdiction
states that enforcement jurisdiction is territorial and consent is needed for acts on foreign soil

items.prompt: (b) Discuss how far one State can enforce its tax claims across borders, referring to the revenue rule, the main treaty and multilateral provisions on assistance in collection, and the difficulties that remain.

answer.model: Traditionally courts in many common law States have refused to enforce the revenue laws of another State, the revenue rule. Government of India v Taylor (House of Lords, 1955) is the usual authority: a claim for foreign tax was not enforceable in the English courts, because enforcing it would be an exercise of foreign sovereign power. The rule rests on respect for sovereignty and on the reluctance of courts to adjudicate on foreign public law. In reply, States have created consensual routes. Article 27 of the OECD Model and Article 27 of the UN Model (assistance in the collection of taxes) provide for the Contracting States to lend assistance in collecting revenue claims. The UN article, added in 2011, follows the OECD article (added in 2003), which obliges assistance to be given subject to safeguards, but the UN Commentary notes that States may limit or omit it where they prefer. Article 26 on exchange of information supports enforcement indirectly by allowing a State to find the taxpayer's assets. The Convention on Mutual Administrative Assistance in Tax Matters (as amended by the 2010 Protocol) extends assistance in recovery and service of documents among many parties, including developing countries. EU Directives provide a further route within the Union. Difficulties remain. Assistance depends on a final enforceable claim in the requesting State and on a treaty or convention in force with the requested State. Safeguards usually let the requested State refuse where this would conflict with public policy or require action contrary to its laws or administrative practice, and a requested State will not usually collect a claim that is still under appeal. Costs, priority against local creditors, and unequal administrative capacity weaken practical value. Some States reserve the right to refuse assistance for taxes owed by their own nationals. Pure unilateral reach by reporting rules and withholding on payments (for example, imposing duties on financial institutions in order to find assets) is often more effective than formal enforcement.

points.point: states the revenue rule and that foreign tax claims are not enforced by domestic courts
cites Government of India v Taylor correctly
explains the reason (sovereignty, non-adjudication of foreign public law)
identifies Article 27 of the OECD and UN Models as the treaty basis for assistance in collection
identifies Article 26 exchange of information as supporting enforcement
identifies the multilateral Convention on Mutual Administrative Assistance
explains at least two limits, e.g. final claim needed, public policy refusal, appeals, priority and cost

answer.grader_note: A statement that the OECD Model contained Article 27 only from 2003 is correct and creditable. Do not require paragraph numbers.

items.prompt: (c) Critically evaluate whether the commentator is right that enforcement, rather than jurisdiction, is the real limit on a State's taxing power, using citizenship-based taxation and reporting obligations on foreign financial institutions as examples.

answer.model: The proposition is largely right on the law but incomplete on the facts. On prescriptive jurisdiction it is correct that public international law does not impose a clear ceiling: a State may tax residents, source income and, if it chooses, its nationals, and it is the lack of a rule of customary law preventing worldwide taxation that explains the wide variety of State practice. Citizenship-based taxation shows both sides. It extends taxation to non-residents on a nationality link only, which most States regard as legitimate in principle but do not use, partly because of administrative burden, double taxation and the difficulty of collecting from persons who live and hold their assets abroad. A State that applies it relies on voluntary compliance, on the taxpayer's remaining assets within the jurisdiction, and on exit and passport consequences, which are practical rather than legal enforcement, and relief from double tax is given by credit and treaty saving clauses. Reporting obligations on foreign financial institutions show that the supposed limit on enforcement can be circumvented without crossing borders: the State imposes duties on institutions that have a link to it, often backed by withholding, and enters intergovernmental agreements that provide reciprocal automatic exchange. This has changed the position of non-compliant taxpayers more than formal assistance in collection ever did. Two points weaken the proposition. First, human rights and constitutional limits, for example on retrospective legislation and on the protection of privacy, restrict how a State may use its powers, and some critics argue that extraterritorial duties on foreign institutions exceed the permitted reach of jurisdiction. Second, enforcement is not wholly absent, since cooperation under Articles 26 and 27 and the multilateral Convention continues to grow. The balanced conclusion is that jurisdiction is wide in law, enforcement is the practical constraint, but modern cooperation and information flows are narrowing the gap, so the commentator describes the traditional position rather than the present one.

points.point: states a clear position on the proposition
explains that international law sets few limits on prescriptive jurisdiction
analyses citizenship-based taxation: link, collection difficulty, double taxation relief
analyses reporting by foreign financial institutions as an indirect enforcement tool (withholding, intergovernmental agreements, automatic exchange)
identifies a counterpoint such as human rights, privacy, constitutional limits or growing cooperation
reaches a reasoned conclusion

answer.grader_note: Any reasoned conclusion is credited if supported. No need to name particular domestic statutes.

title: Standardised returns for routine distribution
scenario: A State with limited transfer pricing capacity is considering whether to apply the OECD simplified and streamlined approach for baseline marketing and distribution activities. Its tax authority says that the approach will give certainty and cut disputes. A multinational group says that it will produce returns that do not reflect the actual facts of its local distributor and may produce double taxation.

items.prompt: (a) Explain the purpose and scope of Pillar One Amount B and how it relates to the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines and the arm's length principle.

answer.model: Amount B is the part of Pillar One designed to simplify and streamline the application of the arm's length principle to in-country baseline marketing and distribution activities, with a particular concern for jurisdictions with limited transfer pricing capacity. It is distinct from Amount A, which would reallocate a share of residual profit of very large multinationals to market jurisdictions but whose multilateral convention was never opened for signature, whereas Amount B is an optional annex to Chapter IV of the Transfer Pricing Guidelines. Amount B does not create a new taxing right and does not depart from the arm's length principle: it is a pricing method for qualifying transactions, and the Inclusive Framework approved the report in February 2024; the OECD published a consolidated report in February 2025 and the text was incorporated into the Transfer Pricing Guidelines as an annex to Chapter IV. Jurisdictions may elect to apply it to fiscal years beginning on or after 1 January 2025. Scope is set by qualitative criteria (a transaction in which a related party buys goods for wholesale resale, or acts as a sales agent or commissionaire, performing baseline distribution activities, with the distributor as the tested party, not owning unique and valuable intangibles or assuming economically significant risks such as those that go beyond ordinary distribution) and by quantitative criteria, including thresholds based on operating expenses against net revenue. Certain transactions such as distribution of commodities or non-tangible goods and services are outside scope. The outcome is a return on sales derived from a pricing matrix based on industry grouping and on operating asset and operating expense intensity, which is applied to the tested party.

points.point: describes Amount B as a simplified approach to baseline marketing and distribution
distinguishes Amount B from Amount A
states that it applies the arm's length principle and creates no new taxing right
states that it is incorporated in the Transfer Pricing Guidelines and optional for fiscal years beginning on or after 1 January 2025
identifies at least two scope conditions (qualitative and quantitative, tested party, no unique intangibles, risk limits, exclusions)

answer.grader_note: Do not credit specific matrix returns or exact quantitative thresholds unless correct for the year; the report allows some choice of jurisdictional thresholds.

items.prompt: (b) Critically evaluate the arguments for and against the approach, taking the positions of the tax authority and of the multinational group.

answer.model: For the tax authority, a rules-based outcome gives certainty and consistency, reduces the need for comparability searches and for scarce database access, shortens audits, and should reduce mutual agreement cases and double taxation because tested parties in different jurisdictions face the same matrix. For a developing State, a conforming return cannot usually be challenged by the group once the approach is applied, so it can move audit resources elsewhere. There is also a safe-harbour feature: qualifying transactions priced in line with the matrix are respected by the other jurisdiction, which should be taxing the distributor's counterparty, if it adopts the approach, or if the matrix is applied by a covered jurisdiction, in which case Inclusive Framework members have committed, subject to their domestic law, to respect the outcome. Against that, the group argues that a matrix built from a global dataset may not fit a specific market: a distributor with high local costs, a market-entry year, a downturn or an unusual local structure may earn a lower return at arm's length, and the application of a uniform return may overstate profit and cause double taxation if the other State does not accept the outcome. Eligibility criteria may exclude marginal cases, producing uncertainty about whether the approach applies at all. There is also a risk of systematic bias: if the tax authority treats the matrix as a floor and the group as a ceiling, a method intended to simplify can become a source of disputes. The approach is optional, and its interaction with domestic rules, with documentation and with Article 9 corresponding adjustments requires care. A reasoned conclusion would say that the approach gives most value to low-capacity States with many small distributors, is least suited to complex or loss-making distributors, and depends for its effectiveness on broad adoption and on whether the data-poor fall-back mechanism is credible.

points.point: tax authority: certainty, consistency and reduced administrative burden
tax authority: fewer disputes and less double taxation if adopted widely
group: matrix may not reflect local facts (costs, market entry, downturn)
group: risk of double taxation if the counterparty State does not accept the outcome
scope and eligibility uncertainty or risk of the matrix being treated as a floor
reaches a reasoned conclusion on suitability or conditions for success

items.prompt: (c) Discuss how an Amount B return should interact with Article 9 and Article 7 of the OECD and UN Models, and what the State should do to protect its position under treaties.

answer.model: Amount B is a pricing approach under the arm's length principle that underlies Article 9 (associated enterprises) and, through the Authorised OECD Approach, Article 7. A return derived from the matrix is therefore intended to be a result which both States can accept as arm's length. However, the treaty obligation to give a corresponding adjustment under Article 9(2) arises where one State adjusts profits and the other agrees that the adjustment is justified. If the distributor's State applies Amount B and the supplier's State does not, the latter could refuse a corresponding adjustment unless it accepts the method. The Inclusive Framework addressed this by a political commitment, subject to each member's domestic legislation and administrative practices, to respect the Amount B outcome where a covered jurisdiction applies it; this is not a treaty obligation. For other cases, the mutual agreement procedure under Article 25 (and arbitration where the treaty provides it) remains the protection. The UN Model Article 9 follows the OECD in paragraphs 1 and 2 (it adds a paragraph 3 on fraud, gross negligence or wilful default) and the UN Practical Manual on Transfer Pricing has traditionally given weight to local conditions, so a State using the UN Model may wish to document that the matrix return reflects local market features. For Article 7, the approach is relevant where a baseline distribution activity is carried on through a permanent establishment, with any attribution still under the AOA (UN Article 7 keeps its limited force of attraction and its rule denying deductions for royalties, fees, commissions and interest paid by the permanent establishment to the head office). Practical steps: legislate the election with clear scope criteria and documentation duties; give notice of the approach to treaty partners; adopt a procedure for taxpayers to rebut where facts differ; and align MAP guidance so that Amount B cases are handled consistently.

points.point: explains that Amount B applies the arm's length principle underlying Article 9
explains the corresponding adjustment issue under Article 9(2) where the other State does not accept the method
identifies MAP under Article 25 as the remedy
notes the commitment by Inclusive Framework members in respect of covered jurisdictions
notes the position under the UN Model or the UN Practical Manual and Article 7 where a PE is involved
gives at least two practical steps for the State

answer.grader_note: Credit any sensible practical steps. A statement that Amount B overrides treaty rules is wrong.

title: Companies that combine across borders
scenario: The board of Tarn Holdings, resident in State R, is considering a merger with a company resident in State S. Tarn Holdings would absorb the target, with the target's shareholders receiving Tarn shares. The target holds assets with large unrealised gains, owns a branch in a third State, and has tax losses. Advisers say that the transaction can be tax neutral if properly structured, but that treaties do not deal with mergers and that anti-abuse rules may deny relief.

items.prompt: (a) Identify and explain the principal tax issues that arise on a cross-border merger for the companies and for their shareholders.

answer.model: The main issues are these. First, the transfer of assets from the absorbed company to the acquirer is, in many States, a disposal at market value, which triggers a charge on unrealised gains (including goodwill and intangibles) unless relief applies. Second, where the absorbed company leaves State S, State S may apply exit taxation to assets which cease to be subject to its taxing rights, and the acquirer may need to establish a base cost in State R. Third, for the shareholders, the exchange of target shares for acquirer shares is a disposal that may give rise to a gain, with the issue of the State in which that gain is taxable (Article 13 of the OECD and UN Models, with differing rules for shares deriving value from immovable property and for substantial holdings). Fourth, tax attributes of the absorbed company, such as losses, credits and reserves, may be lost or limited on a change of control or on the transfer. Fifth, the merged company's residence (Article 4) and the creation of permanent establishments, for example in State S and in the third State where the target holds a branch, determine where profits are taxed afterwards, and the branch may involve its own relief or exit rules in the third State. Sixth, transfer taxes, withholding tax on distributions, and indirect taxes may arise. Finally, treaty benefits may be lost when the identity or residence of the owner changes, which engages the principal purpose test in Article 7 of the MLI and the entitlement to benefits rules in Article 29 of the OECD and UN Models (including the principal purpose test).

points.point: asset transfer treated as disposal at market value
exit taxation by the State of the absorbed company
shareholder gain on exchange and relevance of Article 13
loss of tax attributes such as losses or credits
residence under Article 4 and PE issues, including the third State branch
anti-treaty-shopping or other leakage such as withholding or transfer tax

items.prompt: (b) Explain the solutions that States have adopted to make cross-border mergers tax neutral and the conditions and limits attached to them.

answer.model: The principal solution is deferral through rollover or reorganisation relief: the gain is not taxed at the time of the merger but is carried into the acquirer's base cost, so tax is paid when the assets are later sold. Domestic law commonly extends this to foreign transactions subject to conditions. Within the European Union, the Merger Directive (2009/133/EC) requires Member States to give this deferral for mergers, divisions and transfers of assets between companies of different Member States, and for exchanges of shares, provided assets remain connected to a permanent establishment in the transferor's State, so that the State retains its taxing right over past gains. Where the transferred assets include a permanent establishment in another Member State, Article 10 of the Directive requires the transferor State to give a credit for the tax that would have been charged there; a branch in a non-Member (third) State falls outside the Directive and depends on domestic law. For shareholders, the exchange of shares is not taxed provided the shares are valued for tax by reference to the old shares. The Directive also allows the carry over of certain provisions and reserves. Conditions and limits include the rule that deferral is not available for a gain that leaves the taxing jurisdiction without an assurance of later taxation, so exit tax applies and the Court of Justice has held in National Grid Indus (2011) that exit tax is permitted but immediate recovery without a deferral option is disproportionate. Article 15 of the Directive allows Member States to refuse relief where the main objective or one of the main objectives is tax evasion or avoidance, and relief is typically denied where the merger is not for valid commercial reasons. The Court of Justice in Leur-Bloem (1997) required a case-by-case examination and not a blanket presumption. Outside the Union, bilateral treaties rarely provide relief, so the rule depends on domestic law and ruling practice.

points.point: explains rollover or deferral relief and carry over of base cost
states that domestic relief typically extends to foreign mergers subject to conditions
identifies the EU Merger Directive and its scope
explains that the State of the transferor must retain taxing right via a PE, and credit for tax of another Member State where relevant (third-State branch left to domestic law)
explains exit tax and the National Grid Indus principle
explains Article 15 anti-abuse or valid commercial reasons, and Leur-Bloem case-by-case approach

answer.grader_note: Credit equivalent reasoning for non-EU regimes. Case citations must be accurate: National Grid Indus (C-371/10) concerned immediate recovery on a transfer of place of management.

items.prompt: (c) Evaluate whether the OECD and UN Models and tax treaties deal adequately with cross-border mergers, and what the board should do given the advisers' concerns.

answer.model: Neither Model contains a specific merger article. Treaties address the consequences indirectly. Article 13 allocates taxing rights over gains on alienation, which will cover the asset transfer and the shareholder exchange, but does not itself give deferral: a State may therefore tax a gain that arises on the merger even though no cash has been received, producing a mismatch of timing with the other State's credit. Article 4 determines the residence of the merged entity, and the dual residence of a company is, in the OECD Model since 2017 and in the UN Model 2025, resolved by agreement between the competent authorities (the place of effective management tie-breaker no longer applies), which gives uncertainty. Article 5 governs PEs which result from the merger. Article 24 on non-discrimination may help where a foreign merger is treated less favourably than a domestic one, but the OECD Commentary limits its reach. Article 25 provides MAP for double taxation not otherwise relieved, but depends on a treaty being applicable to the persons and issues concerned. The treaty gap is partly filled by domestic relief and by regional law, but outside the EU it is thin and depends on rulings. The principal purpose test and Article 29 add a risk of denial of benefits. A balanced conclusion is that treaties allocate rights and limit double taxation after the event but do not provide neutrality. The board should obtain advance rulings in both States, document commercial reasons, map the loss and attribute position, consider a staged structure, and model the exit and branch tax position before committing, treating the advisers' concern about anti-abuse rules as a real but manageable risk.

points.point: states that neither Model has a merger-specific article
explains the role of Article 13 and the absence of deferral
Article 4 residence and the competent authority resolution of dual residence
PE issues under Article 5 and non-discrimination or MAP as partial protection
notes anti-abuse risk (principal purpose test or limitation on benefits)
gives reasoned advice such as rulings, documentation of commercial reasons and modelling
reaches an overall conclusion on adequacy

title: Meridian Holdings and its subsidiary in State T
scenario: Meridian Holdings plc is resident in State R. In Year 1 it holds 60 per cent of the votes, capital and profit entitlement of Sable Ltd, resident in State T, a low-tax State; an unrelated State T investor holds the other 40 per cent. Sable Ltd licenses intellectual property that was developed in State R and transferred to it, lends surplus cash to group companies, and also sells products to unrelated customers through its own local premises with 20 employees. State R has introduced controlled foreign company rules following the BEPS Action 3 recommendations. They apply to a foreign company which is controlled (more than 50 per cent of votes, capital or profit entitlement held by resident persons) and whose effective tax rate, measured on income computed under State R rules, is less than three quarters of the State R rate, which is 25 per cent. State R attributes to each resident shareholder the passive income (interest, royalties and similar income) of the CFC, in proportion to its shareholding, but excludes income from genuine trading carried on with local substance and excludes exempt dividends. The attributed income is taxed at the State R rate and State R gives credit for the foreign tax attributable to the attributed income. Meridian Holdings asks whether the rules apply, how much it must pay in State R, and whether it can resist the charge. All amounts are illustrative.

exhibits.caption: Year 1 figures for Sable Ltd (State T), amounts in a common currency unit, illustrative

items.prompt: (a) Explain the building blocks of effective CFC rules recommended in BEPS Action 3 and identify which of them are present in the State R rules described.

answer.model: Action 3 sets out six building blocks. First, rules for defining a CFC, including the definition of control (legal, economic or de facto) and of the entity covered. Second, CFC exemptions and threshold requirements, such as a low-tax exemption or a de minimis rule that focus the rules on entities subject to low tax. Third, a definition of CFC income, which may be a categorical, substance or excess profits approach. Fourth, rules for computing income, usually by the parent's rules, with limits on offsetting losses. Fifth, rules for attributing income to shareholders, by reference to the level of control or influence and the period of holding. Sixth, rules to prevent or eliminate double taxation, for example through credit for foreign tax actually paid and for tax paid on distributions or disposal. The State R rules contain all six: control above 50 per cent held by residents (building block 1), a low-rate test measured at three quarters of the State R rate (2), a categorical definition of passive income with a substance carve out for trading and exempt dividends (3), computation under State R rules (4), proportionate attribution (5) and credit for foreign tax (6).

points.point: lists the six building blocks correctly
identifies control and the low-tax exemption in the State R rules
identifies the CFC income definition, attribution and double tax relief in the State R rules
states that Action 3 offers recommendations and not a minimum standard

answer.grader_note: Credit 1 mark if the six blocks are listed with at most one error.

items.prompt: (b) Calculate whether Sable Ltd is a CFC, the CFC income attributable to Meridian Holdings, and the additional State R tax payable by Meridian Holdings after credit, showing each step.

answer.model: Control: Meridian Holdings, a State R resident, holds 60 per cent, which exceeds 50 per cent, so the control test is met. Effective tax rate: income under State R rules is 9,000,000 (the exempt dividends of 1,000,000 are excluded); State T tax is 540,000; the effective rate is 540,000 ÷ 9,000,000 = 6 per cent. The threshold is 25 per cent × 3/4 = 18.75 per cent. Because 6 per cent is below 18.75 per cent, Sable Ltd is a CFC. CFC income: interest 2,500,000 plus royalties 3,500,000 = 6,000,000. The trading profit of 3,000,000 is excluded on the facts because it is earned with local substance, and the dividends are exempt. Attribution at 60 per cent: 6,000,000 × 60% = 3,600,000. State R tax at 25 per cent: 3,600,000 × 25% = 900,000. Foreign tax attributable to the CFC income: State T tax of 6 per cent on 6,000,000 = 360,000 (6% × 6,000,000); Meridian's 60 per cent share of that = 216,000. Credit is limited to the State R tax on the same income, 900,000, so the full 216,000 is creditable. Additional State R tax = 900,000 − 216,000 = 684,000.

points.point: states that 60% exceeds the 50% control threshold so Sable is controlled
computes the effective rate of 6% (540,000 ÷ 9,000,000) using income net of exempt dividends
computes the threshold 18.75% and concludes that Sable is a CFC
identifies CFC income as 6,000,000 (interest and royalties) excluding trading profit and exempt dividends
attributes 60% giving 3,600,000
computes State R tax of 900,000
computes credit of 216,000 and net tax of 684,000

answer.grader_note: Allow follow-through marks. Using 360,000 as the credit without the 60% share is an error (credit would be 360,000 and net tax 540,000) and loses the final mark only if the candidate fails to apply the shareholding.

items.prompt: (c) Advise Meridian Holdings on the arguments it might raise against the charge and the risks of the State R tax authority challenging the treatment of the trading profit, including the position under treaties.

answer.model: The group could argue three points. First, that the royalty and interest income are not mobile passive income but result from real activity. This is unlikely to succeed under a categorical approach because the rule does not ask about substance for those items, and the IP was developed in State R and transferred to a low-tax entity, which is the situation that the rules aim at, although a substance based or excess profits approach under Action 3 would have asked whether Sable performs the important functions. Second, a treaty argument that the State R charge conflicts with Article 7 of the treaty with State T, because it taxes the profits of a State T enterprise. The OECD Commentary on Article 1 states that CFC rules are not contrary to the Models because they tax residents on their own shareholding income, and the UN Commentary takes the same view; most States accept this. A treaty may nevertheless contain a clause limiting the application of domestic anti-avoidance rules, and Meridian should check. Third, if State R were bound by regional law of the European Union type, a rule that catches more than wholly artificial arrangements could be challenged under Cadbury Schweppes (CJEU 2006), but the facts here, a 60 per cent holding in a company which licenses IP and lends to the group, would probably fall within the justified scope. As to the trading profit of 3,000,000, the exclusion depends on genuine substance: Meridian must evidence the premises, 20 employees, management decisions, and that the sales are not diverted from group customers. If the authority finds the trading is merely a conduit, it could attribute up to 1,800,000 (60% of 3,000,000) more income, and the extra State R tax would be 450,000 before credit of State T tax (6% on 3,000,000 = 180,000; 60% = 108,000) so net 342,000. Double tax is limited because credit is given and a later dividend should be relieved.

points.point: rejects or weighs substance argument for passive royalty and interest under a categorical approach
treaty argument and the OECD or UN Commentary view that CFC rules do not conflict with treaties
mentions Cadbury Schweppes or regional law limits correctly and their likely limited help here
explains evidence needed to keep the trading profit outside CFC income
quantifies the risk on the trading profit: 1,800,000 attributed, 450,000 tax, 108,000 credit, net 342,000

answer.grader_note: Quantification marks need correct recomputation: 3,000,000 × 60% = 1,800,000; × 25% = 450,000; credit 6% × 3,000,000 × 60% = 108,000; net 342,000.

title: Halden Group and its foreign income
scenario: Halden Group plc is resident in State R. In Year 1 it receives a dividend from Orrin Co, a State S company in which it holds 40 per cent of the voting shares, and it also has a branch in State U. State R taxes residents on worldwide income at 30 per cent. Under State R law, relief for foreign tax is given by credit, including underlying tax on dividends where the recipient holds at least 10 per cent of the voting power, and the credit is limited to the State R tax on the foreign income (the overall limit applies to all foreign income taken together). Dividends and branch profits are included in State R taxable income at their gross amount, and underlying tax is added to the dividend (grossed up). The government of State R is considering moving to an exemption for foreign dividends, while keeping credit for branch profits. The relevant figures are in Table 1. Orrin Co distributes only part of its after-tax profit. Halden asks how much State R tax it will pay on this income under the current rules, whether the answer differs under a per-source limit, and how the proposed exemption compares. Assume that the underlying tax is the part of State S corporate tax attributable to the dividend, and that excess credits are lost.

exhibits.caption: Year 1 foreign income of Halden Group plc, illustrative amounts in a common currency unit

items.prompt: (a) Explain how relief by credit works, including the rationale for an underlying credit and the effect of a credit limit, and contrast it with relief by exemption by reference to Articles 23A and 23B of the OECD and UN Models.

answer.model: Under the credit method the residence State taxes worldwide income but gives credit for foreign tax against its own tax on that income. Article 23B provides an ordinary credit, limited to the residence State tax on the income taxed in the source State. The limit prevents the residence State from bearing the cost of a higher foreign rate; excess foreign tax is not refunded, though some States allow carry forward. A dividend suffers two layers of tax: tax on the company's profit and withholding tax on the distribution. An underlying credit relieves the first layer so that the shareholder is treated as if it had earned the profit directly. Article 23B itself speaks of tax paid in the source State on income or capital; underlying credit is not required by the Article but the Commentary recognises it and States commonly give it under domestic law or treaty. Under exemption, as in Article 23A, the residence State does not tax the income at all, which gives capital import neutrality, while credit tends to give capital export neutrality up to the residence rate. The UN Model is in similar terms, and both Models leave the choice to States.

points.point: describes credit method and the ordinary credit limit under Article 23B
explains the double layer of tax on dividends and the purpose of underlying credit
describes exemption under Article 23A
notes both Models give the choice to States or that the UN Model is equivalent

items.prompt: (b) Calculate Halden Group's State R tax after relief under (i) the overall limit and (ii) a limit applied separately to each source of income, showing the dividend gross up, and state any excess credit lost.

answer.model: Dividend received by Halden: 1,800,000 × 40% = 720,000 gross. State S withholding tax at 5% = 36,000. Orrin Co tax: 4,000,000 × 10% = 400,000; after-tax profit 3,600,000. Underlying tax attributable to Halden's dividend: 400,000 × 720,000 ÷ 3,600,000 = 80,000. Grossed up dividend income: 720,000 + 80,000 = 800,000. Foreign tax eligible on the dividend: 36,000 + 80,000 = 116,000. State R tax on dividend income at 30%: 800,000 × 30% = 240,000. Branch: profit 2,000,000; State U tax 38% = 760,000; State R tax 30% = 600,000. Total foreign income 2,800,000; State R tax before credit 840,000. Foreign tax available: 116,000 + 760,000 = 876,000.
