(i) Overall limit: credit is the lesser of 876,000 and 840,000, so 840,000; State R tax payable = 840,000 − 840,000 = 0; excess credit lost = 876,000 − 840,000 = 36,000. (ii) Separate limits: dividend credit = lesser of 116,000 and 240,000 = 116,000; branch credit = lesser of 760,000 and 600,000 = 600,000; total credit 716,000; State R tax payable = 840,000 − 716,000 = 124,000; excess lost on the branch = 760,000 − 600,000 = 160,000. The difference of 124,000 shows that the overall limit allows the unused capacity on the low-taxed dividend to absorb the excess on the high-taxed branch.

points.point: dividend gross 720,000 and withholding 36,000
after-tax profit 3,600,000 and underlying tax 80,000
gross up 800,000 and State R tax 240,000 on the dividend
branch State R tax 600,000 and State U tax 760,000
total State R tax before credit 840,000 and foreign tax 876,000
overall limit: credit 840,000, residual tax 0, excess lost 36,000
separate limits: credit 116,000 plus 600,000 = 716,000, residual tax 124,000
states the excess lost under separate limits (160,000) or explains the cross-crediting effect

answer.grader_note: Follow-through marks allowed. Accept an answer that computes underlying tax on a different but stated basis only if the stated assumption in the question is respected.

items.prompt: (c) Advise Halden on how the proposed exemption for foreign dividends would change its position, comparing exemption and credit in terms of capital import and capital export neutrality, and identify practical difficulties of the credit method shown by these facts.

answer.model: If dividends were exempt and the branch profit stayed on credit, the dividend would drop out of State R tax and the 240,000 of State R tax on it would disappear, together with the credit of 116,000. The branch would then stand alone: State R tax 600,000, credit limited to 600,000, State R tax payable 0, excess 160,000 lost. Total State R tax is therefore 0, the same as under the overall limit, and 124,000 lower than under separate limits. Halden would however lose the cross-crediting. Here the foreign taxes borne are the same (36,000 withholding, 80,000 underlying tax in Orrin's hands and 760,000 on the branch), so the exemption removes the residence tax on the dividend, and the group pays only foreign tax at the source rates. Exemption supports capital import neutrality: Halden's investment in State S competes on the same tax footing as local investors. Credit approaches capital export neutrality by taxing at the higher of the two rates, so that investment decisions between States R and S are not driven by tax, but only up to the residence rate and with the limit weakening it where foreign rates exceed 30 per cent. Practical difficulties illustrated: computing underlying tax needs foreign accounts and tax records, and a pro rata of profit to distribution; timing differences between the years in which tax is paid and income arises; exchange rate conversion; the choice between overall and separate limits; lost excess credits (36,000 or 160,000); and the effect of deferral where profits are retained. The advice is that the overall limit is as good as exemption for Halden on these figures, so the proposal matters mostly for the future, when Orrin is low-taxed and the group has no high-tax branch.

points.point: states the result under exemption for dividends with credit for the branch (residual tax 0, excess 160,000 lost)
compares with the overall limit and separate limits outcomes
explains capital import neutrality and exemption
explains capital export neutrality and credit with its limit
identifies at least two practical difficulties illustrated by the facts
gives a reasoned recommendation

title: Comparables and capacity in transfer pricing
scenario: A finance ministry official from a developing country writes: 'The arm's length principle assumes that reliable comparable transactions exist. In our market they rarely do, and the multinational groups operating here enjoy cost savings and market advantages that no foreign benchmark captures. Either the principle must be abandoned for us, or the guidance must become far more practical.' You are asked to comment on this statement for a tax policy seminar.

items.prompt: (a) Explain why a tax administration in a developing country may find it difficult to apply the arm's length principle using comparables, identifying the practical obstacles.

answer.model:
The arm's length principle in Article 9 of the OECD and UN Models, as elaborated in the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines, requires the controlled transaction to be compared with uncontrolled transactions between independent parties in comparable circumstances. The comparability analysis needs reliable information about the functions performed, assets used and risks assumed, the contractual terms, the economic circumstances and the business strategies.

Several obstacles arise in a developing country. First, the local market may be small, so few independent companies perform the relevant functions and public financial data about them is scarce. Commercial databases are expensive and are weighted towards data from larger, more developed economies, so benchmarking sets are often drawn from foreign companies. Secondly, the tax administration usually has less information than the taxpayer: the group holds the global information and the local authority may lack the skilled staff, experience or legal powers to test the functional analysis. Thirdly, economic circumstances differ: market size, labour and input costs, infrastructure, government incentives, and the level of risk (political, currency, regulatory) affect profitability, so comparables from other markets may not be comparable without adjustment. Fourthly, the group may realise location savings or access a local market premium that foreign comparables do not reflect. Fifthly, some transactions, such as the sale of commodities, intangibles or services performed by a single local entity, may have no comparable at all, and the administration may be forced to depend on the group's own documentation. The UN Practical Manual on Transfer Pricing for Developing Countries was prepared to address these difficulties, including limited data and capacity.

points.point: States that Article 9 and the arm's length principle require comparison with comparable uncontrolled transactions assessed through the comparability factors (functions, assets, risks, contract terms, economic circumstances, strategies)
Identifies scarcity of local comparables and cost or bias of commercial databases
Identifies information asymmetry and limited administrative capacity or skills
Identifies differences in economic circumstances, risk or market conditions that undermine foreign comparables, and location savings or market premium
Identifies transactions with no comparable (intangibles, commodities) and refers to the UN Practical Manual as a response

items.prompt: (b) Discuss the role of comparability adjustments in this setting, including how the UN Practical Manual approaches location-specific advantages. Assess whether adjustments solve the problem.

answer.model:
Comparability adjustments are made to the profit or price of the comparable, or to the tested party's results, to eliminate material differences that affect the comparison. The OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines accept that reasonably accurate adjustments may improve reliability, for example for differences in accounting practices, working capital (payment terms, inventory and receivables levels) and in some cases country risk. The adjustment must be made only where it is expected to increase reliability; an unreliable adjustment does not improve comparability and can introduce further error, and the Guidelines treat adjustments with caution, particularly where they rest on subjective judgement.

In a developing country the main uses are working capital and country risk adjustments, where a comparable set from a lower-risk economy would otherwise understate the return needed in a riskier market. The UN Practical Manual goes further in recognising that conditions specific to the country, such as location savings (cost savings from relocating production to a lower cost location) and a local market premium (a higher price or margin available because of the characteristics of the local market), can be relevant to the analysis. Its position, put broadly, is that the allocation of location savings and market premium depends on the facts and on comparability, considering the functions, assets and risks of each party and what independent parties would have agreed, and that where comparables are not available the savings may need to be shared between the parties on that basis. The OECD Guidelines treat location savings and market characteristics as comparability factors too, but the practical weight and the allocation approach differ in emphasis, so some countries state their own position in their guidance.

Adjustments do not solve the problem fully. They presuppose a reasonably comparable starting set; they require data the administration may not have; they open to dispute because each adjustment, particularly country risk, relies on judgement and on methods (such as sovereign bond spread proxies) that can be criticised; and where taxpayers and administrations use different adjustments, double taxation or double non-taxation can follow. Adjustments are therefore a valuable but partial response and need to be combined with simplified approaches and better data. A reasoned conclusion should state that adjustments improve a defective comparison but cannot cure the absence of one.

points.point: Explains that adjustments eliminate material differences between the tested and comparable transactions and may be made only where they increase reliability
Gives examples of accepted adjustments (working capital, country risk)
Notes the risk that unreliable or subjective adjustments reduce reliability
Explains that the UN Practical Manual recognises location savings and local market premium as relevant to comparability and allocation, depending on functions, assets, risks and facts
Contrasts the OECD and UN emphasis or notes both treat them as comparability factors with different weight
Evaluates limits: needs a comparable starting set, data and judgement, dispute and double taxation risk
Reasoned conclusion that adjustments are useful but partial

answer.grader_note: Credit candidates who say the Manual reflects practical country experience and who do not overstate it as binding law. Do not credit a claim that the OECD Guidelines ignore location savings. Do not require a specific numeric method for country risk.

items.prompt: (c) Evaluate whether simplification measures, such as safe harbours and fixed margins, offer a better route than the full comparables analysis for developing countries. Refer to developments for baseline marketing and distribution activities.

answer.model:
Simplification reduces the dependence on comparables by using a pre-set result. Safe harbours allow a taxpayer that meets stated conditions to price a specified transaction at a prescribed margin or rate, with the administration accepting the result. Fixed margins or a presumptive range for routine activities such as distribution, contract manufacturing or low value-adding services are the main examples. The attractions are administrative: lower compliance cost for taxpayers, lower audit cost for administrations, and greater certainty. The OECD Guidelines contain a chapter recognising safe harbours as having a place, and the simplified approach for low value-adding intra-group services is the best known example.

The weaknesses are equally clear. A unilateral safe harbour can produce a result away from arm's length, creating double taxation where the counterparty State disagrees, or double non-taxation where the rate is set too low. It may be exploited if taxpayers choose it only where it favours them. A rate set too high may attract complaints; set too low it loses revenue. Bilateral or multilateral safe harbours reduce these problems, but are rare.

The OECD and the Inclusive Framework have developed a simplified and streamlined approach for baseline marketing and distribution activities (often referred to as Amount B), under which a pricing matrix setting a return on sales by industry grouping, adjusted for operating asset intensity and operating expense intensity (with an operating expense cross-check), can be used in place of a full comparables search for qualifying transactions. Participation is voluntary for jurisdictions, scope limits and qualifying criteria apply, and the June 2024 additional guidance and the February 2025 consolidated report extend the approach to covered low and middle income jurisdictions, with a modified operating expense cross-check and a data availability adjustment for qualifying jurisdictions. A critical view is that the approach favours certainty over precision, and that the matrix may be less suited to markets with unusual characteristics.

Conclusion: simplification is a better route for routine, high volume, low risk transactions where comparables are weakest and administrative cost is highest, but it is a supplement not a substitute, since complex or intangible transactions will still need a facts based analysis supported by access to information and capacity building.

points.point: Explains simplification (safe harbours, fixed or presumptive margins) as a pre-set result replacing a full comparables search
Identifies advantages: lower compliance and audit cost, certainty, suitability for routine activities
Identifies disadvantages: departure from arm's length, double taxation or non-taxation, self-selection, unilateral design
Describes the simplified and streamlined approach for baseline marketing and distribution activities (Amount B) as a pricing matrix or fixed return approach, and its voluntary or conditional nature
Reasoned conclusion distinguishing routine from complex transactions

answer.grader_note: Candidates are not expected to recite the matrix values. Credit any accurate reference to the low value-adding services simplified approach as a comparable example.

title: Cross-border collection of tax debts
scenario: 'A tax debt is only as valuable as the State's ability to collect it. Where the debtor and the assets have moved abroad, the traditional position that one State will not enforce another's revenue claims leaves taxpayers able to escape. Treaties and conventions have changed this, but the changes are limited and much of their potential is unused.' Discuss.

items.prompt: (a) Explain the traditional position on the enforcement of foreign tax claims and why it was seen as a problem for tax administrations.

answer.model:
The traditional position is the revenue rule: courts of one State will not directly or indirectly enforce the revenue laws of another State. The rule reflects the view that taxation is an exercise of sovereign power, so that enforcement by a foreign court would amount to recognising the exercise of that power outside the territory of the State that imposed it, and it is associated in common law systems with cases such as Government of India v Taylor (House of Lords, 1955). Civil law systems reached similar results through public law principles. The rule means that a tax authority has no direct means of enforcing against a debtor's assets abroad, and a taxpayer who moves assets or residence to another State may escape recovery of an assessed tax.

In modern conditions this is a significant problem. Cross-border wealth, mobile individuals and companies, and offshore holding structures mean that enforcement powers that stop at the border leave many assessments uncollectable. Exchange of information may reveal the assets but does not authorise the State to seize them. The administrative need for cooperation therefore grew, and States responded by agreeing, by treaty, to assist each other in collection, since a sovereign State may by agreement waive the rule for another with reciprocal arrangements.

points.point: States the revenue rule: a State will not enforce another State's tax claims
Explains the sovereignty rationale or cites a recognised case such as Government of India v Taylor
Explains the problem: assets and debtors abroad escape recovery, information exchange alone does not authorise enforcement
Explains that States respond by treaty and reciprocal agreement

items.prompt: (b) Compare the assistance in collection provisions of the OECD and UN Models (Article 27) with the multilateral Convention on Mutual Administrative Assistance in Tax Matters, explaining the main limits on the requested State's obligation.

answer.model:
Article 27 of the OECD Model and of the UN Model provides that the Contracting States lend assistance to each other in the collection of revenue claims, with the revenue claim defined broadly as an amount owed in respect of taxes of every kind and description imposed on behalf of the States, together with interest, administrative penalties and costs of collection. Under the OECD Model the obligation covers revenue claims that are enforceable under the law of the applicant State and owed by a person who cannot, at that time, prevent collection in that State. Measures of conservancy are also available, and the requested State's own time limits and priority rules for its revenue claims do not apply to the accepted claim. The UN Model follows the same structure, and I understand that Article 27 is not included in every treaty, because many States are reluctant to commit their administrations, so the Model's provision is optional in practice.

The multilateral Convention developed by the OECD and the Council of Europe, as amended by the 2010 Protocol, contains assistance in recovery (a chapter covering recovery of tax claims, measures of conservancy, documents accompanying requests, time limits, and priority). It goes beyond a bilateral treaty because it provides one instrument which applies between all parties, covers a wide range of taxes, and permits reservations on the taxes covered. Parties may opt out of assistance in recovery by a reservation, so participation does not guarantee recovery assistance.

The main limits are these. The claim must be finally determined or enforceable and not be under challenge, since the requested State will not collect a claim which the debtor can still dispute under the law of the applicant State, though conservancy measures may be taken. The requested State need not carry out measures that are at variance with its laws or administrative practice or contrary to public policy (ordre public). It need not provide assistance where the burden is clearly disproportionate to the benefit to the applicant State, and the assistance may be refused where the applicant State has not exhausted reasonable domestic measures. Assistance is generally not available for claims relating to the earlier time period beyond stated time limits, and the accepted claim receives no priority in the requested State by reason of its nature as a revenue claim. Costs are generally borne by the requested State for ordinary costs and by the applicant State for extraordinary costs, according to agreement. Nationals of the requested State are not necessarily excepted, and the Model contains no general exception for the requested State's own nationals.

points.point: Describes Article 27 OECD and UN: mutual assistance in collection of revenue claims (taxes, interest, penalties, costs)
States that the claim must be enforceable and the debtor unable to prevent collection, with conservancy measures
Notes that Article 27 is optional in practice and that the Convention is a multilateral instrument which permits reservations including opting out of recovery
Identifies at least three limits: claim not contested, measures contrary to law or public policy, disproportionate burden, time limits, own rules on priority and deferral

answer.grader_note: Do not require article numbers within the Convention. Credit a correct reference to the 2010 Protocol. A candidate who says the OECD Model has no Article 27 is wrong; do not credit that.

items.prompt: (c) Evaluate the contribution of regional cooperation (for example, in the European Union and Africa) and assess whether the potential of collection assistance remains unused. Reach a conclusion.

answer.model:
Regional arrangements add to the global framework by offering deeper integration. In the European Union, the Recovery Assistance Directive (Council Directive 2010/24/EU) obliges Member States to assist in the recovery of tax claims, with a uniform instrument permitting enforcement, standard forms, and a common set of rules on time limits, so recovery within the Union is more automatic than under a bilateral treaty. Other regional instruments exist, such as the Nordic convention on assistance in tax matters, and in Africa the Agreement on Mutual Assistance in Tax Matters developed by the African Tax Administration Forum, which is modelled on the multilateral Convention and is intended to provide a framework for States with limited treaty networks. Regional arrangements gain from shared legal traditions, trust, and common IT, which reduce the friction that limits bilateral requests.

The claim in the question that potential is unused has force. Reports on the practice of the multilateral Convention indicate that the number of recovery requests has been low compared with information exchange, though I cannot give figures with confidence. Reasons include reluctance of administrations to bear costs for another State's claims, a requirement that claims be final, the narrow range of reciprocal treaties containing Article 27, reservations by parties, lack of administrative capacity to process requests (particularly in developing countries which are net requesters), the cost of local proceedings, concern for taxpayer rights and data protection, and political concerns that a requested State loses little by being passive. Moreover, assistance depends on knowing where assets are, so it is linked to information exchange.

A critical assessment should also recognise safeguards: taxpayers retain the right to contest the claim in the applicant State and to be protected from disproportionate measures in the requested State, so limits protect legitimate interests. Conclusion: collection assistance is legally well developed but underused in practice; its potential depends on political will, capacity building (including technical support for developing countries), simplification of procedures, and wider participation, rather than further treaty drafting.

points.point: Explains the EU Recovery Directive or another regional instrument and why it is more effective (uniform enforcement instrument, common rules)
Refers to an African or Nordic regional arrangement accurately
Identifies reasons for limited use: cost, finality requirement, optional treaty clause or reservations, capacity, reliance on information on assets
Recognises protections for taxpayers and legitimate limits
Reasoned conclusion on the gap between law and practice with a recommendation

answer.grader_note: Do not credit invented statistics. A candidate who admits uncertainty about usage figures but argues from reasons should receive full marks for the relevant point.

title: Entitlement to treaty benefits
scenario: 'Treaty shopping has become the central problem of the treaty network. The principal purpose test gives States a flexible weapon, but a weapon so flexible creates uncertainty for legitimate investors, while a detailed limitation on benefits clause is certain but crude. No State should agree to both.' Critically discuss this statement.

items.prompt: (a) Explain what is meant by treaty shopping and describe the structure of a limitation on benefits provision and of the principal purpose test in Article 29 of the OECD Model.

answer.model:
Treaty shopping occurs where a person who is not entitled to the benefits of a treaty obtains them indirectly, typically by interposing a resident of a treaty State, such as a conduit or shell company, between the income source and the real investor, so that the reduced withholding rates or exemptions of the treaty apply. It is usually seen as inconsistent with the purpose of a bilateral treaty, which is to relieve double taxation between two States, not to reduce taxation of third State residents.

Article 29 of the OECD Model (introduced in 2017 following the BEPS Action 6 minimum standard) combines two techniques. A limitation on benefits (LOB) provision makes a resident entitled to benefits only if it is a qualified person, through tests addressing, for example, the nature of the person (individual, publicly listed company, certain charities and pension funds), ownership and base erosion (a company with ownership by qualified residents and without large deductible payments to non-qualified persons), and an active conduct of business test for income derived in connection with an active trade or business, with a discretionary relief provision for the competent authority. The principal purpose test (PPT) provides that a benefit is not granted if it is reasonable to conclude, having regard to all relevant facts and circumstances, that obtaining the benefit was one of the principal purposes of any arrangement or transaction that resulted directly or indirectly in that benefit, unless it is established that granting the benefit in these circumstances would be in accordance with the object and purpose of the relevant provisions of the treaty. The detailed LOB is a mechanical objective test, while the PPT is a general anti-abuse rule based on purpose.

points.point: Defines treaty shopping (use of an intermediary resident to obtain benefits intended for residents of the treaty States)
Identifies Article 29 and its origin in BEPS Action 6
Describes LOB: qualified person tests (ownership, base erosion, active business, listed companies etc.) and discretionary relief
States the PPT: one of the principal purposes, reasonable to conclude, all facts and circumstances
States the object and purpose exception

items.prompt: (b) Discuss the relationship between the treaty provisions and the other tools used against treaty shopping: the beneficial owner requirement, domestic anti-abuse rules and judicial abuse of law doctrines. Refer to decided cases where you are confident of the holdings.

answer.model:
The beneficial owner requirement in Articles 10, 11 and 12 restricts the reduced rate to the person who has the right to use and enjoy the dividend, interest or royalty, unconstrained by a contractual or legal obligation to pass the payment to another person. The OECD Commentary clarifies that a conduit with very narrow powers, acting as a nominee or administrator on behalf of the interested parties, is not the beneficial owner. The requirement catches back to back arrangements where the intermediate company passes on the income, but not every case of treaty shopping, since an intermediary that is an owner with full rights may still be a shell used to reach a better treaty; that gap is the reason for the LOB and PPT.

Domestic anti-abuse rules (general anti-avoidance rules, substance over form, sham, and domestic law that denies treaty benefits to artificial arrangements) are applied alongside treaties. A central question is whether a State may apply domestic rules to deny treaty benefits. The Commentary on Article 1 states that there is no conflict between domestic anti-abuse rules and the treaty because treaties do not prevent application of such rules, and the 2003 text relies on the principle that benefits are not intended where the arrangement is abusive. Courts have reached differing conclusions on the application of domestic rules. In Indofood v JPMorgan (English Court of Appeal, 2006) the court interpreted the term beneficial owner in an interest article by reference to its international fiscal meaning and held that a Dutch conduit would not have been the beneficial owner, so that a substitution of an issuer was not a reasonable measure to avoid the withholding. In Prevost Car (Canada, 2008 to 2009) the courts, in contrast, rejected the argument that the conduit holding company was not a beneficial owner and declined to find abuse because the parent company in the Netherlands was entitled to its dividends in law and no obligation to pass them on existed. In the Danish cases (Court of Justice of the European Union, 26 February 2019) the court held that there is a general principle of EU law that abuse of rights cannot be relied on, and that national authorities may deny benefits under the Parent Subsidiary and Interest and Royalties Directives even in the absence of a domestic rule, and it described the beneficial owner concept as an anti-abuse concept to be interpreted in light of the OECD Model Commentary.

The tools are therefore overlapping rather than alternative. The treaty-based rules offer a more predictable footing for the treaty position, domestic rules are a fallback, and abuse doctrines may bring about uncertainty.

points.point: Explains the beneficial owner requirement (right to use and enjoy, not a mere conduit) and its limits as an anti-treaty-shopping measure
Explains that the Commentary and many States accept that domestic anti-abuse rules may apply alongside treaties, and the debate about conflicts
Accurately describes Indofood or Prevost as contrasting approaches to the beneficial owner and conduit questions
Accurately states the Danish cases (CJEU 2019) on general abuse principle and the beneficial owner as anti-abuse notion
Concludes the tools overlap, with the treaty clauses added to fill the gap and increase certainty

answer.grader_note: Credit any accurate case reference. Do not credit a statement that Prevost applied a PPT, since it pre-dated it. Do not penalise a candidate for describing the Danish cases only in outline.

items.prompt: (c) Evaluate the statement that no State should adopt both a detailed LOB and the PPT. Consider the minimum standard, the position of the UN Model, and the Multilateral Instrument, and reach a reasoned conclusion.

answer.model:
The BEPS Action 6 minimum standard requires jurisdictions to include in their treaties an express statement that the treaties are not intended to be used to generate double non-taxation, including through treaty shopping, and to implement this by one of three options: a PPT alone, a PPT combined with either a simplified or a detailed LOB, or a detailed LOB supplemented by a mechanism dealing with conduit arrangements not otherwise caught. The Multilateral Instrument (Articles 6 and 7) implements the preamble statement and the PPT, with an optional simplified LOB provision, and most signatories chose the PPT alone as the default, showing the practical preference for the flexible rule. So the minimum standard itself permits the combination, the claim that no State should agree to both is a normative view rather than a legal limit, and it is open to challenge.

The argument for the claim is that the PPT gives broad discretion and thereby uncertainty and the risk of inconsistent interpretation, with results turning on assessments of purpose and 'reasonable' conclusions that taxpayers cannot easily predict, with the OECD guidance on examples supplying only partial comfort. The detailed LOB, based on legal form, gives certainty but can deny benefits to legitimate investors whose structures fail the mechanical tests (for example, with widely held funds or companies whose ownership is diffuse), thereby acting crudely and complicating compliance, and requiring a discretionary relief provision. Combining both therefore multiplies cost and creates two layers of denial.

The argument against the claim is that the two address different problems. The LOB provides certainty for those who clearly qualify, which reduces PPT uncertainty for the majority of genuine investors, while the PPT closes gaps which a mechanical test cannot anticipate. Many treaties of the United States carry detailed LOB provisions while other States rely on the PPT. The UN Model (2021 and 2025 editions alike) includes an Article 29 on entitlement to benefits, introduced in the 2017 update, which combines a qualified-person limitation on benefits with a principal purpose test, which is consistent with a view that a developing country source State benefits from a flexible provision. For developing countries with limited capacity, a simple PPT is easier to administer than a detailed LOB, although administrative guidance and capacity are needed to apply the test consistently.

Conclusion: the statement is too absolute. A combination may be justified in treaties with a State which is a major source of conduit investment, where certainty for qualified persons and a backstop for abuse are both useful. For most treaties the PPT with clear guidance, and a competent authority consultation process to give comfort to investors, strikes the better balance of certainty and flexibility.

points.point: States the minimum standard and its three options, including the combination of a PPT with an LOB
States that the MLI implements the preamble and PPT, with an optional simplified LOB, and that the PPT is the common choice
Develops the argument that the PPT creates uncertainty and the detailed LOB is crude or costly
Develops a counter argument: the tools address different problems, the LOB gives certainty to genuine investors, the PPT is a backstop
Compares the UN Model's approach (Article 29, a qualified-person LOB plus a PPT, in both the 2021 and 2025 editions) and discusses suitability for developing countries
Reasoned conclusion that is not merely descriptive

answer.grader_note: The MLI Article 7 simplified LOB is optional and only applies if both parties choose it. Do not penalise a candidate who is cautious about the UN Model text, but do not credit an assertion that the UN Model has no LOB at all (its Article 29 is a qualified-person LOB plus a PPT) or that it is identical to the United States model.

title: Corvane group services and platform
scenario: The Corvane group is headed by Corvane Holdings Ltd (Holdings), resident in State R, which also operates a central service company within the same legal entity. In Year 1 the central service company incurred the costs in Table 1 and provided services to its three subsidiaries, Corvane S, Corvane T and Corvane U, whose headcount (the allocation key used by the group) is in Table 2. The group proposes to recharge costs for human resources administration, payroll, IT help desk and accounting, adding a mark-up of 5% on the cost pool, and not to recharge the other items. State U has recently introduced rules on intra-group service charges. Separately, in Year 1 the three subsidiaries and Holdings agreed in writing to develop jointly a customer analytics platform under a cost contribution arrangement. The expected annual cost of development is 800,000. The participants will each use the platform in their own markets, and expected benefits are measured by projected sales: State S 45%, State T 35% and State U 20%. Contributions actually made in Year 1 were State S 400,000, State T 280,000 and State U 120,000, measured at the arm's length value of the contributions. State U's tax authority has queried the charge for the services and the platform arrangement and says that its position is influenced by the UN Model, including Article 12A of the 2021 UN Model on fees for technical services (replaced in the 2025 UN Model by Article 12AA on fees for services). Advise the group. All numbers are illustrative.

exhibits.caption: Annual costs of the central service company in State R (all figures in currency units, illustrative)
Recipients and allocation key (average headcount)

items.prompt: (a) Calculate the amount to be charged to each subsidiary for the low value-adding services under the 5% simplified approach, explaining which cost pools qualify and why the others do not.

answer.model:
The OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines (Chapter VII, 2022) allow a simplified approach for low value-adding intra-group services: supportive services of a routine nature, not part of the core business of the group, not involving unique and valuable intangibles and not involving the assumption or control of substantial risk. Listed examples include accounting and auditing, human resources, IT support and payroll. Excluded categories include services constituting the core business, research and development, manufacturing and production, purchasing, sales and marketing, financial transactions and senior corporate management; acquisition support is outside the approach because it is not routine supportive activity. Shareholder activities (costs of board reporting and shareholder meetings) are not services for the recipients at all since they benefit Holdings in its capacity as shareholder, so no charge arises.

Qualifying pool: human resources 300,000 + payroll 200,000 + IT help desk 250,000 + accounting 150,000 = 900,000. Not charged: board and shareholder costs 100,000 (shareholder activity), acquisition support 220,000 (not low value-adding, and also it benefits the group at holding level, so a benefit test would have to be applied separately) and development of new products 280,000 (research and development and potentially intangible related, outside the simplified approach). Check: 900,000 + 100,000 + 220,000 + 280,000 = 1,500,000.

Mark-up: 900,000 × 5% = 45,000; total charge 945,000. Allocation by headcount, on the facts given: total headcount 250 + 150 + 100 = 500 (Holdings' own use of the services is not in the key, which a tax authority could challenge). Shares: State S 250/500 = 50%, State T 150/500 = 30%, State U 100/500 = 20%.
Corvane S: 945,000 × 50% = 472,500.
Corvane T: 945,000 × 30% = 283,500.
Corvane U: 945,000 × 20% = 189,000.
Total 472,500 + 283,500 + 189,000 = 945,000.

The simplified approach removes the need for a benchmarking study for the mark-up, but a documentation requirement remains (description of the service, identification of recipients, the rationale for the allocation key, calculations). The mark-up is applied to the cost pool and not to pass through costs without services.

points.point: Identifies that services qualify only if routine, supportive and not core business, with the excluded categories
Correctly includes HR, payroll, IT and accounting (900,000) and excludes shareholder activity costs, acquisition support and product development, with reasons
Computes mark-up 45,000 and total 945,000
Computes allocation shares 50%, 30%, 20% from headcount
Computes the charges 472,500, 283,500 and 189,000

answer.grader_note: Allow a candidate who treats acquisition support as potentially chargeable under a normal benefit test, provided it is excluded from the simplified pool. The simplified approach is optional for jurisdictions to adopt, as tax administrations may have a different position; credit a candidate who notes this.

items.prompt: (b) Analyse the cost contribution arrangement. Calculate whether any balancing payment is required for Year 1 and explain the principles on which contributions and benefits are assessed.

answer.model:
Chapter VIII of the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines applies the arm's length principle to a CCA: a participant's proportionate share of the overall contributions must be consistent with its proportionate share of the overall expected benefits, and each participant must have a reasonable expectation of benefit and the ability and authority to control the risks and exercise decision making in respect of the arrangement. Contributions are measured at their value, which may be based on the cost for services but at value for contributions such as pre-existing intangibles, and cost may be used as a proxy for the value of services contributed only where that is reliable. Expected benefits are estimated using a reliable allocation key, such as projected sales, projected profits or headcount, according to the type of benefit.

Proportionate shares of expected benefits applied to the actual total contributions: total contributions 400,000 + 280,000 + 120,000 = 800,000.
State S: 45% × 800,000 = 360,000; contributed 400,000; excess 40,000.
State T: 35% × 800,000 = 280,000; contributed 280,000; difference nil.
State U: 20% × 800,000 = 160,000; contributed 120,000; shortfall 40,000.
Total differences net to zero (40,000 over, nil, 40,000 under).
A balancing payment of 40,000 is therefore needed from Corvane U to Corvane S. The payment is treated as an increase in the contribution of the payer and a reimbursement to the recipient, and not as a royalty or service fee, though tax treatment depends on domestic rules.

The analysis assumes that Holdings is not a participant, though the facts mention that Holdings agreed to the arrangement. If Holdings contributes nothing and expects no benefit, it is not a participant; if it exploits the platform, it should have a share. Projected sales are only one proxy for expected benefits; if the platform is more valuable where data volumes are higher, other keys may be better, and the allocation should be reviewed when actual results differ materially from projections.

points.point: States the CCA principle: share of contributions consistent with share of expected benefits, with expectation of benefit and control
States that contributions are measured at value (not necessarily cost) and benefits by a reliable allocation key
Computes entitlement shares 360,000, 280,000, 160,000
Identifies the balancing payment of 40,000 from State U to State S
Notes the question about Holdings as participant or the need to review the key when projections and results differ

answer.grader_note: Accept a candidate who identifies Holdings as a participant with a share, provided the point is argued. Do not require recitation of paragraph numbers.

items.prompt: (c) Advise the group on the challenges that State U is likely to make, including the benefit test, the treatment of the platform arrangement and the relevance of Article 12A of the 2021 UN Model (now Article 12AA in the 2025 UN Model), and assess the group's strongest and weakest positions.

answer.model:
State U may raise several lines of challenge. First, the benefit test: under the OECD Guidelines an intra-group service exists only if the activity provides the recipient with economic or commercial value to enhance its commercial position, which an independent enterprise in comparable circumstances would have been willing to pay for. State U may argue that its subsidiary already has local staff for HR or accounting, so the central charge is duplicative, or that the IT help desk is a shareholder-type service. The group's position is strongest where it can show actual use (tickets handled, payroll runs processed) and is weakest where the recharge rests only on the headcount key without evidence of use. Secondly, State U may query the allocation key, which for payroll may be reasonable but for the accounting or IT services may be better by transactions or user numbers. Thirdly, deductibility under State U's domestic rules, including a cap on service charges or documentation requirements, is a matter of domestic law; the treaty does not override those rules but Article 9 and Article 24 (non-discrimination, deduction on the same conditions as to residents) may limit discriminatory rules, with the OECD and UN Models similar in this respect.

On withholding, State U may seek to tax the service fee. Under the OECD Model, a fee for services is not a royalty and, where the recipient has no permanent establishment in State U, it is taxable only in State R under Article 7. The UN Model 2021 contained Article 12A, which allowed the source State to tax fees for technical, managerial or consultancy services; the 2025 UN Model replaces Articles 12A and 14 with Article 12AA on fees for services, at a rate negotiated in the treaty, on a gross basis, but only if the treaty includes the article. Whether the services here are technical, managerial or consultancy services within the Article 12A definition would need to be examined: an automated payroll or standard accounting service may or may not be, and the definition contains exclusions (for example for services ancillary to other income and for employees) that would need to be checked against the text. Whether the State R and State U treaty contains Article 12A (2021 UN Model numbering; Article 12AA in the 2025 UN Model) or a service permanent establishment rule (as in Article 5(3)(b) of the UN Model, which is based on presence for more than 183 days) is a fact for which the instructions do not provide, and the advice should be conditional. The CCA payment in State U's hands is a contribution, not a royalty, but the platform may contain intangibles, and any payment to State R for use of existing intangibles would be a royalty under Article 12.

On the platform, State U may argue that its 20% share is overstated by projected sales and that it should have a lower share, or that the group has not shown that State U has control of risk. The group's strongest argument is the written agreement with a benefit key and a balancing payment that is correct on the facts. Its weakest points are the headcount key and thin documentation of the cost for State U. Recommendation: prepare contemporaneous documentation, add evidence of service use, review the keys, and consider an advance pricing agreement or a mutual agreement procedure where double taxation is risked.

points.point: Explains the benefit test and shows how State U might apply it (duplication, shareholder-type activity), with evidence of use as the response
Considers the allocation key and domestic deduction rules, with the treaty non-discrimination or Article 9 relevance

Explains that under the OECD Model a service fee without a PE is taxed in the residence State under Article 7, and describes Article 12A of the 2021 UN Model or Article 12AA of the 2025 UN Model (gross basis, negotiated rate, treaty dependent)
Notes the conditional nature of the answer (treaty content unknown) and the UN service PE alternative
Evaluates the CCA challenge: expected benefit share, control, documentation
Assesses strongest and weakest positions and gives practical recommendations (documentation, MAP, APA)

answer.grader_note: Accept alternative analysis of Article 12A (2021 UN numbering; Article 12AA in the 2025 UN Model) scope if reasoned. Do not credit a statement that either article is in the OECD Model.

title: Dunlin Ltd and payments to Marrow Finance
scenario: Dunlin Ltd (Dunlin) is resident in State S and manufactures specialist packaging. Marrow Finance Ltd (Marrow) is resident in State T and is a wholly owned subsidiary of Delta Holdings Ltd (Delta), resident in State Z, which also owns 40% of Dunlin through a separate holding. Marrow has 12 employees, a leased office and funds itself from Delta by an intra-group loan on matching terms. In Year 1 Dunlin made the payments in Table 1 to Marrow, which also holds the process patent under a licence from Delta. The State S and State T treaty follows the OECD Model in form for Articles 5, 7, 11 and 12 but the agreed withholding rates are those in Table 2, and Article 11 contains a paragraph addressing special relationships in the form of the Model. Assume the treaty contains no principal purpose test and that Marrow has no permanent establishment in State S. Dunlin asks (i) what withholding tax it must deduct on each payment and (ii) whether Marrow can invoke the treaty. Advise, discussing both the OECD and UN Models where the treatment differs. All numbers are illustrative.

exhibits.caption: Payments by Dunlin Ltd (State S) to Marrow Finance Ltd (State T) in Year 1 (currency units, illustrative)
Other data

items.prompt: (a) Calculate the State S withholding tax on the interest on the basis that Marrow is entitled to the treaty, explaining the effect of the special relationship provision, and then calculate the tax if the treaty is not available.

answer.model:
Article 11 of the Model (OECD and UN) defines interest as income from debt claims of every kind, and allows the source State to tax interest at a rate capped by the treaty (in the OECD Model at 10%, in the UN Model at a rate to be negotiated), provided the recipient is the beneficial owner of the interest. The rate here is 10%. Article 11 (paragraph 6) provides that where, because of a special relationship between the payer and the beneficial owner or between both of them and some other person, the amount of the interest exceeds the amount which would have been agreed in the absence of the relationship, the article applies only to the last mentioned amount; the excess remains taxable according to the laws of each Contracting State, with due regard to the other provisions of the treaty. Marrow and Dunlin are connected through Delta: Delta owns Marrow wholly and 40% of Dunlin, so a special relationship may exist, which includes relationships by common control. It is for the facts to say that the connection influences the rate; the benchmark of 6% suggests that it did.

Arm's length interest: 5,000,000 × 6% = 300,000. Excess: 450,000 minus 300,000 = 150,000.
Scenario 1 (treaty applies): treaty rate on 300,000 at 10% = 30,000. The excess 150,000 is not within the treaty rate and is taxed according to domestic law at 25% = 37,500 (State S may treat the excess as a dividend or other payment according to its law, with the treaty provisions on that category, for example Article 10, to be considered; assume here domestic 25%). Total tax 30,000 + 37,500 = 67,500.
Scenario 2 (treaty not available): 450,000 × 25% = 112,500.
Difference 112,500 minus 67,500 = 45,000.
The relationship also raises the possibility of a domestic transfer pricing or thin capitalisation adjustment, and a corresponding deduction issue for Dunlin.

points.point: States the treaty definition of interest and the rate cap, with the beneficial owner condition
Explains Article 11(6): the treaty rate applies only to the arm's length amount, with the excess taxable under domestic law having regard to other provisions
Computes arm's length interest 300,000 and excess 150,000
Computes treaty case: 30,000 + 37,500 = 67,500
Computes non-treaty case 112,500 and the difference 45,000

answer.grader_note: Allow an alternative treatment of the excess (for example a dividend under Article 10) if the candidate states the rate assumption and calculates consistently.

items.prompt: (b) Characterise each of the payments for licence fees and technical assistance under Article 12 of the OECD Model and the UN Model, and calculate the State S tax on each, on the basis that the treaty applies.

answer.model:
Article 12 of the OECD Model provides for taxation of royalties only in the State of residence of the beneficial owner (a nil source rate), while here the treaty rate of 5% has been agreed, which follows the pattern of the UN Model where the source State may tax royalties at a negotiated rate. The royalties definition covers payments for the use of, or the right to use, any copyright of literary, artistic or scientific work, any patent, trade mark, design or model, plan, secret formula or process, or for information concerning industrial, commercial or scientific experience (know-how). The UN definition includes, in addition, the use of or right to use industrial, commercial or scientific equipment, and the cinematographic film coverage is wider in wording, but equipment is not relevant to these facts.

Licence fee 1: the OECD Commentary on Article 12 states that payments for software are royalties only where the payment is for the right to use a copyright in the program in a way which, without the licence, would be an infringement, such as reproducing or distributing it commercially. Payments in which the user obtains only the right to make a copy needed for operating the program, such as installing on its own servers and a back-up copy, are not royalties; they are treated as business profits (Article 7) (or as the sale of a copy). As Marrow has no PE in State S, State S has no right to tax. Tax: nil. Some States take a different view on some software payments, so the position should be flagged. Under the UN Model 2025 the Article 12 royalty definition covers payments for the use of software even where no copyright is used, so a treaty following that text would make licence fee 1 a royalty and the tax would be 400,000 × 5% = 20,000. The OECD Model and the UN Model 2021 text do not go that far, and this treaty is in OECD form.
Licence fee 2: the right to use a patented process and know-how is a royalty. Treaty rate 5%: 200,000 × 5% = 10,000 (domestic 25% would be 50,000). The beneficial owner requirement applies, see part (c).
Technical assistance fee: payment for services, not information concerning experience already acquired (the know-how line is that the supplier does not do work for the user, which the services do). It is business profits under Article 7, so no State S tax in the absence of a PE: nil. The distinction is the one made in the Commentary between a payment for the supply of existing know-how and for the performance of services. Under the UN Model, if the treaty included Article 12A (2021 UN Model numbering; replaced by Article 12AA in the 2025 UN Model), a fee for services could be taxable at source; this treaty is in OECD form so no such article is assumed.

Total State S tax: nil + 10,000 + nil = 10,000. If all three were royalties: 700,000 × 5% = 35,000; at the domestic rate without the treaty: 700,000 × 25% = 175,000.

points.point: States the Article 12 definition including know-how and patents, and contrasts OECD (residence only) with UN (source tax allowed)
Characterises licence fee 1 as not a royalty (copy needed for use only), so business profits and nil tax without a PE
Characterises licence fee 2 as a royalty and computes 10,000
Characterises the technical assistance fee as services (not know-how supply), with nil tax, and notes Article 12A (2021 UN Model numbering; Article 12AA in the 2025 UN Model) as an alternative
Total tax 10,000, with comparators of 35,000 and 175,000, or flags the alternative characterisation of software 20,000

answer.grader_note: Credit a candidate who identifies the mixed nature of the technical assistance (partly know-how) if reasoned. Do not credit a statement that the OECD Model permits source State tax on royalties.

items.prompt: (c) Advise whether Marrow can be treated as the beneficial owner of the interest and royalties, and whether the treaty benefits could be denied on other grounds. Give your judgement.

answer.model:
The beneficial owner requirement in Articles 11 and 12 restricts the treaty rate to the person who has the right to use and enjoy the income, free of a contractual or legal obligation to pass it on. The OECD Commentary says that a conduit company with very narrow powers, which in relation to the income is a mere fiduciary or administrator acting on account of the interested parties, is not the beneficial owner, and it confirms that the requirement does not apply to every case of back to back arrangement but looks to who really has the benefit. The Commentary also indicates that the test looks at the recipient's powers over the income in substance, not only at a legal obligation to pass it on, though a contractual or de facto obligation is a strong indicator. In the Danish cases (CJEU, 26 February 2019) the court treated the concept as an anti-abuse concept and indicated that pass-through within a short time, lack of substance and economic activity, and matching terms point towards denial.

The facts point both ways. Against Marrow: it passes 90% of each interest payment to Delta within 30 days, funds itself on matching terms, has only 12 employees, and is owned by a State Z company which has no treaty with State S, so the structure looks like a conduit and the treaty rate would be unavailable on the interest, giving tax of 112,500 on the interest as in (a). For Marrow: it has a leased office and staff, it is not obliged contractually to pass on the money (the facts do not state an obligation), it retains 10% and bears credit and currency risk of its own on a loan, and a margin of 10% might indicate real activity. A tribunal in a State following the Prevost Car approach, focusing on the legal entitlement, may find in favour of Marrow, whereas a tribunal following Indofood and the Danish cases may deny. For the royalties, Marrow holds the patent under a licence from Delta, so it may be a sub-licensor paying on royalties to Delta and so a conduit for the process payments (the facts do not say). It is not apparent that it passes them on.

Other grounds: the treaty as stated has no PPT, so denial would depend on the domestic general anti-abuse rule, whose compatibility with the treaty is a question under the Commentary on Article 1 and on the national law. If the treaty were amended by the Multilateral Instrument to include a PPT, it would be reasonable to conclude that one of the principal purposes of interposing Marrow was to obtain the 10% rate in place of 25%, and the PPT exception would require showing that granting the benefit was in accordance with the object and purpose. Judgement: on the interest, the denial risk is high; Dunlin should consider withholding at 25% or obtaining a ruling from the State S authority, because the withholder is liable for under-withholding. On the royalties, the risk is lower on the facts given but needs facts about the onward payments.

points.point: States the beneficial owner test and the conduit concept from the Commentary, with reference to the Danish cases or Indofood
Applies the facts against Marrow: 90% pass through in 30 days, matching terms, no treaty with State Z, limited substance
Applies the facts for Marrow: staff, office, no stated obligation, retained margin and risk, and the Prevost Car approach
Considers other grounds (domestic anti-abuse rules, MLI PPT if applicable) and the royalties position
Gives a reasoned judgement and practical advice for the withholder

answer.grader_note: Either conclusion on the interest may be credited if supported by facts on both sides. A statement that Marrow is the beneficial owner merely because it is the legal owner of the loan is not sufficient for full marks.

title: Amount A and the reach of a new taxing right
scenario: A finance minister argues: "Amount A gives market jurisdictions a share of the profits of the largest groups without the need for a permanent establishment, so the old connecting factors are finished. Nothing more is needed from the rest of the international tax system except signature of the Multilateral Convention." You are asked to assess the claim for a briefing paper.

items.prompt: (a) Explain the scope rules, the nexus rule and the revenue sourcing approach of Pillar One Amount A, and how the share of profit reallocated to market jurisdictions is determined.

answer.model: Amount A applies to a group, and not to each entity, so the starting point is consolidated financial accounts. A multinational enterprise group is in scope when its total revenues exceed EUR 20 billion and its profit before tax divided by revenue exceeds 10 per cent, tested on an averaging basis over the relevant periods. The text provides for the revenue threshold to fall to EUR 10 billion later, but only if implementation of the first phase, including tax certainty, is judged successful after a review that starts several years after entry into force. Extractives and regulated financial services are excluded, and segmentation is available only in limited circumstances. The Amount A mechanism does not depend on physical presence. A jurisdiction qualifies to receive Amount A only if the group derives at least EUR 1 million of revenue sourced to it, with a lower figure of EUR 250,000 for smaller economies, defined by reference to GDP below EUR 40 billion. This is a revenue nexus, in place of a permanent establishment. Revenue is allocated to a jurisdiction by detailed sourcing rules that follow the type of goods or services supplied, such as the place of delivery or consumption for finished goods, the location of the user or device for many digital services, and the location of the property for real property services, applying a hierarchy of reliable indicators and not a single test. The amount reallocated is 25 per cent of residual profit, where residual profit is the profit before tax above 10 per cent of revenue. The 10 per cent is treated as a routine return on revenue and the excess as the profit attributable to market-related intangibles and scale. The 25 per cent is then divided among the qualifying market jurisdictions in proportion to the revenue sourced to each. A marketing and distribution profits safe harbour limits the Amount A taxable profit in a market where the group already earns a return on baseline marketing and distribution activities. The candidate should point out that the design is formulaic, and that it is a new taxing right in addition to, and not a modification of, Articles 5 and 7.

points.point: states the two scope tests: global revenue above EUR 20 billion and profitability above 10 per cent, on a group basis
notes the later reduction of the revenue threshold to EUR 10 billion only after a successful review, and the extractives and regulated financial services exclusions
states the nexus rule: at least EUR 1 million of sourced revenue (EUR 250,000 for jurisdictions with GDP below EUR 40 billion) and that no permanent establishment is needed
explains revenue sourcing by category of supply using reliable indicators in a hierarchy
states that 25 per cent of profit above 10 per cent of revenue is reallocated, split by sourced revenue

answer.grader_note: Figures are the thresholds in the October 2023 text of the Multilateral Convention; the candidate need not recall the lower figure for small economies for full marks if the main thresholds are right. Do not credit a claim that Amount A changes Article 5.

items.prompt: (b) Explain how the Multilateral Convention is intended to deliver Amount A and how double taxation and disputes are meant to be handled, and critically evaluate the minister's statement that signature alone is enough.

answer.model: Amount A cannot be introduced by changing bilateral treaties one by one, because it overrides the allocation rules of Articles 5, 7 and 9 in existing treaties and needs a common rule for the group as a whole. The Multilateral Convention is a treaty, concluded by the Inclusive Framework, that parties would sign and ratify, with entry into force dependent on a critical mass of parties: a minimum number of jurisdictions, which must include those that are the residence of a given share of the in-scope parent entities. Parties would also undertake to remove digital services taxes and similar measures and not to introduce new ones. Double taxation of the reallocated profit is addressed by an elimination mechanism: jurisdictions that are identified as bearing the burden, by reference to profits and a return on depreciation and payroll, must give relief by exemption or credit. Tax certainty is a central element. A panel process is meant to give early, binding, group-wide determinations of scope and of related matters, so that the same question is not decided differently in each market. The minister's statement is open to several objections. Signature is not ratification, and entry into force needs enough ratifications, including those of the home jurisdictions of the largest groups. Domestic legislation will be needed in many States, and the Convention does not apply itself to tax liabilities without domestic implementation. The text contained identified reservations by some jurisdictions, and consensus on it had not been reached at the January 2025 Co-chairs statement; the Multilateral Convention was never finalised or opened for signature, so at November 2026 there is nothing to sign or ratify, and the United States withdrew in 2025. Amount B was finalised separately in February 2024 as an optional annex to Chapter IV of the Transfer Pricing Guidelines, available for fiscal years beginning on or after 1 January 2025. Whether any large home jurisdiction will ratify is uncertain. Without that, the threshold of 30 ratifying jurisdictions including the parents of at least 60 per cent of in-scope groups is not reached. A strong answer also notes that Amount A sits on top of the rest of the system: the existing arm's length principle and treaty allocation continue to apply to the residual profit in the hands of each entity, the Pillar Two rules interact with it, and the tax certainty panel needs administrative capacity that many developing States lack, which is a reason why the UN has pursued its own digital taxation options.

points.point: explains why a multilateral instrument is needed: Amount A overrides treaty allocation under Articles 5, 7 and 9 and needs a coordinated rule
describes entry into force by a critical mass of ratifying jurisdictions including home jurisdictions of in-scope groups
notes the commitment to withdraw digital services taxes and similar measures
explains elimination of double taxation by exemption or credit for specified jurisdictions
explains the tax certainty panels and their purpose of binding, group-wide, early determination

evaluates the statement: signature is not ratification, domestic legislation is needed, and reservations or lack of consensus mean the outcome is uncertain (credit for stating that status must be checked and giving a reasoned position)

answer.grader_note: The Convention text was released in October 2023; as at the January 2025 Inclusive Framework statement consensus had not been reached and work has since stalled. Accept an answer that says status is uncertain and gives reasons. Do not credit a flat statement that the Convention is in force or open for signature, since it was never opened for signature. The precise ratification thresholds are not required.

items.prompt: (c) "Amount A gives market jurisdictions a taxing right that does not depend on a permanent establishment." Critically assess whether Amount A achieves the aims of the project, and compare it briefly with the approach of the UN Model in Article 12B.

answer.model: The claim is accurate as far as it goes: for an in-scope group the revenue nexus replaces physical or agency presence, and the reallocated profit is not tested against Article 5. The question is whether this meets the aims. In favour, Amount A responds directly to the argument that value is created by users and markets, it uses a formula that is simple to apply compared with a functional analysis, and it comes with a binding certainty process, which is intended to reduce disputes. Against, the scope is so narrow, with a EUR 20 billion revenue test and a 10 per cent margin test, that only around 100 groups are expected to be affected, and many digital businesses fall outside. The share allocated is modest, 25 per cent of residual profit, so the amount moved is small for many market States, and small and developing economies receive little. The elimination of double tax shifts cost to a few residence States, and the dependence on ratification by major economies makes the whole structure fragile. Administrative complexity, including segmentation, revenue sourcing and the panel process, is heavy. The UN Model takes a different path. Article 12B lets the source State tax income from automated digital services by withholding on the gross amount at a rate to be negotiated, or the beneficial owner may elect to be taxed on its qualified profits, a fixed percentage of the profit derived from applying its profitability ratio to the gross annual revenue from such services, at the domestic rate. It is bilateral, requires no group threshold and is much easier for a developing State to administer, but gross-basis tax raises risks of over-taxation and double taxation without relief, and it has only effect where it is included in a treaty. A good conclusion states that the two are not exact substitutes: Amount A is a multilateral, formulaic, group-wide reallocation with a high threshold, Article 12B a bilateral source-State right with a low administrative burden.

points.point: accepts that the claim is correct for in-scope groups: a revenue nexus replaces Article 5 for Amount A
gives at least two reasoned arguments that Amount A meets its aims (formula, certainty, response to market value creation)
gives at least two reasoned limits (narrow scope, small share of profit, dependence on ratification, administrative burden, cost borne by few residence States, little benefit for small States)
describes Article 12B correctly: source taxation of automated digital services, gross basis at a negotiated rate, or the qualified profits election at the domestic rate
reaches a reasoned comparison and conclusion

answer.grader_note: Accept 30 per cent of the profit derived from applying the profitability ratio to ADS revenue for qualified profits; the percentage is not required for full marks.

title: National rules and the arm's length principle
scenario: "Article 9 of the Models tells States what they may do, not what they must do. The real content of transfer pricing law lives in domestic legislation, and the differences between States are the main source of double taxation." Discuss with reference to the practice of at least three of the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany and Australia.

items.prompt: (a) Explain the content of Article 9(1) and 9(2) and the sense in which Article 9 permits, but does not itself require, an adjustment. Note any difference in the UN Model.

answer.model: Article 9(1) applies where two associated enterprises, one in each Contracting State, are linked by conditions in their commercial or financial relations that differ from those that would be made between independent enterprises. Profits that would have accrued to one of them, but for those conditions, may be included in its profits and taxed accordingly. It is a permission addressed to the State that makes the adjustment. The treaty is not self-executing here: a State can only adjust to the extent that its domestic law provides for an adjustment, and Article 9 does not create a charge that does not exist in domestic law. Article 9(2) deals with the other State. Where one State includes in the profits of an enterprise profits on which an enterprise of the other State has been charged to tax, and the profits so included would have accrued to the first enterprise if the conditions had been arm's length, the other State shall make an appropriate adjustment to the tax charged on those profits. In making that adjustment the competent authorities consult each other where necessary. The corresponding adjustment is therefore a duty only where the other State agrees that the first adjustment was justified in principle and in amount, and the mechanism that makes it effective is the mutual agreement procedure in Article 25. The UN Model has the same structure but adds a paragraph 3 which provides that paragraph 2 does not apply where judicial, administrative or other legal proceedings have resulted in a final ruling that, by actions giving rise to an adjustment under paragraph 1, one of the enterprises concerned is liable to penalty with respect to fraud, gross negligence or wilful default.

points.point: states Article 9(1): arm's length test between associated enterprises permits an upward profit adjustment
explains that the treaty does not create the charge; domestic law must allow the adjustment
states Article 9(2): corresponding adjustment by the other State where it agrees the first adjustment is justified in principle and amount
identifies the UN Model difference: paragraph 3 removing the obligation in cases of fraud, gross negligence or wilful default

answer.grader_note: Do not require paragraph numbers of the Commentary. Credit a link to Article 25 and MAP.

items.prompt: (b) Compare the way in which at least three of the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany and Australia legislate for transfer pricing, identifying one real difference of approach in each.

answer.model: The United States applies section 482 of the Internal Revenue Code, which allows the tax authority to allocate income among commonly controlled taxpayers to prevent evasion or to reflect income clearly, supported by detailed Treasury regulations. The regulations adopt the best method rule, choose between methods including the comparable uncontrolled price method, the comparable profits method and the profit split, and use an interquartile range, with adjustment to the median if the result is outside it. For intangibles, the statute requires that income be commensurate with the income attributable to the intangible, which supports periodic adjustment based on later results, and the regulations contain cost sharing rules and strict contemporaneous documentation requirements which, when followed, protect against penalties. The United Kingdom has Part 4 of the Taxation (International and Other Provisions) Act 2010, which requires that provisions be construed in the way that best secures consistency with the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines, so that the Guidelines are in effect part of the interpretation of the statute. The rules apply both to cross-border and domestic transactions, a small and medium-sized enterprise exemption is available (not for transactions with non-qualifying territories, broadly those without a treaty containing a non-discrimination article), and the participation condition covers control and certain joint ventures. Germany relies on section 1 of the Foreign Tax Act, the Aussensteuergesetz, which adopts the arm's length principle and a hierarchy of methods, allows the range to be narrowed to the interquartile range where comparability is limited, and requires an adjustment to the median where the result lies outside the range, includes specific rules on transfers of functions, and imposes detailed documentation rules in an ordinance with penalties and a presumption against the taxpayer where documentation is missing. Australia has Subdivision 815-B of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1997, which applies the arm's length conditions with regard to the relevant treaty where one applies and to the OECD guidance specified in section 815-135, with a power to reconstruct a transaction in limited circumstances, and a separate Subdivision 815-A for the application of treaty Article 9 and its rules for what the arm's length conditions are. The best answers do not list statutes but show that the common root, the arm's length principle, is applied with different standards for documentation, ranges, intangibles and the status of the OECD Guidelines.

points.point: United States: names section 482 and one correct feature (best method rule, commensurate with income standard, regulations, interquartile range or documentation)
United Kingdom: Part 4 TIOPA 2010 and construction consistent with the OECD Guidelines, with one correct feature (domestic coverage or SME exemption)
Germany: section 1 of the Foreign Tax Act, with one correct feature (median adjustment, function transfer rules, documentation presumptions)
Australia: Division 815 and use of treaty and OECD Guidelines with reconstruction power
shows that approaches are not identical and links to the common arm's length root

answer.grader_note: Credit any three jurisdictions at the stated marks, with the fourth as extra credit within the 10 marks. Do not credit invented thresholds. These domestic descriptions are given from general knowledge and should be checked against current legislation.

items.prompt: (c) Evaluate whether divergence between national transfer pricing rules is the main cause of double taxation, and explain how it can be resolved.

answer.model: Divergence is an important source of economic double taxation but not the only one. Where one State adjusts and the other does not make the corresponding adjustment, the same profit is taxed twice. Differences in methods, in acceptance of ranges and the point to which adjustments are made, in the treatment of intangibles and of location savings, in documentation penalties, and in time limits for adjustments each produce disagreement. Differences in how a State uses the OECD Guidelines make this worse: a State which treats them as binding interpretation will adjust differently from a State which treats them as persuasive. Other causes also matter, including differences in the facts found, different views of who performs the important functions, differences in timing, and the absence of treaty provisions. Divergence is a real cause but arguably only the technical form of a more basic conflict of revenue interests, because each State chooses a rule that supports its own tax base. Resolution is by several routes. Following the Guidelines reduces divergence in principle. Article 25 provides the mutual agreement procedure, and Article 9(2) the corresponding adjustment; mandatory binding arbitration, where it is included in a treaty, ensures a result (for example under the Multilateral Instrument, for the States that chose Part VI). Advance pricing agreements, particularly bilateral and multilateral ones, address the problem before it arises. Safe harbours and the simplified approach for low value-adding services reduce the need for adjustment. Joint audits and the OECD's forum on tax administration work can help. For developing States, the UN Practical Manual and the UN Model give a somewhat different emphasis, for example on location savings. The conclusion should weigh these: no mechanism removes divergence, and dispute prevention is cheaper than resolution.

points.point: explains that adjustment without corresponding adjustment causes economic double taxation
gives at least two concrete sources of divergence (methods, ranges, intangibles, documentation, time limits, status of the Guidelines)
recognises other causes and offers a reasoned view of whether divergence is the main cause
identifies resolution: MAP under Article 25, Article 9(2), arbitration, APAs, safe harbours
reaches a reasoned conclusion

title: Source taxation of services under the UN Model
scenario: A developing State asks its negotiators to include Article 12A (replaced in the 2025 UN Model by Article 12AA) and Article 12B of the UN Model in all new treaties, on the grounds that service providers and digital businesses earn large profits from the State without a permanent establishment there. A trade association of the exporting State objects that gross-basis withholding on services will be unworkable. Advise on the content of the provisions and the strength of the competing arguments.

items.prompt: (a) Explain how Article 12A of the UN Model (2021 numbering; replaced by Article 12AA in the UN Model 2025) works and how it differs from the treatment of the same payments under the OECD Model.

answer.model: Article 12A of the 2021 UN Model, which the 2025 UN Model replaces with Article 12AA (covering any payment for any service, and absorbing Article 14), allows the State of source to tax fees for technical services, which are defined as payments of any kind for services of a managerial, technical or consultancy nature, subject to listed exclusions.
