The right belongs to the State from which the payment arises, and the treaty provides that the tax shall not exceed an agreed rate, which the Contracting States settle in bilateral negotiation, so that it is a gross-basis withholding right which does not depend on any presence in the source State. Article 12A is not a part of the OECD Model. Under the OECD Model, fees for services are generally business profits under Article 7, taxable in the State of source only if the provider has a permanent establishment, subject to the rule for employment under Article 15, the artistes and sportspersons rule in Article 17 and the Article 5 services rules, where they are included in a treaty. Without a permanent establishment, a provider of consultancy services performed outside the source State pays no tax there. The UN Model already deals with some services through an Article 5(3)(b) services permanent establishment, which treats the furnishing of services by an enterprise through employees or other personnel as a permanent establishment where the activities continue for more than a stated period, usually 183 days in any twelve month period, within the State. Article 12A is wider because it needs no days test. The usual relationship with the other Articles is that the provisions of Article 12A do not apply where the fees are attributable to a permanent establishment, in which case Article 7 applies. The text also contains a source rule, deeming the fees to arise where the payer is resident or has a permanent establishment bearing the expense, and a rule that restricts the amount to an arm's length figure where the parties are specially related.

points.point: defines fees for technical services: managerial, technical or consultancy services

states that Article 12A (2021 numbering; Article 12AA in the 2025 UN Model) gives the source State a right to tax, limited by a bilaterally agreed rate on a gross basis, without a permanent establishment
contrasts the OECD Model: fees are business profits under Article 7 taxed only through a permanent establishment

explains the relationship with the UN Article 5(3)(b) services permanent establishment and with permanent establishment attribution (Article 12A is disapplied where a permanent establishment bears the fees)
mentions the source rule or the special relationship rule

answer.grader_note: Exclusions, paragraph numbering and the final form of the source rule should be checked against the current UN Model; credit general descriptions.

items.prompt: (b) Explain how Article 12B works, including the definition of automated digital services and the election available to the taxpayer.

answer.model: Article 12B was added to the UN Model in 2021. It allows the State of source to tax income from automated digital services, which are services provided on the internet or another electronic network, requiring minimal human involvement from the service provider, and listed in the Article. The list includes online advertising services, the supply of user data, online search engines, online intermediation platform services, social media platforms, digital content services, online gaming, cloud computing services and standardised online teaching services. The general rule is that the source State may tax the gross payments for those services at a rate fixed by bilateral negotiation, which does not depend on a permanent establishment. The beneficial owner may, however, request that its qualified profits be taxed, at the domestic rate of the source State, instead of the gross withholding. Qualified profits are a fixed percentage, which is 30 per cent in Article 12B of the UN Model, of the profit obtained by applying the profitability ratio of the beneficial owner or of its automated digital services segment to the gross annual revenue from those services in the source State. The point of the election is to reflect profit instead of revenue, so that an enterprise with a thin margin is not taxed on gross receipts, and the Article is intended for use mainly by groups with significant consolidated revenue. As with other income Articles, the right does not apply where the income is effectively connected with a permanent establishment in the source State, in which case Article 7 applies. The source rule looks to the payer's residence or the permanent establishment which bears the payment, and the rules about the beneficial owner of the income also apply.

points.point: states the date or origin: UN Model 2021 addition permitting source taxation without a permanent establishment
defines automated digital services: internet or electronic network, minimal human involvement, with at least three listed examples
states the gross-basis withholding at a negotiated rate
describes the election for taxation of qualified profits at the domestic rate
explains qualified profits: fixed percentage of the profit derived by applying a profitability ratio to the gross annual revenue
notes disapplication where there is a permanent establishment and the beneficial owner requirement

answer.grader_note: The 30 per cent figure is the one in Article 12B of the UN Model; credit without the figure.

items.prompt: (c) Assess the arguments for and against the negotiators' proposal and advise whether it should be pursued.

answer.model: For the proposal, the developing State argues that the permanent establishment threshold is a poor fit for services and digital business, in which a foreign provider can earn large amounts from the State through remote activity. Article 12A (2021 numbering; Article 12AA in the 2025 UN Model) and Article 12B restore a source taxing right without a physical presence test, they are simple to administer compared with an Article 7 attribution inquiry, and withholding is collected by the payer in the State, which matters where the administration has limited resources. The UN Model recognises that source States need such rights in treaties with capital-exporting States. Against the proposal, the association's argument has substance. Gross-basis taxation can exceed the profit when margins are low, and the State of residence may not give a credit for all of it, so double taxation results. Services are often a cost of the payer's own business, and a withholding tax raises the cost of services to local business, which may bear it through gross-up clauses. Identifying fees, where mixed services, software and royalties are supplied together, creates classification disputes. The negotiating partners that follow the OECD Model resist such rules, so that inclusion may cost concessions elsewhere. The election for qualified profits in Article 12B mitigates over-taxation but needs information on the group margin and may be hard to verify. A reasoned recommendation would advise pursuing the provisions, with a moderate rate, a clear definition of the scope, rules on credit in the partner State, a net-basis election, and a review of the interaction with the existing Articles 5, 7, 12 and the services permanent establishment rule, and treats Pillar One Amount A as an alternative to which the State may not obtain access, so that its position should be set out in the light of the multilateral process.

points.point: gives at least two arguments for: PE threshold inadequate, administrative simplicity, source State revenue
gives at least two arguments against: gross-basis over-taxation, cost to local payers, classification, partner resistance, credit and double taxation
recognises that the Article 12B election and a moderate rate mitigate the objections
links to the existing rules (Articles 5, 7, 12) or to Amount A as an alternative
gives a clear reasoned recommendation

title: Daro Optics and its State S distributor
scenario: Daro Optics Ltd is resident in State R and makes branded spectacle lenses. Since Year 1 it has sold the lenses to its wholly owned subsidiary Daro Sales S.A., resident in State S, which resells them to opticians and retail chains and, under a group marketing mandate, runs advertising campaigns in State S for the brand. Daro Sales S.A. has no manufacturing function, does not own the brand and bears normal inventory risk. The State R and State S treaty follows the OECD Model. The State S tax authority has opened an audit and says that the profit of Daro Sales S.A. is below an arm's length level. The group has no benchmarking study for the sales entity and has used the same transfer price for all years. Management points to two things: an internal transaction in which Daro Optics sold the same lens to an unrelated distributor in State T, and a set of independent distributors identified by a database search. Exhibit 1 gives the Year 1 figures. All amounts are illustrative and in a common currency unit. Assume no other differences affect the comparisons unless the Exhibit says so. The gross margin data of the independent distributors were collected from accounts in which some distributors include marketing costs in cost of sales, and others do not.

exhibits.caption: Year 1 data for Daro Sales S.A. and comparables

items.prompt: (a) Explain the factors that determine the selection of the most appropriate transfer pricing method under the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines, and state which of the comparable uncontrolled price method, the resale price method, the transactional net margin method and the profit split method best suit the facts of Daro Sales S.A. and why.

answer.model: Since the 2010 revision, retained in 2017 and 2022, there is no strict hierarchy of methods: the taxpayer selects the most appropriate method for the circumstances, taking account of the strengths and weaknesses of each method, the nature of the controlled transaction as shown by the functional analysis, the availability of reliable information, in particular on uncontrolled comparables, and the degree of comparability, including the reliability of any adjustments. The traditional transaction methods are still preferred where they can be applied reliably as well as other methods can. The comparable uncontrolled price method compares the price in the controlled transaction with that in a comparable uncontrolled one, and needs close product and contractual comparability. The resale price method starts from the resale price to independent parties and deducts an appropriate gross margin, and is suited to distributors that add little value to the product, but it needs consistent accounting of the cost items in gross margins. The transactional net margin method compares the net profit indicator of the tested party with that of comparable independent enterprises, is less sensitive to product differences and to differences in functions, and is usually applied to the least complex party. The profit split is suitable where both parties make unique and valuable contributions or operations are highly integrated, which does not fit here since Daro Sales S.A. is a distributor without intangibles. The facts point to the transactional net margin method, with Daro Sales S.A. as the tested party, because the gross margin data are not reliable owing to inconsistent classification of marketing costs, and Daro Sales S.A. performs marketing under a mandate that the comparables may not, so net profit is a more robust indicator. The comparable uncontrolled price method remains a cross-check. The resale price method on the Exhibit data gives a gross margin of 24 per cent, inside the 22 to 30 per cent range and so no adjustment, but that result is unreliable because the comparables classify marketing costs inconsistently.

points.point: states there is no hierarchy and the most appropriate method is chosen on the facts (2017 Guidelines)
lists the selection factors: strengths and weaknesses, functional analysis, availability of reliable information, comparability and adjustments
explains why profit split is not suitable (no unique contributions or integration)
selects TNMM with the distributor as the tested party and gives reasons based on the facts (inconsistent gross margin data, marketing functions)

answer.grader_note: Accept resale price method as the answer if the candidate justifies it and deals with the cost classification problem, but expect a cross-check using the net margin. The 2017 Guidelines kept a preference for traditional transaction methods where equally reliable.

items.prompt: (b) Calculate the operating profit margin of Daro Sales S.A. in Year 1, test it against the interquartile range, and calculate the adjustment and the additional State S tax if the profit is brought (i) to the median and (ii) only to the bottom of the range. State the arm's length purchase price under (i).

answer.model: Gross profit is 50,000,000 less 38,000,000, which is 12,000,000, a gross margin of 12,000,000 ÷ 50,000,000 = 24.0 per cent. Operating profit is 12,000,000 less 10,000,000 = 2,000,000, so the operating margin is 2,000,000 ÷ 50,000,000 = 4.0 per cent. The interquartile range of the comparables is 5 per cent to 9 per cent, so 4.0 per cent is below the range and an adjustment is open to the tax authority. (i) Adjusting to the median of 7 per cent requires operating profit of 7% × 50,000,000 = 3,500,000. The shortfall is 3,500,000 less 2,000,000 = 1,500,000. Additional State S tax is 1,500,000 × 25% = 375,000. The arm's length purchase price falls by the same 1,500,000 to 38,000,000 less 1,500,000 = 36,500,000, or 36,500,000 ÷ 300,000 = 121.67 per unit against the actual 126.67 per unit. (ii) Adjusting to the bottom of the range, 5 per cent, requires operating profit of 5% × 50,000,000 = 2,500,000, so the adjustment is 2,500,000 less 2,000,000 = 500,000, and the additional tax is 500,000 × 25% = 125,000. The purchase price would then be 37,500,000. A candidate should note that the Guidelines allow a point within the range, and that the median is a common approach, or the State may argue for the median where the taxpayer's result is outside the range, while the taxpayer may argue for the least adjustment.

points.point: gross profit 12,000,000 and gross margin 24.0 per cent
operating profit 2,000,000 and operating margin 4.0 per cent
states that 4.0 per cent is below the 5 to 9 per cent range so an adjustment can be made
(i) median target profit 3,500,000 and adjustment 1,500,000
(i) tax 375,000 and arm's length purchase price 36,500,000
(ii) target profit 2,500,000 and adjustment 500,000

answer.grader_note: Allow follow-through. Credit per unit price 121.67 as a bonus within the marks.

items.prompt: (c) Management says the price of 118 per unit paid by the State T distributor is a reliable comparable that should be used to test the transfer price. Evaluate this CUP evidence, including a calculation of the effect of the different credit terms on the price comparison, and compare the result with your answer in (b)(i).

answer.model: The comparison is of the controlled price of 38,000,000 ÷ 300,000 = 126.67 per unit and the independent price of 118. The independent distributor receives 180 days' credit against 30 days for Daro Sales S.A., a difference of 150 days. The credit has value, so the 118 is higher than the price that would apply with 30 day terms. The adjustment is 118 × 6% × 150 ÷ 365 = 2.91 per unit, so the adjusted comparable price is about 115.09 (118 less 2.91). Against this, the controlled price of 126.67 is about 11.58 or 10.1 per cent higher, so the CUP, as adjusted, suggests that the controlled price is too high, which is consistent with the tax authority's view and with the result of the net margin analysis at 121.67 per unit, which is 6.58 per unit above the adjusted CUP, so both point the same way but do not coincide. Management's unadjusted 118 is not on comparable terms, and even unadjusted it lies below the controlled price of 126.67, so it supports State S rather than management. The reliability of the CUP is still limited: the volume is 120,000 units against 300,000, there may be exclusive territory, currency and marketing differences, and no reliable adjustment for these is given, so it can only be a corroborating cross-check. Both methods show the controlled price is too high, though the adjusted CUP of about 115 and the net margin result of 121.67 differ, so a range is more defensible than a point.

points.point: computes the controlled price 126.67 per unit
recognises that 150 days of extra credit means the comparable price must be reduced to equate terms
calculates the adjustment 118 × 6% × 150 ÷ 365 = 2.91 and adjusted price about 115.09
compares 115.09 with 126.67 and the TNMM result 121.67, concluding both indicate the controlled price is too high and management's argument fails
notes remaining comparability limits (volume, territory, marketing) and that CUP is a cross-check only

answer.grader_note: Accept 2.90 or 2.91 and 115.09 or 115.10. If the candidate applies the credit adjustment in the wrong direction, credit method but not the conclusion.

items.prompt: (d) Advise Daro Optics on the consequences for the group if State S makes the adjustment in (b)(i), and what steps can be taken to avoid double taxation.

answer.model: If State S increases the profit of Daro Sales S.A. by 1,500,000, State R still taxes the revenue of Daro Optics based on the original price, so the same 1,500,000 is taxed twice, in State S through the adjustment and in State R through the sale. Article 9(2) of the treaty requires State R to make a corresponding adjustment, reducing the profit of Daro Optics by 1,500,000, if State R agrees that the adjustment is justified in principle and amount. Daro Optics should present the case to the competent authority of State R under Article 25, within the time limit, with a request for a corresponding adjustment, and the competent authorities will try to reach an agreement, possibly followed by arbitration if the treaty provides for it. State R is not bound to follow State S, and it might argue for a lower adjustment, for example at the bottom of the range, in which case the unrelieved difference remains double tax. Interest and penalties on the State S assessment may be levied on top. Going forward, the group should prepare benchmarking and transfer pricing documentation, and consider a bilateral advance pricing agreement to fix the method and range for later years.

points.point: identifies economic double taxation of 1,500,000 if there is no corresponding adjustment
explains Article 9(2) corresponding adjustment and MAP under Article 25, noting State R is not automatically bound
recommends documentation and a bilateral APA for the future

title: Orrin Holdings and a disputed treaty term
scenario: Calloway Ltd is resident in State S. Since Year 1, it has been wholly owned by Orrin Holdings Ltd, resident in State R. Orrin Holdings Ltd is a holding company with two employees which is wholly owned by Zarin Group Plc of State T. The State R and State S treaty was signed in Year 1 and follows the OECD Model of that time. Article 10 limits State S tax on dividends to 5 per cent where the beneficial owner is a company holding at least 25 per cent of the capital of the payer, and 15 per cent in other cases. The treaty does not define 'beneficial owner' and contains no principal purpose test. In Year 8 State S enacted a statutory definition of beneficial owner for domestic and treaty purposes, which denies that status to a recipient that has no right to use and enjoy the dividend, being under a contractual or practical obligation to pass it on. In Year 9 Calloway Ltd paid a dividend, and Orrin Holdings Ltd passed on the stated share to Zarin Group Plc within 30 days under an informal group cash management policy, not a written obligation. State S applied withholding tax at the domestic rate. Orrin Holdings Ltd says that the treaty must be read as at Year 1, when the OECD Commentary said little about conduit arrangements, and that the Year 8 definition cannot reduce treaty benefits. Exhibit 1 gives the figures, which are illustrative and in a common currency unit.

exhibits.caption: Facts and rates for the Year 9 dividend

items.prompt: (a) Explain the rules that govern the interpretation of the treaty, including Articles 31 and 32 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties and Article 3(2) of the OECD Model, and how they relate to each other.

answer.model: Treaty interpretation is governed by customary international law, as reflected in Articles 31 to 33 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, and the courts of many States apply them even where the State is not a party. Article 31(1) requires a treaty to be interpreted in good faith in accordance with the ordinary meaning of its terms in their context and in the light of its object and purpose. The context includes the text, preamble and annexes, and any agreement or instrument made in connection with the treaty. Article 31(3) requires account to be taken of any subsequent agreement between the parties on interpretation or application, subsequent practice that establishes the agreement of the parties, and relevant rules of international law. Article 32 permits recourse to supplementary means, including the preparatory work and the circumstances of the conclusion of the treaty, to confirm the meaning from Article 31 or where it leaves the meaning ambiguous or obscure or leads to a manifestly absurd or unreasonable result. Article 3(2) of the OECD Model is a rule specific to tax treaties for terms not defined in the treaty. Any such term has, unless the context otherwise requires, the meaning that it has at the time of application under the law of the State applying the treaty for the purposes of the taxes to which the treaty applies, with the meaning under tax law prevailing over other laws. The two sets of rules work together. The phrase 'unless the context otherwise requires' brings in the interpretation under Article 31, so domestic meaning is the second step, taken only where context does not supply an answer, and a term with an established international meaning may not be left to domestic law.

points.point: states that Articles 31 and 32 VCLT apply as customary rules: good faith, ordinary meaning in context, object and purpose
mentions subsequent agreement or practice (Article 31(3)) and supplementary means including preparatory work (Article 32)
states Article 3(2): undefined term takes the domestic meaning at the time of application unless the context otherwise requires, tax law prevailing
explains the relationship: context comes first and Article 3(2) is a fall-back

items.prompt: (b) Discuss whether the treaty term should be read as at Year 1 (the static approach) or as applying at the time of application (the ambulatory approach), and what weight the later versions of the OECD Commentary and the Year 8 definition should have.

answer.model: Orrin Holdings Ltd relies on the static approach, under which the meaning is fixed at the time of conclusion, so later domestic changes cannot affect the treaty bargain. There is force in this where the treaty term is not given the meaning of domestic law, since a State could otherwise change the treaty benefit unilaterally. The ambulatory approach, which Article 3(2) itself adopts through the words 'at that time', applies the domestic law at the time of application, and the OECD Commentary has endorsed it since 1995. But it applies only where the context does not otherwise require, and 'beneficial owner' is an example of a term whose context points to an international meaning from the treaty system rather than to national law. Courts in several jurisdictions have taken this view: in Indofood v JPMorgan (UK Court of Appeal, 2006) the term was given an international fiscal meaning, not a narrow technical domestic one, and in Prevost Car (Canada, 2008 and 2009) the courts used the Commentary, including the later conduit companies clarifications, as an aid. For the Commentary, the Introduction explains that changes which clarify the meaning of existing text, as opposed to those that reflect substantive change, can be applied to earlier treaties, so later Commentary may be used for guidance, though it does not bind the court. The Year 8 domestic definition therefore cannot be treated as automatically determining a treaty term: if it merely reflects the international meaning, it is consistent with the treaty, but if it goes further, the treaty meaning prevails. The better view is that the term is read in line with the international meaning and clarifications of the Commentary, with the domestic definition given weight only to the extent that it is consistent.

points.point: explains the static approach and the argument for it (the treaty bargain should not be changed unilaterally)
explains the ambulatory approach in Article 3(2) and the Commentary endorsement
explains that 'unless the context otherwise requires' and the international meaning of beneficial owner limit domestic law, with an accurate reference to Indofood or Prevost Car
explains the status of later Commentary: clarifications may be applied to earlier treaties but are not binding; the domestic definition does not override the treaty meaning

answer.grader_note: Credit either conclusion if reasoned. Do not credit invented paragraph numbers.

items.prompt: (c) Calculate the withholding tax under the treaty at the 5 per cent and the 15 per cent rate, and under domestic law, and the amount in dispute in each case. Advise whether Orrin Holdings Ltd is likely to be treated as the beneficial owner of the dividend, taking account of the facts that cut each way.

answer.model: At 5 per cent, tax is 8,000,000 × 5% = 400,000. At 15 per cent, it is 8,000,000 × 15% = 1,200,000. Under domestic law at 25 per cent it is 8,000,000 × 25% = 2,000,000. State S withheld 2,000,000, so the amount in dispute if Orrin Holdings Ltd is the beneficial owner is 2,000,000 less 400,000 = 1,600,000. If it is not, and Zarin Group Plc is treated as the owner entitled to the treaty rate between State S and State T, tax is 1,200,000 and the refund due is 800,000. The amount Orrin Holdings Ltd retained is 10% × 8,000,000 = 800,000, and 90% × 8,000,000 = 7,200,000 was passed on. On the facts, the points for State S are that Orrin Holdings Ltd is a holding company with two employees, that 90 per cent of the dividend is passed on within 30 days, that this follows a group policy, and that it is wholly owned by Zarin Group Plc. The points for Orrin Holdings Ltd are that no written or legal obligation exists, that the group cash management policy is informal, that Orrin retains 10 per cent and may use the funds, that it has held the shares since Year 1, long before the Year 8 change, and that the Commentary treats a conduit as a recipient with very narrow powers as a mere fiduciary or administrator, not one that is merely passing on income as a matter of group policy. The rapid pass-through, the minimal substance, and the high share passed on make State S's position credible, but without a legal obligation, the better view is that Orrin Holdings Ltd is more likely than not to be the beneficial owner under the international meaning, though the Year 8 statutory definition, which mentions a practical obligation, makes the position uncertain. A prudent adviser would recommend appeal, seeking a mutual agreement procedure under Article 25 with State R, and noting that a principal purpose test is absent.

points.point: tax at 5 per cent 400,000, at 15 per cent 1,200,000, at 25 per cent 2,000,000
amount in dispute: 1,600,000 if Orrin is the owner; refund 800,000 if the treaty rate of 15 per cent applies through Zarin Group Plc
amounts passed on 7,200,000 and retained 800,000
identifies facts for State S: minimal substance, 90 per cent passed on quickly, group policy
identifies facts for Orrin: no legal obligation, informal policy, retains 10 per cent, holding since Year 1
reaches a reasoned conclusion on beneficial ownership and next steps (MAP, appeal)

answer.grader_note: Allow either conclusion if reasoned. State S could also argue the 15 per cent rate for a different reason; credit only if the candidate explains it.

title: Automatic exchange of information as a compliance tool
scenario: A finance minister of State R says: "Between them, the Common Reporting Standard and country-by-country reporting have ended the era in which wealth and profit could be hidden offshore. Everything now reaches the tax authority automatically." A tax adviser replies that automatic exchange of information is a powerful tool but that it neither detects every case nor, on its own, changes where multinational groups report their profit.

items.prompt: (a) Explain how the Common Reporting Standard operates, including the roles of financial institutions and of competent authorities, and outline the main changes made by the amended Standard that took effect from 2026.

answer.model:
The Common Reporting Standard (CRS) is the OECD standard for automatic exchange of financial account information, approved in 2014 and built on the Model Competent Authority Agreement and the Standard's Commentaries. It has two parts. The first is a reporting and due diligence obligation placed on financial institutions: banks, custodians, certain investment entities and specified insurance companies. Each reporting financial institution must identify the tax residence of its account holders, using self-certifications and documentary evidence, with different procedures for pre-existing and new individual accounts and for entity accounts. For passive non-financial entities it must also look through to the controlling persons, which is the link to beneficial ownership. The institution then reports the details of reportable accounts (identity, tax identification number, balance, and income such as interest, dividends and gross proceeds) to its own domestic tax authority.

The second part is the exchange itself. The domestic authority sends the information annually to the competent authority of each jurisdiction in which a reportable account holder or controlling person is resident. The legal basis for the exchange is a bilateral or multilateral instrument that allows exchange, most commonly the Convention on Mutual Administrative Assistance in Tax Matters or a double tax convention with an exchange of information article (Article 26 of the OECD and UN Models), combined with the multilateral Competent Authority Agreement under which each pair of jurisdictions activates the exchange. The exchange is not reciprocal in every case: some jurisdictions with no personal income tax participate without receiving data on the basis of non-reciprocal arrangements. The United States does not participate in the CRS and relies on its own FATCA regime, which is a significant gap in coverage that the minister overlooks.

The Standard was amended by the OECD in 2023 with effect from 1 January 2026 in the earliest adopting jurisdictions (the domestic start date varies by jurisdiction), with first exchanges of the new data expected during 2027 for the first wave of committed jurisdictions and 2028 for a second wave. The amendments bring specified electronic money products and central bank digital currencies within the Standard, bring certain indirect investments in crypto-assets (for example through derivatives or investment vehicles) into the reporting net, strengthen the due diligence procedures, including a requirement for a valid self-certification, and expand the information reported, including the role of each controlling person. They are designed to work alongside the Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework, which covers transactions rather than account holdings.

points.point: states that the CRS is an OECD standard for automatic exchange of financial account information, approved in 2014
explains the due diligence role of financial institutions: identifying tax residence by self-certification and documentary evidence, with a look through to controlling persons of passive entities

explains that institutions report account details (identity, TIN, balance, income) to their domestic authority, which then exchanges annually with the competent authority of the residence jurisdiction
identifies the legal basis: a multilateral or bilateral exchange instrument (Convention on Mutual Administrative Assistance or Article 26 of the Models) plus the Competent Authority Agreement
notes the United States is outside the CRS and uses FATCA, or that some participants are non-reciprocal
states that the amended CRS applies from 1 January 2026 in the earliest adopting jurisdictions, with first exchanges in 2027
outlines at least two substantive amendments, such as electronic money and central bank digital currency, crypto-assets held as investments, stronger due diligence or additional reporting fields

answer.grader_note: Accept different wording for the amendments provided at least two are accurate. Do not credit a claim that the CRS exchanges transaction data on crypto-assets (that is the Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework). No penalty for omitting FATCA if the other points are made.

items.prompt: (b) Describe country-by-country reporting under BEPS Action 13, including who must file, the information reported, how it is exchanged and the limits placed on its use.

answer.model:
Country-by-country (CbC) reporting is a minimum standard of the BEPS project under Action 13, which also introduced the three-tier documentation approach of master file, local file and CbC report. The CbC report must be filed by the ultimate parent entity of a multinational enterprise group whose consolidated group revenue in the preceding fiscal year is at or above the threshold of EUR 750 million, or a local currency equivalent. Jurisdictions may, and many do, apply backup rules: a surrogate parent entity may file, and where the parent's jurisdiction does not require or exchange the report, local filing can be required from a constituent entity in the jurisdiction (the secondary mechanism). The report is generally due within twelve months of the end of the fiscal year.

The report is aggregated by tax jurisdiction. It shows, for each jurisdiction in which the group operates, revenues (split between related and unrelated parties), profit or loss before income tax, income tax paid on a cash basis, income tax accrued for the current year, stated capital, accumulated earnings, number of employees and tangible assets other than cash. A second table lists each constituent entity of the group by jurisdiction and its main business activities.

The report is filed with the tax authority of the jurisdiction of the ultimate parent. It is then exchanged with the other jurisdictions in which the group has entities, under the multilateral Competent Authority Agreement on the exchange of CbC reports, a double tax convention or the Convention on Mutual Administrative Assistance, subject to confidentiality and appropriate use safeguards. The standard limits use. The report is intended for high level transfer pricing risk assessment and for assessment of other BEPS related risks. It is not conclusive evidence that transfer prices are or are not appropriate, and tax administrations must not propose adjustments to income on the basis of the CbC report alone, nor apply a formulary apportionment of income based on its data. Separately, some jurisdictions, notably within the European Union, now require certain groups to publish a CbC report under public reporting rules, which goes beyond the OECD minimum standard.

points.point: identifies CbC reporting as a BEPS Action 13 minimum standard alongside the master file and local file
states the EUR 750 million consolidated revenue threshold and that the ultimate parent entity files
mentions surrogate or secondary (local) filing mechanisms as a backstop
lists at least four data items by jurisdiction, such as revenue, profit before tax, tax paid and accrued, employees, tangible assets, capital and earnings
explains exchange to other jurisdictions under the CbC MCAA, a DTC or the Convention, with confidentiality safeguards
states that the report is a risk assessment tool and not a basis on its own for transfer pricing adjustments or formulary apportionment

answer.grader_note: Accept any reasonable local currency or threshold wording but the 750 million euro figure must be stated for the mark. The mention of public CbC reporting is creditable as extra detail in point 3 or 6 but does not carry a separate mark.

items.prompt: (c) Critically evaluate the minister's claim and the adviser's reply. Conclude on how far automatic exchange has addressed offshore evasion and profit shifting.

answer.model:
The minister's claim is strongest for offshore evasion by individuals, and weakest for profit shifting by multinationals. The distinction is the heart of a good answer.

For evasion, the CRS has changed behaviour on a large scale. A bank in a former secrecy jurisdiction now reports account balances and income to the account holder's State of residence, so a resident who holds an undeclared account faces a high chance of detection, and the existence of the exchange has itself driven voluntary disclosure programmes and the closing of accounts. The standard is also stronger than earlier bilateral exchange on request because it does not depend on the receiving State already suspecting a particular taxpayer. The limits are nonetheless real. Coverage is incomplete: the United States is outside the CRS, some jurisdictions are only partial participants or are non-reciprocal, and investment migrated into asset classes the early standard did not cover, such as real estate, art and, until recently, crypto-assets and electronic money, which is why the standard has been amended and why the Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework was added. Data quality depends on self-certification, so an account holder who misstates residence, or who uses nominees, trusts or entities whose controlling persons are not identified, may escape the net. Receiving authorities must also have the capacity to match and use data, which is a particular burden for lower income States, so the benefit is uneven.

For profit shifting, CbC reporting provides information, not a rule. It lets a tax authority see the mismatch between a group's revenue, employees and tangible assets in a jurisdiction and the profit it reports there, which helps risk assessment and has probably deterred the most aggressive structures. But the report cannot itself found an adjustment, and the OECD limits its use for that purpose. It does not change the substantive rules on where profit is allocated: only the transfer pricing rules, the permanent establishment rules and, where implemented, Pillar Two do that (Pillar One Amount A has not entered into force: its Multilateral Convention was never opened for signature). The EUR 750 million threshold leaves out smaller groups, and the report shows only aggregate data, with comparability issues from differing accounting rules. Public CbC reporting in some jurisdictions (for example under the EU public reporting Directive, applying to financial years beginning on or after 22 June 2024) adds reputational pressure but also raises concerns on confidentiality.

The adviser is therefore right. Automatic exchange is an information measure. It increases the probability of detection and so changes incentives, but it does not decide taxing rights. The minister overstates the case: the claim that "everything" reaches the authority is untrue given gaps in coverage, in asset classes, in entity look through and in the threshold. A balanced conclusion is that exchange has substantially reduced undeclared offshore holdings by individuals, that it has contributed to transparency about multinational profit allocation, and that tackling profit shifting depends on substantive rules, supported by exchange.

points.point: distinguishes evasion by individuals (CRS) from profit shifting by groups (CbC reporting)
gives at least two reasons the CRS has been effective, such as automatic rather than on request exchange, deterrence or voluntary disclosure

identifies at least two limits of the CRS, such as non-participation of the United States, non-reciprocal participants, uncovered assets, reliance on self-certification, nominees or capacity of receiving States
explains that CbC data is for risk assessment and cannot alone support adjustments, so it does not change where profit is taxed
reaches a reasoned conclusion that supports the adviser and explains why the minister's claim is overstated

answer.grader_note: Full marks need both sides of the argument and a conclusion that is reasoned. A candidate who simply lists the features of CRS and CbC without evaluation should not exceed 4.

title: Transparency about owners, assets and sustainability
scenario: Tax transparency began with the exchange of information about bank accounts. It has since spread to three further areas: public and tax authority access to information on who ultimately owns and controls companies and trusts, reporting by providers of crypto-asset services, and voluntary or mandatory disclosure of tax information in sustainability and ESG reporting. Critics say that each step adds compliance cost and privacy risk faster than it adds tax revenue.

items.prompt: (a) Explain why information on beneficial ownership matters to tax administrations and describe the international standards that address it. Discuss the privacy limits that have emerged.

answer.model:
A tax administration cannot tax a person it cannot identify. Legal entities and arrangements such as companies, trusts and foundations can interpose layers between income and the individual who ultimately benefits, and a chain of nominees or entities in different States can make it hard to establish who is liable, who is entitled to treaty benefits and who is a controlling person for exchange purposes. Beneficial ownership information therefore supports four tax functions: finding the true taxpayer, applying anti-abuse rules and treaty entitlement tests that depend on ownership (the beneficial owner requirement in Articles 10, 11 and 12 and the limitation on benefits and principal purpose tests), carrying out the CRS look through to controlling persons, and responding to requests for exchange of information.

Two sets of international standards address it. The Financial Action Task Force (FATF) Recommendations 24 and 25 require countries to ensure adequate, accurate and up to date information on the beneficial ownership of legal persons and legal arrangements, available to competent authorities in a timely way; the FATF strengthened Recommendation 24 in March 2022 to push countries towards registers or equivalent mechanisms, and revised Recommendation 25 on legal arrangements in 2023. Secondly, the standard of the Global Forum on Transparency and Exchange of Information for Tax Purposes, in its terms of reference for peer reviews, requires jurisdictions to hold ownership and identity information on legal entities and arrangements, including beneficial ownership information, and to exchange it on request. In the European Union, the Anti-Money Laundering Directive required Member States to establish registers, and later amendments opened them to the public.

Privacy limits have developed. In November 2022 the Court of Justice of the European Union, in WM and Sovim, held that the provision giving the general public access to beneficial ownership information in all cases was invalid, because it was a serious interference with the rights to private life and protection of personal data under the Charter of Fundamental Rights and was not proportionate. Access for competent authorities and those with a legitimate interest remained. The lesson is that transparency for tax authorities is accepted, but wider public access must be justified and proportionate, and a regime must be designed so that data is protected as well as collected. Candidates may also note that a register does not guarantee accuracy unless information is verified, and that trusts and foundations raise particular difficulties.

points.point: explains that tax administrations need to identify the real taxpayer behind entities and arrangements
links ownership information to anti-abuse and treaty entitlement, such as beneficial owner or LOB tests
links ownership information to CRS controlling person look through and to exchange on request
identifies FATF Recommendations 24 and 25 on legal persons and legal arrangements
identifies the Global Forum standard on ownership and identity information
explains the CJEU decision in WM and Sovim (2022) that unrestricted public access was invalid on proportionality and privacy grounds

answer.grader_note: Accept FATF 'revised in 2022' wording; a candidate who states only 'FATF standards' without the Recommendation numbers earns one of the two marks. Do not credit a claim that the CJEU invalidated the registers themselves: only the public access provision was held invalid.

items.prompt: (b) Describe the OECD Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF) and explain why the existing CRS was thought insufficient for crypto-assets.

answer.model:
The Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework was developed by the OECD at the request of the G20 and approved in 2022. It provides for the automatic exchange of tax information on transactions in crypto-assets, and is designed to sit beside the CRS. It has three building blocks: the rules, which define which assets, which service providers and which transactions are covered; the Commentary; and the legal and technical framework for exchange, which includes a multilateral competent authority agreement and an XML schema.

The rules apply to crypto-assets, meaning assets that rely on cryptographically secured distributed ledger technology to validate and secure transactions, subject to exclusions for central bank digital currencies and specified electronic money products, which are dealt with in the amended CRS. They place the reporting obligation on reporting crypto-asset service providers, which are individuals or entities that, as a business, effect exchange transactions for or on behalf of customers: exchanges, brokers, dealers and operators of crypto-asset ATMs. Providers collect due diligence information on users and controlling persons and report annually. The reported transactions include exchanges between crypto-assets and fiat currencies, exchanges between different crypto-assets, and transfers, including reportable retail payment transactions. The provider reports the user's identity, tax residence and the aggregate value, number of units and number of transactions by type, which the receiving administration can use to check the user's gains. The information is exchanged with the jurisdiction of residence of the user, and implementation is intended for exchanges to begin from 2027 in the jurisdictions that committed to the earliest timeline.

The CRS was thought insufficient for four reasons. First, it was built around financial institutions holding financial accounts, but a person may hold crypto-assets in a self-hosted wallet or with a provider who is not a financial institution, so nothing is reported. Secondly, the CRS reports balances and income at year end, whereas the tax issue with crypto-assets is the gain on each disposal, which needs transaction data. Thirdly, crypto-assets are by design borderless and pseudonymous, which can make it hard to identify the residence of the holder. Fourthly, the CRS did not originally cover assets such as electronic money or central bank digital currency, so a package of amendments was needed. The new framework therefore targets the intermediaries who are visible, and collects transaction information that supports self-assessment of capital gains and income.

points.point: states that CARF was developed by the OECD for the G20 and approved in 2022 as a framework for automatic exchange on crypto-asset transactions
identifies the reporting persons: crypto-asset service providers such as exchanges, brokers and dealers
describes reportable transactions: crypto to fiat, crypto to crypto, and transfers or retail payments
describes information reported: user identity and residence plus aggregate value and units by transaction type, exchanged with the residence State
states that implementation has exchanges starting from 2027 for early adopters
explains why the CRS was insufficient: self-hosted wallets and non-financial intermediaries are outside account based reporting
explains that the CRS reports balances and income whereas crypto tax issues turn on gains on disposals and transactions

answer.grader_note: Accept 'around 2027' for the first exchanges. The point about exclusion of CBDC and e-money (dealt with in the amended CRS) is creditable under point 2 if made.

items.prompt: (c) Discuss how tax is now treated within sustainability and ESG disclosure, and assess whether this form of transparency is likely to change the tax behaviour of multinational groups.

answer.model:
Investors, lenders, civil society and regulators increasingly treat tax conduct as part of a business's governance and social contribution, and tax now features in sustainability and ESG reporting in two ways. One is voluntary or standards based disclosure: for example, the Global Reporting Initiative's tax standard (GRI 207, effective for reporting from 2021) asks an entity to describe its approach to tax, its tax governance, control and risk management, how it engages with stakeholders, and to report tax paid by jurisdiction. The other is a regulatory requirement for public reporting in some places, such as the European Union rules requiring large multinational groups to publish a country-by-country report of tax and other data, which goes beyond the confidential CbC report under BEPS Action 13.

The case that this will change behaviour starts with the reputational channel. Information published in a standardised form can be compared by investors and the public, and a group with a large revenue in a State but little profit or tax there may be asked to explain it. Boards may then favour simpler structures and a stated tax policy, and tax risk becomes a board level matter. Public data may also help smaller tax authorities that cannot access confidential exchanged reports, and it supports an argument that paying tax where activity takes place is part of social responsibility.

There are doubts. A voluntary standard can be satisfied by narrative disclosure that does not alter practice, and aggregated figures are hard to interpret: low tax in a jurisdiction can result from lawful incentives, losses, timing differences or the stage of an investment, so data can mislead as well as reveal. Compliance costs fall on the groups least able to bear them, and public data raises concerns on commercial confidentiality, though supporters reply that the risk is low for aggregated data. The effect also depends on whether the audience cares about tax: evidence that consumers or investors act on it is mixed. Behaviour changes more reliably when the substantive rules change, so a minimum tax of the type found in Pillar Two reduces the gain from shifting regardless of reputation.

A sound conclusion is that ESG and public tax disclosure is a supplement. It adds a reputational and governance incentive, and may reinforce the exchange of information between administrations, but it is unlikely on its own to change behaviour materially, and it works best alongside binding rules and exchange between authorities.

points.point: identifies tax as part of governance or social contribution in sustainability reporting and explains why stakeholders care
describes the content of a standards based tax disclosure, for example GRI 207 on approach, governance, risk and country level reporting
identifies public country-by-country reporting as a regulatory form and distinguishes it from the confidential Action 13 report
explains how disclosure may change behaviour: reputational pressure, comparability, board level tax risk, benefit to smaller administrations
identifies at least two limitations: narrative or voluntary disclosure, difficult interpretation of aggregated data, compliance cost, confidentiality, weak evidence that stakeholders act
reaches a reasoned conclusion that places disclosure as a supplement to binding rules such as Pillar Two

answer.grader_note: Do not require GRI 207 specifically: any accurate description of a recognised tax disclosure framework earns the two marks. The word 'Pillar Two' is not essential to the conclusion mark if the candidate argues the point.

title: The development of international tax institutions
scenario: "The rules that decide which State may tax cross-border income were written in the 1920s by a handful of European experts, refined by the OECD for its members, and are now being renegotiated in a forum that developing countries say they never really shaped. International tax law has a history, and the history explains today's disputes."

items.prompt: (a) Trace the work of the League of Nations on double taxation and explain how it influenced the OECD and UN Model Conventions.

answer.model:
After the First World War, rising national tax burdens and growing cross-border investment made double taxation a practical obstacle to trade, and the League of Nations took up the problem. In 1921 it asked experts to study it, and in 1923 four economists (Bruins, Einaudi, Seligman and Stamp) reported. They worked from the idea of economic allegiance, which weighs the contribution of the place where wealth is produced against that of the place where the owner lives, and recommended that residence should in principle be the basis of taxation, with the source State yielding on some classes of income. Technical experts then drafted model provisions in 1925, and a general meeting of government experts in 1928 produced draft bilateral conventions on double taxation and on administrative assistance, which established the template of a model that States could adapt in bilateral treaties. The Fiscal Committee carried on the work, and in 1935 a draft convention on the allocation of business profits between States adopted the separate entity and permanent establishment approach that remains in Article 7 today.

During the Second World War, Mexico City in 1943 and London in 1946 produced two further models. The Mexico Model favoured greater source taxation, reflecting the interests of capital importing countries in Latin America. The London Model leant towards residence taxation. This divergence anticipated the later debate between capital exporters and importers.

The OECD inherited this work. Its predecessor's fiscal committee began work in 1956, and the OECD issued a draft Model Convention in 1963 and a full Model Convention with Commentary in 1977, which has since been updated on a continuing basis rather than replaced, with revisions in 1992 onwards, and most recently including the 2025 update. The OECD Model follows the League's emphasis on residence taxation, a limited source right for business profits through the permanent establishment threshold, and exchange of information. The UN Model Convention began with the Ad Hoc Group of Experts established by the Economic and Social Council in 1967, to produce guidance for treaties between developed and developing countries. It published a Model in 1980. It follows the OECD structure but, in the tradition of Mexico, gives more weight to source taxation: for example, the lower permanent establishment thresholds for building sites and service activities, a force of attraction rule in Article 7, and a wider source taxation of royalties and of fees for technical services (Article 12A of the 2021 UN Model, replaced in the 2025 update by Article 12AA on fees for services, which also absorbed Article 14). In 2004 the Ad Hoc Group became the Committee of Experts on International Cooperation in Tax Matters. Both models therefore owe their structure to the League, and differ in the balance between residence and source.

points.point: explains the League of Nations began work after the First World War because double taxation obstructed trade and investment
describes the 1923 report of four economists and the economic allegiance concept, with a residence based tendency
describes the 1927 or 1928 draft model conventions as the template for bilateral treaties and the 1935 draft on profits allocation with PE approach
identifies the Mexico (1943) and London (1946) models and their source versus residence emphasis
describes OECD development: 1963 draft, 1977 Model, subsequent updates
describes the UN Ad Hoc Group (1967), the 1980 UN Model, and its greater weight on source taxation with at least one example

answer.grader_note: Dates within a year of those stated are acceptable for 1927 and 1928. Do not credit an assertion that the League produced the OECD Model or that the UN Model is a different structure from the OECD Model.

items.prompt: (b) Explain the role of the G20 and the OECD in the BEPS project, and of the UN in the development of international tax cooperation since 2013.

answer.model:
The BEPS project was a response to concern that the existing rules allowed multinational groups to report profits in places of low taxation and little activity. The G20 gave the political mandate: the OECD produced a 2013 report on base erosion and profit shifting and an Action Plan of 15 actions, which the G20 endorsed in 2013, and the G20 endorsed the final reports in 2015. The OECD supplied the technical work. The outputs included minimum standards (on harmful tax practices under Action 5, treaty abuse under Action 6, CbC reporting under Action 13 and dispute resolution under Action 14), common approaches, and best practices. Action 15 produced the Multilateral Instrument, which allows treaty changes to be made in many treaties at once. Because many non-members were affected, the OECD and G20 created the Inclusive Framework on BEPS in 2016, so that any interested jurisdiction could take part on an equal footing in monitoring and in further work. The Inclusive Framework agreed in 2021 on a two pillar solution to the tax challenges arising from the digitalisation of the economy, supported by a large number of jurisdictions: Pillar One reallocating taxing rights (its Amount A convention was never opened for signature, and Amount B is an optional annex to Chapter IV of the Transfer Pricing Guidelines) and Pillar Two providing a global minimum tax.

The UN has had a different role. The Committee of Experts on International Cooperation in Tax Matters continues to maintain the UN Model and Commentary and the practical manual on transfer pricing for developing countries, and gives a voice to developing countries within a tax standard setting process. More recently, in December 2023 the General Assembly (resolution 78/230) set up an ad hoc committee to draft terms of reference for a UN framework convention on international tax cooperation. In December 2024 the General Assembly approved those terms of reference (resolution 79/235), an intergovernmental negotiating committee was established, with final texts due for the General Assembly in 2027 to develop the framework convention and two early protocols, on taxation of cross-border services and on the prevention and resolution of tax disputes. The negotiation is continuing and the outcome is not settled.

points.point: explains the G20 gave the mandate and the OECD supplied the technical work on BEPS, with a 15 point Action Plan in 2013 and final reports in 2015
identifies the types of output: minimum standards, common approaches and best practices, with at least two examples of minimum standard actions
mentions the Multilateral Instrument (Action 15)
explains the Inclusive Framework (2016) and its two pillar agreement in 2021
describes the continuing role of the UN Committee of Experts and the UN Model and its focus on developing countries
describes the UN framework convention process begun in 2023 with the terms of reference of 2024 and the planned protocols on cross-border services and dispute prevention and resolution

answer.grader_note: Accept 2013 or 2015 for the G20 endorsement dates as stated. The statement of the status of the UN process should be hedged as ongoing: do not credit a claim that the convention has been adopted.

items.prompt: (c) Assess the claim that international tax rules have been shaped mainly by capital exporting countries and that the legitimacy of the process is in question. Reach a conclusion.

answer.model:
There is a strong historical case for the claim. The League's experts came largely from Europe and the United States and their approach, which favoured residence taxation, reflected the interests of the major capital exporting States, whose investors wished to be taxed once in the home State. The Mexico Model was a deliberate counterweight and was not adopted as the main template. The OECD, as a club of generally wealthier economies, produced a Model suited to two way investment between similar economies, and in practice many developing countries have followed that Model in their treaties because of its influence and the volume of case law and commentary, even though the UN Model better reflects their interest in source taxation. The BEPS project began among the G20 and OECD members and non-members at first had little say, which prompted the creation of the Inclusive Framework in 2016. Even there, critics argue that the decisions are made by consensus among a body led by OECD members, that the Pillar One and Pillar Two outcomes reflect the interests of larger economies, and that the minimum tax design gives the headquarters State's income inclusion rule priority over the undertaxed profits rule, although a qualified domestic minimum top-up tax lets the source State claim the top-up first.

There are counterarguments. The UN Model has existed since 1980 and takes a source oriented line, and its use in treaties is substantial. The Inclusive Framework has a large membership and gives non-OECD States a seat, and developing countries gained from minimum standards such as treaty abuse prevention and CbC exchange. The OECD's technical resources and the expertise of its secretariat make it efficient, while a UN process, with more than a hundred and ninety States, can be slow and consensus may be harder to reach. The UN framework convention process is itself evidence that States regard the existing arrangements as incomplete, and that the debate is real.

A balanced conclusion is that history supports the claim in respect of agenda setting and the early institutions, but that it is overstated for the present: participation has widened, the UN process may rebalance the debate, and legitimacy now depends on whether the outcomes reflect source State interests as well as efficiency. The test of legitimacy is therefore what is delivered for developing countries over the next decade, not the history alone.

points.point: explains why history supports the claim: League experts and the residence emphasis reflecting capital exporters, Mexico Model as a counterweight
explains the OECD as a club of mostly developed members, with its Model widely followed, and the original BEPS agenda set by the G20 and OECD
identifies the Inclusive Framework as the response and gives at least one criticism of the way decisions are reached or of the distribution of outcomes
gives counterarguments: UN Model, wider membership, gains from minimum standards, efficiency of OECD
refers to the UN framework convention process as evidence of continuing dissatisfaction
reaches a balanced and reasoned conclusion

answer.grader_note: This is a judgement item. Credit any consistent position that deals with both sides. A purely descriptive history should not exceed 3.

title: Delta Assembly and the Corvane Group
scenario: Corvane Holdings plc (Corvane) is resident in State R and owns the design, patents and brand for a range of industrial pumps. In 2026 it contracted with its wholly owned subsidiary Delta Assembly Ltd (Delta), resident in State S, to manufacture the pumps from components that Corvane specifies and sells to Delta at cost, to Corvane's quality standards (the cost of those components forms part of Delta's total operating costs), and to sell the whole output to Corvane. Delta owns no intangibles, holds no inventory beyond three days of work in progress, bears no demand or warranty risk (Corvane indemnifies Delta against claims) and has no research function. Delta's accounts for 2026 show revenue of 42,100,000 and total operating costs of 40,000,000, with State S currency units throughout. The group's transfer pricing policy sets Delta's reward by reference to a net cost plus mark-up on total operating costs, and the State S tax authority is reviewing 2026. Corvane's adviser prepared a benchmarking study of independent contract manufacturers. Nine candidates were identified by database screening. The State S tax rate is 25%. Ignore any other income or deductions of Delta. Figures are illustrative.

exhibits.caption: Net cost plus (operating profit divided by total operating costs) of the nine screened candidates for the same year as the tested party (multiple year data was also reviewed by the adviser); and the reason noted by the adviser
Method for quartiles used by the adviser and the State S authority

items.prompt: (a) Explain which party is the appropriate tested party in the Corvane and Delta transaction and why, and why a one-sided method such as the transactional net margin method is suitable.

answer.model:
The tested party is the party to the controlled transaction for which a profit level indicator can be applied most reliably and for which the most reliable comparable data can be found. That is generally the least complex party, and the one that does not own valuable unique intangibles or assume unique risks. Delta fits: it assembles to Corvane's specification and supplies, owns no intangibles, carries minimal inventory and no demand or warranty risk, and performs no research. Corvane, by contrast, owns the IP and the brand and controls the key risks, and it would be very difficult to find independent companies that are comparable to it. A benchmarking of Delta against independent contract manufacturers is therefore more reliable than any attempt to benchmark Corvane.

Because only Delta is tested, a one-sided method is appropriate. The transactional net margin method (TNMM) compares the net profit margin of the tested party from the controlled transaction relative to a base such as costs, sales or assets, with that earned by independent enterprises in comparable transactions. A cost based profit level indicator is suitable for a service like contract manufacturing in which Delta's costs are the best measure of the value of its input and the contract price does not depend on market prices of the pumps. Net operating profit is used because it is less affected by differences in accounting classification between gross margin items than a gross margin and because interest and tax are excluded. A transactional profit split is not suggested because Delta makes no unique contribution and there is no sharing of significant risk. A one-sided method also has a practical advantage that data on independent manufacturers is accessible from databases.

points.point: states that the tested party is the one for which the profit indicator can be applied most reliably and for which the most reliable comparables can be found, usually the least complex party
applies this to Delta using at least two facts: no intangibles, no demand or warranty risk, minimal inventory, no research
explains that Corvane owns the IP and key risks, so it is hard to find comparables for it
explains that TNMM with a cost based net profit indicator suits a routine contract manufacturer

answer.grader_note: Accept a statement that the OECD Guidelines do not require Delta to be selected where facts differ, but that on these facts it is clearly right. No marks for naming a profit split as appropriate.

items.prompt: (b) Evaluate whether Comp 8 and Comp 9 should be excluded from the set used to compute the arm's length range.

answer.model:
A comparable should be accepted or rejected on whether it is sufficiently comparable in functions, assets and risks, after taking account of the five comparability factors in the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines, and the aim is to exclude results that are not reliable measures of what independent parties would earn in the controlled transaction.

Comp 8 owns patents and sells under its own brand to end customers. Those are functions, assets and risks that Delta does not have, and the returns of an entity that owns valuable intangibles and bears market risk include a return to those assets. Its margin of 12.6% is higher than every other candidate and is consistent with that difference. It should be excluded for lack of comparability in the functional analysis, and not simply because the result is high: a candidate may not be excluded merely because it is an outlier.

Comp 9 is more of a judgement. The Guidelines accept that loss making comparables are not automatically rejected: an independent enterprise cannot sustain losses indefinitely, and a loss may reflect normal business conditions such as a start up or a downturn, in which case the company may be a useful comparable. But the loss may be the result of special circumstances which do not reflect the economic conditions that Delta faces. The adviser's note says the loss was caused by a fire that closed the plant for four months. That is an exceptional event rather than a normal commercial result, a contract manufacturer in a comparable position as Delta would not be expected to earn a loss in a normal period, and its inclusion would depress the range. There is a reasonable case for exclusion. The tax authority, however, might argue that the fire is a risk of the manufacturing business, that insurance proceeds should be considered, and that the multiple year data may show a normal margin in other years. The sound approach is to examine the multiple year results and the insurance position, and, if the fire year is the only year affected, to exclude that year or the company with documented reasons. On the facts given, exclusion is justified, but the reasoning must be documented.

Removing the two leaves seven comparables, which are the seven used below.

points.point: states the test: exclude where functions, assets and risks are not sufficiently comparable, not merely because the result is extreme
excludes Comp 8 because it owns intangibles, uses its brand and bears market risk, so it is functionally different
explains that loss making comparables are not automatically rejected under the Guidelines
assesses Comp 9: the fire is a special circumstance so exclusion is justifiable, and notes the counterargument or the need to check multiple year data and insurance

answer.grader_note: Full marks do not require exclusion of Comp 9 if the argument is balanced and reasoned, but the calculation in (c) assumes exclusion of both. Credit the candidate who excludes only Comp 8 and calculates consistently in (c).

items.prompt: (c) Using the seven remaining comparables and the method in Table 2, calculate the interquartile range and the median. Determine whether Delta's 2026 result falls within the range and, if not, calculate the adjustment to the median. Explain what the position would be if the full range of the seven comparables were used instead.

answer.model:
Step 1: rank the seven comparables: 3.9%, 5.2%, 6.4%, 7.5%, 8.1%, 9.7%, 11.3%. n = 7.

Step 2: quartile positions, using 1 + (n minus 1) × p, so 1 + 6 × p.
First quartile: position 1 + 6 × 0.25 = 2.5, halfway between the second value (5.2%) and the third value (6.4%): 5.2% + 0.5 × (6.4% minus 5.2%) = 5.8%.
Median: position 1 + 6 × 0.5 = 4, which is the fourth value: 7.5%.
Third quartile: position 1 + 6 × 0.75 = 5.5, halfway between the fifth value (8.1%) and the sixth value (9.7%): 8.1% + 0.5 × 1.6% = 8.9%.
The interquartile range is 5.8% to 8.9%, with median 7.5%.

Step 3: Delta's result. Operating profit = revenue minus total operating costs = 42,100,000 minus 40,000,000 = 2,100,000. Net cost plus = 2,100,000 ÷ 40,000,000 = 5.25%.

Step 4: 5.25% is below the lower quartile of 5.8%, so it is outside the interquartile range.

Step 5: where a result is outside the arm's length range, the OECD Guidelines say that the tax administration may adjust to any point within the range, and that where comparability defects remain, a measure of central tendency such as the median may be used to minimise the risk of error (paragraph 3.62). Adjusting to the median: required profit = 40,000,000 × 7.5% = 3,000,000. Adjustment = 3,000,000 minus 2,100,000 = 900,000. Delta's revenue should therefore have been 43,000,000.

Step 6: the full range. The minimum is 3.9% and the maximum is 11.3%. Delta's 5.25% is inside the full range and so no adjustment would arise. The result therefore depends on the statistical method. The Guidelines say that where the comparables have some remaining differences, so that the range is likely to include less reliable results, a statistical tool such as the interquartile range can improve reliability. Here all seven comparables were accepted as sufficiently comparable, so Delta may argue that the full range is appropriate and that the comparables with the lowest and highest results are no less reliable than the others. The authority will argue that the interquartile range is a normal tool, particularly when the data rely on database screening and cannot remove all differences. Both positions are arguable, and the facts about the quality of the screening would decide.

points.point: ranks the seven values in ascending order and applies the stated position formula
computes first quartile 5.8% (interpolation between 5.2% and 6.4%)
computes median 7.5% and third quartile 8.9% (interpolation between 8.1% and 9.7%)
computes Delta operating profit of 2,100,000 and net cost plus of 5.25%
concludes that 5.25% is outside the interquartile range and adjusts to the median: 40,000,000 × 7.5% = 3,000,000, adjustment 900,000
explains that with the full range 3.9% to 11.3% no adjustment arises and that the choice of statistical tool is therefore decisive, with an argument for each side

answer.grader_note: Accept a different consistent interpolation method only if stated, but the exhibit gives the method. A candidate who adjusts to the lower quartile (5.8%) rather than the median should receive credit for the method if stated, with an adjustment of 40,000,000 × 5.8% minus 2,100,000 = 220,000, and one mark less on the adjustment line.

items.prompt: (d) State the additional State S tax arising from the adjustment in (c) and explain, with reference to Article 9 of the Models, what relief Corvane can seek in State R.

answer.model:
Additional taxable profit in State S is 900,000. At 25% the additional State S tax is 900,000 × 25% = 225,000, before any interest or penalty under domestic law.

The adjustment increases Delta's profit and so, if State R does not adjust, the same profit is taxed in State R in Corvane's hands because Corvane's deduction for the price paid to Delta remains the same. That is economic double taxation. Article 9(1) of the OECD and UN Models allows State S to adjust profits of an enterprise where conditions between associated enterprises differ from arm's length conditions. Article 9(2) provides that where State S includes profits on which an enterprise of State R has been charged to tax in State R, and the profits are those that would have accrued to the State S enterprise had the conditions been arm's length, State R shall make an appropriate adjustment to the amount of tax charged on those profits. It applies only where State R agrees that the adjustment is justified in both principle and amount. In practice Corvane would ask State R for a corresponding adjustment, reducing its profit by 900,000 by increasing its deduction, and the competent authorities may be asked to resolve disagreement through the mutual agreement procedure in Article 25. Domestic time limits for making the adjustment, and for the corresponding adjustment, also matter.

points.point: calculates additional State S tax of 225,000 (900,000 × 25%)
explains economic double taxation if State R does not give relief
explains Article 9(2): corresponding adjustment by State R if it agrees that the adjustment is justified in principle and amount
refers to the mutual agreement procedure (Article 25) where the States disagree

answer.grader_note: Statements on arbitration are not required and are not credited.

title: Rivermead Holdings and its State S income
scenario: Rivermead Holdings Ltd (Rivermead) is resident in State R. For 2026 it earned a trading profit in State R and also had income from State S: profits of a branch that is a permanent establishment in State S, a dividend from a State S company in which Rivermead holds 8% of the capital, and interest from a State S borrower. The treaty between State R and State S follows the OECD Model 2025 in Articles 10, 11 and 7, with a maximum State S withholding rate of 15% on dividends and 10% on interest, and State S taxes the branch profits at 20%. State R taxes companies at a flat rate of 25% on worldwide income computed under State R rules, and its domestic law applies any credit separately for each item of income, with no carry forward or carry back of unused credit. The finance director asks how much State R tax is payable for 2026 if the treaty applies Article 23A (exemption) in State R and how much if it applies Article 23B (credit), and which is better for the group. All amounts are in State R currency units and are illustrative. Assume that State S levied tax at the treaty maximum on dividends and interest, the amounts shown in Table 1 are gross, and State R rules compute the PE profit at the same amount as State S.

exhibits.caption: Rivermead's 2026 income and State S tax

items.prompt: (a) Explain the difference between Article 23A and Article 23B of the OECD Model and state how Article 23A(2) treats dividends and interest.

answer.model:
Both Articles require the State of residence to relieve double taxation where the source State may tax under the Convention. Article 23A gives the exemption method: income that may be taxed in the other State under the Convention is exempt from tax in the residence State (paragraph 1), though the residence State may take the exempt income into account in determining the rate of tax on the remaining income (paragraph 3, exemption with progression). Article 23B gives the credit method: the residence State taxes worldwide income and allows as a deduction from its tax an amount equal to the tax paid in the source State, but the deduction cannot exceed the part of the residence State's tax, computed before the deduction, that is attributable to the income that may be taxed in the source State (the ordinary credit limit).

Article 23A(2) provides that for dividends and interest, which may be taxed in the source State under Articles 10 and 11 (at the capped rates), the residence State does not exempt them but allows a credit under the credit method for the source State tax. So even in a treaty with exemption, there is a credit for passive income. The UN Model Articles 23A and 23B follow the same structure.

points.point: states that Article 23A is exemption and Article 23B is credit
explains the credit limit in 23B: deduction not exceeding the residence State tax attributable to the foreign income
