states that under Article 23A(2) dividends and interest are relieved by credit not exemption
mentions exemption with progression in 23A(3) or that the UN Model has the same structure

answer.grader_note: Accept 23A(3) described as allowing the State to take the exempt income into account in fixing the rate on other income.

items.prompt: (b) Calculate Rivermead's State R tax payable for 2026 if Article 23B applies, applying the credit separately to each item of income.

answer.model:
Step 1: worldwide income = 600 + 400 + 100 + 80 = 1,180. State R tax before credit = 1,180 × 25% = 295.

Step 2: State R tax attributable to each foreign item, and the credit allowed (the lower of State S tax and State R tax on the item).
Branch profit: State R tax = 400 × 25% = 100. State S tax = 80. Credit = 80 (the lower).
Dividend: State R tax = 100 × 25% = 25. State S tax = 15. Credit = 15.
Interest: State R tax = 80 × 25% = 20. State S tax = 8. Credit = 8.
Total credit = 80 + 15 + 8 = 103. No credit is limited, because State S tax is below State R tax on each item.

Step 3: State R tax payable = 295 minus 103 = 192.

Step 4: check. State R tax of 192 = 25% × 600 (150) plus the top up on foreign items: branch 100 minus 80 = 20, dividend 25 minus 15 = 10, interest 20 minus 8 = 12; 150 + 20 + 10 + 12 = 192. Total tax in both States = 192 + 103 = 295, which equals 25% of 1,180, so the credit method brings the total burden to the State R rate.

points.point: computes worldwide income 1,180 and tax before credit 295
computes the State R tax attributable to each foreign item (100, 25, 20)
applies the limit item by item and obtains the credits 80, 15 and 8, total 103
concludes State R tax payable is 192
shows the total tax burden as 295 or equivalent check

answer.grader_note: Accept an alternative that applies the limitation overall rather than item by item only if the answer states that it is an assumption: the figures are the same here since no item is limited.

items.prompt: (c) Calculate Rivermead's State R tax payable for 2026 if Article 23A applies (with credit where Article 23A(2) requires it), and compare the total tax burden under the two methods.

answer.model:
Step 1: under Article 23A(1) the branch profit of 400 is exempt in State R, because it may be taxed in State S under Article 7 (the treaty permanent establishment rule). The dividend and the interest are not exempt but fall under Article 23A(2), so they remain taxable in State R with a credit.

Step 2: taxable income in State R = 600 + 100 + 80 = 780. Tax before credit = 780 × 25% = 195.

Step 3: credit for State S tax on the dividend and interest: dividend, lower of 15 and 25 = 15; interest, lower of 8 and 20 = 8. Total credit = 23.

Step 4: State R tax payable = 195 minus 23 = 172.

Step 5: total burden. State S tax is 80 + 15 + 8 = 103 in both cases. Under Article 23A the total is 172 + 103 = 275, which is 20 lower than the total of 295 under Article 23B. Rivermead pays 20 less State R tax under exemption (172 against 192) because the 5 percentage point gap between the State R rate (25%) and the State S branch rate (20%), applied to the branch profit of 400, is 20, and exemption relinquishes that top up.

The exemption method therefore leaves the branch profit bearing only the State S rate of 20%, and favours the taxpayer when the source State rate is lower. If the source State rate were higher than 25%, total tax would be the same under both methods (the higher State S rate applies and no State R tax is due on the branch), except that under credit the excess of State S tax over 25% would be unrelieved and, because credit is applied item by item without carry forward, could not be set against other items.

points.point: exempts the branch profit of 400 under Article 23A(1) and keeps the dividend and interest taxable under 23A(2)
computes taxable income 780 and tax before credit 195
computes credits of 15 and 8 (total 23) and tax payable 172
compares total tax burden 275 against 295 and explains the 20 difference using the 5 point rate gap on 400

answer.grader_note: Do not penalise the last sentence of the model on a higher source rate if a candidate omits it.

items.prompt: (d) Advise the finance director which method is better for Rivermead, and discuss the policy arguments for each method. Comment on what would change if State S had a 0% rate on branch profits through a domestic incentive.

answer.model:
On these figures, exemption is better for Rivermead because it pays 172 against 192 in State R, a saving of 20 a year. But the choice between 23A and 23B is made by the treaty and domestic law of State R, not by the taxpayer, so the advice concerns how to plan and what to expect, for example when the investment is made through a branch, or a subsidiary.

The policy arguments differ. The credit method supports capital export neutrality: an investor is taxed at the same total rate whether it invests at home or abroad, so location decisions are not distorted by tax. The exemption method supports capital import neutrality: all businesses operating in the source State bear the same tax there, whether owned by local or foreign investors, so competitiveness in the market is not distorted. Exemption is administratively simpler because no foreign tax computation is needed, but it makes a low tax State attractive for locating business income. Credit is more complex, and, where the credit is limited, can leave the investor bearing the higher rate.

If State S taxed the branch profit at 0% by incentive, under exemption State R would give up taxing it and the profit would bear no tax at all, which is why many treaties and domestic laws restrict exemption by subject to tax conditions or switch to credit (Article 23A(4) of the OECD Model deals with a related case in which State S treats the income as exempt under the Convention). Under credit State R would tax at 25% with nothing to credit, producing tax of 100 on the branch profit. An incentive in State S would therefore be neutralised under credit but would remain fully effective under exemption. Tax sparing credit is a possible treaty feature for this, which is more usual in treaties with developing countries and which the UN Model Commentary treats more favourably than the OECD Commentary.

points.point: concludes exemption is better for Rivermead here: 172 against 192, a saving of 20, noting the method is set by the treaty
explains CEN for credit and CIN for exemption
identifies a practical or policy point such as simplicity of exemption or distortion of location
explains the 0% scenario: under exemption no tax anywhere, under credit State R taxes at 25% (100 on the branch profit)
mentions anti-abuse or subject to tax conditions, Article 23A(4), or tax sparing as a response

answer.grader_note: A judgement item. Credit sound alternatives. The statement that the UN Commentary is more favourable on tax sparing is background and not required for a mark.

title: Equal treatment of foreign taxpayers
scenario: A commentator writes: "Article 24 gives foreign investors only a thin shield. It forbids discrimination on paper but lets a State treat non-residents worse in almost every way that matters, because the comparison is always made with 'the same circumstances' and because the most important distinctions are expressly carved out." State R, which has a treaty with State S based on the OECD Model, taxes a branch of a State S company at the same rate as its resident companies but gives the branch no personal allowances, and denies a deduction for interest paid by a State R company to a non-resident parent when its debt to equity ratio exceeds 3 to 1 while applying no such test to loans from resident lenders.

items.prompt: (a) Explain the structure of Article 24 of the OECD Model, identifying the type of discrimination addressed by each paragraph.

answer.model: Article 24 contains six paragraphs. Paragraph 1 prohibits discrimination on grounds of nationality: nationals of one State must not be subjected in the other State to taxation or connected requirements that are other or more burdensome than those applied to nationals of that other State in the same circumstances, in particular with respect to residence. It applies whether or not the person is a resident of either State, so it is not limited by Article 1. Paragraph 2 gives stateless persons resident in a State equivalent protection. Paragraph 3 deals with permanent establishments: the taxation of a PE of an enterprise of one State in the other State must not be less favourable than that of enterprises of the other State carrying on the same activities. It does not oblige a State to grant to non-residents the personal allowances, reliefs and reductions it gives to its own residents for family or civil status reasons. Paragraph 4 requires interest, royalties and other disbursements paid by an enterprise of one State to a resident of the other to be deductible on the same conditions as if paid to a resident of the first State, except where Article 9(1), 11(6) or 12(4) applies; the same applies to debts. Paragraph 5 protects enterprises of one State whose capital is wholly or partly owned or controlled by residents of the other State from more burdensome taxation than similar domestic enterprises. Paragraph 6 states that the Article applies to taxes of every kind and description, not just those covered by the Convention under Article 2. The UN Model Article 24 follows the same architecture with broadly similar wording, although its paragraph 4 cross references follow the UN numbering: in the UN Model 2021 they include Article 12A on fees for technical services, and in the UN Model 2025 they refer to Article 12AA on fees for services instead (Article 14 was deleted in 2025).

points.point: paragraph 1 nationality discrimination, 'same circumstances, in particular with respect to residence', applies irrespective of Article 1
paragraph 2 stateless persons
paragraph 3 PE non-discrimination and the personal allowances proviso
paragraph 4 deductibility of payments to non-residents with the Articles 9(1), 11(6), 12(4) exceptions
paragraph 5 foreign-owned or controlled enterprises
paragraph 6 all taxes of every kind and description, wider than Article 2; UN Model broadly the same

items.prompt: (b) Critically evaluate the commentator's claim that the 'same circumstances' comparison and the express exceptions strip Article 24 of most of its force.

answer.model: There is real force in the claim. First, the comparator under paragraph 1 is a national of the other State in the same circumstances including residence, so a rule that depends on residence (for example taxing residents on worldwide income and non-residents only on source income, or applying different rates to non-residents) does not breach paragraph 1: a non-resident national of State R and a non-resident national of State S are treated alike, and the comparison with residents fails because the circumstances differ. Second, paragraph 3 is limited to PEs, accepts that a PE is taxed only on profits attributable to it, and expressly does not require personal allowances. Third, paragraph 4 is subject to Articles 9(1), 11(6) and 12(4), so arm's length limits and transfer pricing adjustments survive, and thin capitalisation rules framed in arm's length terms may be defended on that basis. Fourth, Article 24 contains no most favoured nation clause: a State need not extend to residents of one treaty partner the benefits it gives another under a separate treaty. Fifth, the Article reaches only differential treatment, not an unfair tax applied to all. Against this, the claim overstates the position. Paragraph 1 does catch rules turning on nationality alone, paragraph 3 catches discrimination in rates, deductions and loss relief against the PE, paragraph 5 prevents ownership based burdens (for example a harsher thin capitalisation regime applying only to State R companies owned or controlled by non-residents, subject to the paragraph 4 carve outs), and paragraph 6 extends the reach to all taxes including sub national ones. The Commentary treats the Article as targeted at differences of treatment on prohibited grounds, not as a general guarantee of equality. A balanced conclusion: the protection is real but narrow and form based, and its value to an investor depends on which paragraph is engaged and how the domestic rule is drafted.

points.point: residence based distinctions are not caught by paragraph 1 because circumstances differ; non-resident nationals of both States are compared
paragraph 3 limited to PE; no obligation to give personal allowances
paragraph 4 exceptions for Articles 9(1), 11(6), 12(4) keep arm's length and transfer pricing rules
no most favoured nation obligation
counter argument: nationality, PE rates and deductions, ownership and all taxes under paragraph 6 are caught
reasoned conclusion that protection is real but narrow and drafting dependent

items.prompt: (c) Advise whether State R's treatment of the State S company's branch and its interest deduction restriction is likely to breach Article 24, and identify the arguments on each side.

answer.model: Branch rate: taxing the branch at the same rate as resident companies satisfies paragraph 3 on rates. Denying personal allowances is expressly permitted by the final sentence of paragraph 3, and in any case a company could not claim such allowances, so no breach. Interest restriction: the rule treats a loan from a non-resident parent less favourably than one from a resident lender, which prima facie falls within paragraph 4 (deductibility on the same conditions) and, because the borrower is a State R company owned by a State S resident, paragraph 5 as well. State R's defence is the exception for Article 9(1) and 11(6): if the 3 to 1 ratio is a proxy for the arm's length amount of debt, the restriction may fall within those carve outs. The weakness is that a fixed ratio applied only to non-resident lenders, regardless of whether the borrower could obtain such debt at arm's length, is not obviously an arm's length test, and the Commentary has traditionally taken the view that restrictions beyond Articles 9(1) and 11(6) are not permitted, although the 2025 update revised the Article 9 and 24(4) Commentary on thin capitalisation and interest limits. A stronger position for State R would be to apply the same ratio to all related lenders, resident or not. On the facts as given, the interest restriction is the vulnerable measure; the branch treatment is likely compliant. The conclusion is a judgement because the outcome turns on how closely the ratio can be justified as an arm's length proxy.

points.point: branch taxed at the resident rate satisfies paragraph 3
denial of personal allowances is permitted by paragraph 3
interest restriction is prima facie within paragraph 4 and 5
State R defence that Articles 9(1) and 11(6) apply
weakness: fixed ratio applied to non-residents only is not an arm's length test; remedy of applying to all related lenders
reasoned conclusion distinguishing the two measures

answer.grader_note: Accept alternative conclusions if reasoned. Do not credit statements that Article 24 requires most favoured nation treatment.

title: Preferential regimes, substance and nexus
scenario: State R introduces a patent box under which qualifying income from intellectual property is taxed at 5 per cent against the general rate of 25 per cent. A group has a State R company, Lumora Ltd, that earned overall IP income of 2,000 in the year. Lumora's research and development expenditure for the IP was: own in-house activity 500; outsourced to unrelated parties 100; outsourced to related parties 100; and acquisition cost of the IP 300. All figures are illustrative. A government adviser argues that the OECD's harmful tax practices work now does little more than police regimes that tax authorities elsewhere already counter through Pillar Two.

items.prompt: (a) Describe the criteria applied by the OECD Forum on Harmful Tax Practices in identifying a harmful preferential regime, including the role of the substantial activity requirement.

answer.model: The 1998 Report on Harmful Tax Competition set out four key factors for identifying a harmful preferential regime: no or low effective tax rates on the relevant income; ring fencing of the regime from the domestic economy; lack of transparency; and lack of effective exchange of information. Eight further other factors were used in assessing harm. The Forum on Harmful Tax Practices (FHTP), which is a subsidiary body of the Committee on Fiscal Affairs and works within the Inclusive Framework on BEPS, reviews regimes of members and associates on that basis. The BEPS Action 5 report of 2015 refocused the work on substance: the first factor of no or low taxation acts as a gateway, and a regime is then assessed under the substantial activity requirement, so that a preferential regime must be linked to real economic activity by the taxpayer rather than the mere location of income. For IP regimes the substantial activity requirement is applied through the modified nexus approach; for other regimes the test is whether the income benefited is matched by core income generating activities by the taxpayer in the jurisdiction. The Action 5 work also introduced a framework for the compulsory spontaneous exchange of information on rulings that give rise to BEPS concerns. The substantial activities factor is also applied to jurisdictions with no or only nominal tax.

points.point: 1998 Report four key factors listed correctly
low or no tax as gateway; assessment of harm by other factors
FHTP and its review role
Action 5 substantial activity requirement linked to real activity
ruling transparency framework or no tax jurisdictions mentioned

items.prompt: (b) Explain the modified nexus approach and calculate the proportion of Lumora's 2,000 IP income that qualifies for the 5 per cent rate, and the tax payable on the whole 2,000 of IP income if the remainder is taxed at the general rate.

answer.model: The modified nexus approach allows IP income to benefit from a preferential regime only in proportion to the qualifying expenditure the taxpayer itself incurred on R&D. Nexus ratio = (qualifying expenditures + uplift) ÷ overall expenditures. Qualifying expenditures are in-house R&D plus R&D outsourced to unrelated parties: 500 + 100 = 600. Non-qualifying expenditures are related party outsourcing and acquisition costs: 100 + 300 = 400. Overall expenditures = 600 + 400 = 1,000. The uplift is the lesser of 30 per cent of qualifying expenditures (30% × 600 = 180) and the non-qualifying expenditures (400), so it is 180. Numerator = 600 + 180 = 780. Nexus ratio = 780 ÷ 1,000 = 78 per cent. Qualifying income = 78% × 2,000 = 1,560, taxed at 5% = 78. Non-qualifying income = 2,000 − 1,560 = 440, taxed at 25% = 110. Total tax = 78 + 110 = 188, an effective rate of 9.4 per cent on 2,000.

points.point: formula (qualifying + uplift) ÷ overall expenditure explained
qualifying 600, overall 1,000, uplift 180 (lesser of 30% of 600 and 400)
ratio 78% and qualifying income 1,560

items.prompt: (c) Critically evaluate the adviser's argument that the work on harmful tax practices has been overtaken by Pillar Two.

answer.model: The argument has some force. Pillar Two's GloBE rules set a 15 per cent minimum effective rate on large groups, so a preferential regime delivering a low rate to an in scope group may simply trigger top-up tax, via a qualified domestic minimum top-up tax in the regime State, the IIR or the UTPR. This reduces the incentive to offer such regimes to in scope groups and has led States to redesign their incentives, for example towards refundable credits and expenditure based incentives, which the GloBE rules treat more favourably. Also, the Action 5 peer review process has already produced a large number of abolished or amended regimes, so much of the original work has been done. However, the argument is incomplete for several reasons. First, Pillar Two applies only to groups above the EUR 750 million revenue threshold, so the FHTP's remit still matters for smaller groups and for regimes available to all taxpayers. Second, the FHTP continues to review new regimes, to monitor substantial activity in no or only nominal tax jurisdictions, and to apply a revised review methodology, so its work complements rather than duplicates the minimum tax. Third, the two approaches have different objectives: Pillar Two sets a floor on rate, while the nexus and substantial activity requirements test the link between income and real activity and deal with ring fencing and transparency. Fourth, a regime consistent with the nexus approach can still deliver an effective rate below 15 per cent, as Lumora's 9.4 per cent shows, and so interacts with Pillar Two; this makes the continuing consistency of the two frameworks a live policy question, for example for developing countries that rely on incentives. A balanced conclusion: Pillar Two weakens the commercial value of low rate regimes for large groups but does not displace the FHTP, which retains a distinct role on substance, transparency and smaller groups.

points.point: Pillar Two minimum rate and QDMTT/IIR/UTPR reduce the value of low tax regimes for in scope groups
States redesign incentives; Action 5 reviews have already led to changes
threshold of EUR 750 million leaves smaller groups outside Pillar Two
FHTP continues to review regimes and monitor substantial activities
different objectives: floor on rate versus substance, ring fencing, transparency
interaction illustrated by Lumora effective rate of 9.4%; developing country concerns optional
reasoned conclusion

answer.grader_note: Credit any well argued position. The EUR 750 million figure is the correct GloBE threshold.

title: Tax crime, laundering and foreign revenue claims
scenario: A professional adviser in State R is asked by a client to help move funds from a bank account in State S that holds the proceeds of unreported business income. State S treats deliberate under reporting of tax as a criminal offence; State R has anti money laundering legislation under which tax evasion is a predicate offence. Traditionally, courts have been unwilling to enforce the revenue laws of another State, yet recent policy has moved sharply towards treating foreign tax offences as a matter for domestic anti laundering rules.

items.prompt: (a) Explain how tax evasion has come to be treated as a predicate offence for money laundering and outline the traditional rule that courts do not enforce foreign revenue laws.

answer.model: The FATF Recommendations, revised in 2012, listed tax crimes relating to direct and indirect taxes among the designated categories of predicate offence, so that the proceeds of tax evasion are the proceeds of crime and handling them can itself be money laundering. States implement this in their own legislation. In the UK, for example, the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 defines criminal conduct to include conduct overseas that would be an offence if committed in the UK, which has the effect of bringing the proceeds of some foreign tax offences within the laundering offences, subject to dual criminality. The traditional position is the revenue rule: courts will not directly or indirectly enforce the penal, revenue or other public laws of a foreign State. The classic authority in English law is Government of India v Taylor (House of Lords, 1955), concerning a claim for foreign tax in a liquidation. The rule rested on sovereignty and on the view that one State's tax claims are for its own courts. The modern erosion of the rule comes from treaties (Articles 26 and 27 of the Models on exchange of information and assistance in collection), the Convention on Mutual Administrative Assistance, and anti laundering law that reaches the proceeds of foreign tax crime without enforcing the foreign tax debt itself.

points.point: FATF 2012 revision includes tax crimes as predicate offence
handling proceeds is laundering; domestic implementation with dual criminality
revenue rule statement and rationale
Government of India v Taylor correctly cited
treaty and Convention exchange and collection assistance as erosion

items.prompt: (b) Discuss the position of the State R adviser, including the reporting duties and the distinction between evasion and avoidance.

answer.model: The adviser is in a regulated position. Where the adviser knows or suspects that the funds are the proceeds of tax evasion, handling or transferring them may constitute the laundering offence of concealing, transferring or acquiring criminal property, and the adviser may also commit an offence by failing to file a suspicious activity report where the regime imposes such a duty on regulated professionals. Disclosing the suspicion to the client may amount to the offence of tipping off, so the adviser must file the report without alerting the client. Legal professional privilege may protect advice given to a client in connection with litigation or legal advice but not advice used to further a crime, so that the crime fraud exception is relevant. The central question is whether the funds are criminal property. Evasion, meaning deliberate dishonest non payment, is a crime; avoidance, meaning arrangements within the letter of the law that frustrate its purpose, is not generally criminal, although a particular scheme may fall on either side, and an adviser who believes a scheme is merely aggressive but lawful will not be liable. Here the facts say the income was unreported, so the client's intent is likely central: unreported business income points to evasion. Professional standards also require the adviser to decline the engagement. The conclusion is that the adviser should not move the funds, should consider a report under the regime, and should not tip off the client.

points.point: handling funds that are proceeds of evasion may be a laundering offence
duty to report suspicion by regulated professionals
tipping off risk
privilege and the crime fraud exception
evasion versus avoidance distinction applied to facts
reasoned conclusion on the adviser's position

answer.grader_note: Do not require statutory section numbers. Reporting regimes differ by State; credit general statements.

items.prompt: (c) Evaluate the effect of the dual criminality requirement and of the evasion versus avoidance line on the effectiveness of this approach in tackling cross border tax non compliance.

answer.model: Dual criminality means a foreign tax offence generates criminal property only if the conduct would also be a crime in the State applying the laundering law. This limits effectiveness in three ways. First, States differ in what they treat as criminal: some require a particular level of dishonesty or amount, some reach negligent under reporting only civilly. Second, what is evasion in State S may be lawful tax planning or a civil matter under State R's rules, so an adviser may be told that dual criminality is not satisfied. Third, the evasion versus avoidance line is not fixed, as a scheme found to be abusive by a court may be treated as avoidance and so is not a predicate offence, while a sham or concealed account is evasion. The result is uncertainty for advisers and an inconsistent reach between States, which weakens deterrence. In its favour, the approach adds a practical enforcement tool that does not depend on the foreign State's own debt claim being enforced abroad, supports the information exchange that follows from suspicious activity reports, and aligns incentives for banks and advisers to conduct due diligence. It does not replace treaty cooperation, however, because collection of the foreign tax itself still depends on Article 27 or domestic assistance legislation. Overall the approach is a useful complement to exchange of information and automatic reporting, with its weakest point being the divergence in national definitions.

points.point: meaning of dual criminality
divergence in national definitions limits reach
evasion versus avoidance line uncertainty
benefits: new tool without enforcing foreign debt, supports information flows
conclusion noting complement to treaty cooperation

title: A federal company with foreign branch income
scenario: Delta Ltd is a company resident in Province P of State F, a federal State. State F has a federal corporate income tax at 20 per cent and Province P levies its own corporate income tax at 7 per cent on the same profits, collected by its own tax agency. Delta also pays a municipal business tax of 1 per cent of gross turnover to the city of Corvia where it is managed. Delta carries on a manufacturing business through a branch in State S, a unitary State. The branch earned profits of 1,000 in the year, taxed in State S at 30 per cent. A treaty between State F and State S is based on the OECD Model and uses the credit method in Article 23B. State F's domestic law gives credit for foreign tax against federal tax only, but the provincial tax law says that the province will follow whatever the treaty requires. State F's constitution gives each province the power to levy income tax; the treaty was signed by the federal government and approved by the federal parliament but not by the provinces. All figures are illustrative. Delta's directors ask for advice on whether the two layers of tax in State F and the tax in State S are all covered by the treaty, on how much double taxation remains, and on whether a different method of relief would be better.

exhibits.caption: Rates and profits (illustrative currency units)

items.prompt: (a) Calculate the tax charged on the branch profits in State S, in State F federally, and in Province P, and the total State F tax and total relief if credit is given (i) against federal tax only and (ii) against federal and provincial tax together.

answer.model: State S tax = 30% × 1,000 = 300. State F federal tax = 20% × 1,000 = 200; Province P tax = 7% × 1,000 = 70; total State F tax before relief = 270. (i) Credit against federal tax only: the credit is the lower of foreign tax (300) and federal tax on that income (200), so 200. Federal tax payable = 0; provincial tax payable = 70 with no relief. Total tax = 300 + 70 = 370, effective rate 37%. (ii) Credit against federal and provincial tax: the limit is the State F tax on that income, 270, so credit = lower of 300 and 270 = 270. State F tax payable = 0. Total tax = 300 (all paid in State S), effective rate 30%. Unrelieved State S tax = 300 − 270 = 30. Double taxation remaining: 70 in case (i) and none in case (ii), though 30 of State S tax is unrelieved and is a permanent cost unless carry forward is allowed.

points.point: State S 300, federal 200, provincial 70, total 270
case (i) credit 200, total tax 370
case (ii) credit 270, total tax 300, unrelieved 30

items.prompt: (b) Explain, by reference to this scenario, how federal structures, sub national taxes and the differences in states' rules cause international double taxation.

answer.model: Double taxation arises where two jurisdictions tax the same income of the same person. The classic causes are residence/source conflict, here Delta resident in State F and the branch profits sourced in State S, with State S taxing the branch profits at source and State F taxing Delta on worldwide income as resident. A federal structure adds layers: State F's federal government and Province P each tax the profits, so Delta's profits bear three layers of tax. Sub national taxes complicate relief because the treaty is made by the national government, the provinces have constitutional taxing power, and domestic credit rules may cover only federal tax, as here. This is a source of internal as well as international double taxation: the interaction between provinces and the federal level, and between provinces where profits are allocated by formula, can leave income taxed twice or not at all. The municipal tax on turnover is a further layer: a turnover tax is not obviously a tax on income and so may fall outside the credit and the treaty. Other causes include conflicting definitions of connecting factors: if State S treated Delta as resident through its management or if State F's definition of source differed from State S's, both could claim the same profits. Differences in the tax base (timing, deductions, depreciation) lead to economic rather than legal double taxation. The conflict between residence and source is the principal cause here, and the federal layers aggravate it.

points.point: residence versus source conflict applied to Delta and State S
federal and provincial layers each tax the profits
treaty made by national government while provinces have taxing power; domestic credit limited to federal tax
municipal turnover tax and coverage question
conflicting definitions of connecting factors or base differences mentioned
conclusion identifying principal cause

items.prompt: (c) Advise Delta whether the provincial and municipal taxes are covered by the treaty, whether the treaty requires State F to relieve the provincial tax, and whether exemption would be preferable to credit.

answer.model: Coverage: Article 2(1) of the OECD Model applies to taxes on income imposed on behalf of a Contracting State or of its political subdivisions or local authorities, irrespective of the manner of levy, so the Province P income tax is a covered tax even though levied by the province; Article 2(3) lists existing taxes but the list is not exhaustive. The municipal tax on gross turnover is not clearly a tax on income: Article 2(2) treats as taxes on income those on total income or on elements of income, including taxes on gains and total wages; a tax on gross turnover that is not computed by reference to profit is unlikely to be covered by the credit under Article 23B, though State F may allow a deduction for it domestically. Relief: Article 23B(1) requires State F to allow as a deduction from the tax on income of the resident an amount equal to the income tax paid in State S, limited to the part of the tax, as computed before the deduction, which is attributable to the income that may be taxed in State S. The State F tax on that income includes the provincial tax if the provincial tax is a tax of State F within the Article, so the treaty arguably requires the 270 limit. The constitutional difficulty is that the treaty binds State F as a State in international law whatever its internal division of powers, and a federal clause is relevant only if included in the treaty; State F cannot rely on internal law to avoid the treaty obligation (Vienna Convention, Article 27), although the practical route is the provincial law that follows the treaty, which here supports case (ii). Conclusion on credit: the credit should be 270, leaving 30 of State S tax unrelieved. Exemption: under Article 23A State F would exempt the branch profits, so no State F federal or provincial tax would arise and Delta would bear 300; credit gives the same 300 here because State S's rate exceeds State F's combined 27 per cent, so exemption gives no extra advantage on these figures. Exemption would be better only if State S's rate were lower than State F's, since credit then tops up to the State F rate. Exemption, by contrast, gives capital import neutrality and credit capital export neutrality. Delta is therefore indifferent between the methods on these figures, and the advice should focus on securing the 270 credit and checking the turnover tax deduction.

points.point: Province P tax covered under Article 2(1) as tax of a political subdivision
municipal turnover tax likely outside Article 2(2) coverage
Article 23B(1) credit limited to State F tax attributable to the income
State F cannot rely on internal division of powers; practical route via provincial law
exemption comparison: equal outcome at 300 because State S rate exceeds 27%
conclusion and practical advice

answer.grader_note: Vienna Convention Article 27 (internal law not a justification for failure to perform a treaty) is a creditable point but not required. The Models' rules on credit are Articles 23A and 23B in the OECD Model and the UN Model.

title: Top-up tax across a multinational group
scenario: The Quorra group has consolidated revenue well above EUR 750 million and is in scope of the GloBE rules. Its ultimate parent entity is Parentco in State A. Parentco owns 100 per cent of Sub B in State B and 100 per cent of Sub C in State C. Sub C owns 100 per cent of Sub D in State D. Sub E is a small subsidiary of Parentco in State E with no GloBE income but with employees and tangible assets. State A has not introduced an income inclusion rule. State C has implemented the IIR and the UTPR. State E has implemented the UTPR only. States B and D have not introduced a qualified domestic minimum top-up tax. Assume the minimum rate is 15 per cent, all numbers are for one year, there are no deferred tax adjustments and no other adjustments, and the substance based income exclusions are as shown. State A has no income inclusion rule in this question, so Parentco's own jurisdiction raises no IIR top-up tax. All figures are illustrative. The group's tax director asks the adviser to compute the top-up tax for each low taxed jurisdiction, say which State collects it, and explain how the position would change if a qualified domestic minimum top-up tax were introduced in State D.

exhibits.caption: GloBE data by jurisdiction (illustrative currency units)
UTPR allocation keys (illustrative)

items.prompt: (a) Calculate the effective tax rate and the top-up tax for each of States A to D.

answer.model: ETR = adjusted covered taxes ÷ GloBE income. State A: 250 ÷ 1,000 = 25 per cent, above 15 per cent, so no top-up tax. State B: 40 ÷ 400 = 10 per cent; top-up percentage = 15% − 10% = 5%; excess profit = GloBE income − substance based income exclusion = 400 − 80 = 320; top-up tax = 5% × 320 = 16. State C: 90 ÷ 600 = 15 per cent, equal to the minimum rate, so top-up percentage nil and no top-up tax. State D: 10 ÷ 200 = 5 per cent; top-up percentage = 10%; excess profit = 200 − 20 = 180; top-up tax = 10% × 180 = 18. Total top-up tax = 16 + 18 = 34.

points.point: ETRs 25%, 10%, 15%, 5% calculated
State B excess profit 320 and top-up 16
State D excess profit 180 and top-up 18
states A and C no top-up; total 34

items.prompt: (b) Explain the order in which the IIR and UTPR apply on these facts, which State collects the top-up tax of each of Sub B and Sub D, and allocate any UTPR top-up tax between States C and E.

answer.model: The IIR is applied top down: the parent entity highest in the ownership chain located in an implementing jurisdiction applies it, and the UTPR is a backstop that applies only to top-up tax not collected under the IIR (or a qualified domestic tax). Sub D's top-up tax of 18: the UPE is in State A, which has no IIR, so the next parent down the chain, Sub C in State C (an intermediate parent entity holding 100 per cent), applies the IIR in State C for Sub D. State C therefore collects the 18. Sub B's top-up tax of 16: Sub B is held directly by Parentco in State A, which has no IIR, and no intermediate parent entity in an implementing State owns it, so the IIR does not collect it. It is therefore subject to the UTPR in the UTPR jurisdictions. The UTPR allocation key is 50 per cent by number of employees and 50 per cent by net book value of tangible assets in each UTPR jurisdiction relative to the total across all UTPR jurisdictions. Total employees = 100, total tangible assets = 400. State C: 0.5 × 60/100 + 0.5 × 300/400 = 0.30 + 0.375 = 0.675, so 67.5% × 16 = 10.8. State E: 0.5 × 40/100 + 0.5 × 100/400 = 0.20 + 0.125 = 0.325, so 32.5% × 16 = 5.2. Check: 10.8 + 5.2 = 16. The UTPR is implemented by denying deductions or an equivalent adjustment, so each State collects its share through its domestic mechanism.

points.point: IIR applied top down; UTPR is a backstop
Sub D top-up 18 collected by State C as intermediate parent entity
Sub B top-up 16 not caught by IIR; falls to UTPR
allocation key 50% employees and 50% tangible assets
State C 10.8 and State E 5.2 with correct workings
total check 16

items.prompt: (c) Advise the tax director how the position would change if State D introduced a qualified domestic minimum top-up tax, and comment on how the January 2026 side-by-side package could affect the group.

answer.model: A qualified domestic minimum top-up tax (QDMTT) lets the source State collect the top-up tax computed under GloBE rules on its own constituent entities, and the amount paid is credited against the group's top-up tax for that jurisdiction. If State D introduced a QDMTT, Sub D's 18 would be paid in State D, and the IIR top-up tax for Sub D in State C would fall to nil, so State C would lose the 18 but State D would gain it. The group's total tax would be unchanged; what changes is which State collects. A QDMTT also generally ensures a source State is not left behind by IIR and UTPR States, and many States prefer it for that reason. It would not alter the Sub B position unless State B also introduced one. Side by side: on 5 January 2026 the OECD Inclusive Framework agreed a package of four safe harbours (side by side, UPE, simplified ETR and substance based tax incentive) and extended the transitional CbCR safe harbour by a year. The side by side safe harbour, the one relevant here, in outline allows a group whose ultimate parent is in a jurisdiction identified as having a qualifying tax system to be treated as not subject to the IIR and UTPR top-up tax in respect of the group, subject to eligibility assessment and applying from income years beginning on or after 1 January 2026. Its application to Quorra would depend on whether State A were found eligible, which on these facts is unlikely, since only the United States regime was recognised as a qualified side by side regime at 1 January 2026, and State A has no minimum tax of its own. The conclusion is that the QDMTT would shift collection to State D without increasing group tax, while the side by side package depends on State A's status and should be checked against the OECD's detailed text.

points.point: QDMTT collects top-up tax in the source State and reduces IIR and UTPR top-up tax
State D would collect 18; State C IIR amount falls to nil; group total unchanged
Sub B position unaffected unless State B introduced a QDMTT
side by side package: agreed in January 2026, applies to income years from 1 January 2026, eligibility by central assessment
application to State A depends on eligibility; conclusion

answer.grader_note: The detail of the side by side package should be treated with care; credit general statements of its purpose and effect.
